The main challenge of this problem is that the learner no longer has a simulator or ``environment oracle'' as in most reinforcement learning settings. To solve this problem, we propose a monotonic advantage reweighted imitation learning strategy that is applicable to problems with complex nonlinear function approximation and works well with hybrid (discrete and continuous) action space. The method does not rely on the knowledge of the behavior policy, thus can be used to learn from data generated by an unknown policy. Under mild conditions, our algorithm, though surprisingly simple, has a policy improvement bound and outperforms most competing methods empirically. Thorough numerical results are also provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methodology.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from historical trajectories presents a different problem from learning through ongoing interaction. The learner has recorded experience but cannot ask a simulator or environment to test new behavior. This paper studies deep policy learning in that setting, including cases where the policy that generated the records is unknown.

The proposed strategy reweights imitation learning according to advantage, giving different emphasis to recorded behavior based on its assessed value. Its exponentially weighted formulation is designed for complex nonlinear models and works with action spaces containing both discrete and continuous choices. It does not require knowledge of the original behavior policy.

Under conditions described as mild, the algorithm has a policy-improvement bound. Numerical results also show that it outperforms most of the competing methods examined. The theoretical statement remains conditional, while the comparisons provide empirical support. Together, they suggest that carefully weighted learning from recorded actions can be an effective route to policy improvement when new environment interaction is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Advantage-weighted imitation learns policies from fixed historical trajectories without requiring a simulator or knowledge of the behavior policy.

title: Exponentially Weighted Imitation Learning for Batched Historical Data

abstract: Holistic 3D indoor scene understanding refers to jointly recovering the i) object bounding boxes, ii) room layout, and iii) camera pose, all in 3D. The existing methods either are ineffective or only tackle the problem partially. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end model that simultaneously solves all three tasks in real-time given only a single RGB image. The essence of the proposed method is to improve the prediction by i) parametrizing the targets (e.g., 3D boxes) instead of directly estimating the targets, and ii) cooperative training across different modules in contrast to training these modules individually. Specifically, we parametrize the 3D object bounding boxes by the predictions from several modules, i.e., 3D camera pose and object attributes. The proposed method provides two major advantages: i) The parametrization helps maintain the consistency between the 2D image and the 3D world, thus largely reducing the prediction variances in 3D coordinates. ii) Constraints can be imposed on the parametrization to train different modules simultaneously. We call these constraints "cooperative losses" as they enable the joint training and inference. We employ three cooperative losses for 3D bounding boxes, 2D projections, and physical constraints to estimate a geometrically consistent and physically plausible 3D scene. Experiments on the SUN RGB-D dataset shows that the proposed method significantly outperforms prior approaches on 3D layout estimation, 3D object detection, 3D camera pose estimation, and holistic scene understanding.

paragraphs: Understanding an indoor image in three dimensions requires estimating objects, room layout, and the camera's pose together. These predictions must describe a compatible scene. The paper introduces an end-to-end model that estimates all three from a single RGB image in real time, treating their relationships as part of the prediction problem.

The model represents three-dimensional object boxes through predictions from modules for camera pose and object attributes. This parameterization helps preserve agreement between the image and the reconstructed world, reducing variation in predicted three-dimensional coordinates. It also creates a way to impose shared constraints across modules, so training can account for their combined geometric consequences.

They support joint training and inference toward geometrically consistent, physically plausible scenes. On SUN RGB-D, the authors report significant improvements over prior approaches in layout estimation, object detection, camera pose estimation, and overall scene understanding. These results support coordinating the component predictions through shared structure rather than evaluating each component's training objective in isolation.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained model uses shared geometric and physical constraints to recover indoor objects, room layout, and camera pose from one image.

title: Cooperative Holistic Scene Understanding: Unifying 3D Object, Layout, and Camera Pose Estimation

abstract: A fundamental goal of systems neuroscience is to understand how neural activity gives rise to natural behavior. In order to achieve this goal, we must first build comprehensive models that offer quantitative descriptions of behavior. We develop a new class of probabilistic models to tackle this challenge in the study of larval zebrafish, an important model organism for neuroscience. Larval zebrafish locomote via sequences of punctate swim bouts--brief flicks of the tail--which are naturally modeled as a marked point process. However, these sequences of swim bouts belie a set of discrete and continuous internal states, latent variables that are not captured by standard point process models. We incorporate these variables as latent marks of a point process and explore various models for their dynamics. To infer the latent variables and fit the parameters of this model, we develop an amortized variational inference algorithm that targets the collapsed posterior distribution, analytically marginalizing out the discrete latent variables. With a dataset of over 120,000 swim bouts, we show that our models reveal interpretable discrete classes of swim bouts and continuous internal states like hunger that modulate their dynamics. These models are a major step toward understanding the natural behavioral program of the larval zebrafish and, ultimately, its neural underpinnings.

title: Point process latent variable models of larval zebrafish behavior

abstract: In many platforms, user arrivals exhibit a self-reinforcing behavior: future user arrivals are likely to have preferences similar to users who were satisfied in the past. In other words, arrivals exhibit {\em positive externalities}. We study multiarmed bandit (MAB) problems with positive externalities. We show that the self-reinforcing preferences may lead standard benchmark algorithms such as UCB to exhibit linear regret. We develop a new algorithm, Balanced Exploration (BE), which explores arms carefully to avoid suboptimal convergence of arrivals before sufficient evidence is gathered. We also introduce an adaptive variant of BE which successively eliminates suboptimal arms. We analyze their asymptotic regret, and establish optimality by showing that no algorithm can perform better.

paragraphs: On some platforms, satisfying one group of users makes similar users more likely to arrive later. The paper studies multiarmed bandit learning with this self-reinforcing behavior, called positive externalities. A decision therefore affects both its immediate outcome and the preferences of the population the learner will encounter in the future.

This feedback changes the exploration problem. The authors show that standard methods such as UCB may incur linear regret, meaning their accumulated performance gap can grow proportionally with time. Their proposed Balanced Exploration algorithm explores carefully to avoid steering arrivals toward a suboptimal outcome before enough evidence has been collected. An adaptive version also progressively eliminates inferior arms.

The authors analyze the algorithms' asymptotic regret and establish optimality through a bound showing that no algorithm can do better in the studied setting. The contribution is thus both an exploration strategy and a characterization of achievable performance. It explains why learning must account for how present choices reshape future arrivals, rather than treating that feedback as incidental.
summary.tldr: Balanced Exploration achieves asymptotically optimal regret in a bandit setting where satisfied users influence future arrivals.

title: Bandit Learning with Positive Externalities

abstract: Optimal transportation, or computing the Wasserstein or ``earth mover's'' distance between two $n$-dimensional distributions, is a fundamental primitive which arises in many learning and statistical settings. We give an algorithm which solves the problem to additive $\epsilon$ accuracy with $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$ parallel depth and $\tilde{O}\left(n^2/\epsilon\right)$ work. \cite{BlanchetJKS18, Quanrud19} obtained this runtime through reductions to positive linear programming and matrix scaling. However, these reduction-based algorithms use subroutines which may be impractical due to requiring solvers for second-order iterations (matrix scaling) or non-parallelizability (positive LP). Our methods match the previous-best work bounds by \cite{BlanchetJKS18, Quanrud19} while either improving parallelization or removing the need for linear system solves, and improve upon the previous best first-order methods running in time $\tilde{O}(\min(n^2 / \epsilon^2, n^{2.5} / \epsilon))$ \cite{DvurechenskyGK18, LinHJ19}. We obtain our results by a primal-dual extragradient method, motivated by recent theoretical improvements to maximum flow \cite{Sherman17}.

paragraphs: Optimal transport measures the cost of moving probability mass from one distribution to another, giving the Wasserstein or earth mover’s distance. This paper develops a direct algorithm for computing that quantity to a chosen additive accuracy. Its focus is both the total computation required and how much of that computation can run in parallel.

For two distributions of dimension n and accuracy epsilon, the algorithm has parallel depth of roughly 1/epsilon and total work of roughly n squared divided by epsilon, suppressing polylogarithmic factors. Parallel depth describes the sequential stages that remain even when work is distributed. The method uses primal-dual extragradient updates, motivated by theoretical advances in maximum flow.

Earlier reduction-based algorithms achieved the same work bound through positive linear programming or matrix scaling. The new approach matches that bound while either improving parallelization or avoiding linear-system solves required by those routes. It also improves the stated bounds for previous first-order methods. The contribution therefore concerns the computational structure of achieving accurate transport solutions, alongside the work guarantee.
summary.tldr: A direct extragradient algorithm computes optimal transport with strong work bounds while improving parallelization or avoiding linear-system solves.

title: A Direct tilde{O}(1/epsilon) Iteration Parallel Algorithm for Optimal Transport

abstract: Segmentation algorithms are prone to make topological errors on fine-scale struc- tures, e.g., broken connections. We propose a novel method that learns to segment with correct topology. In particular, we design a continuous-valued loss function that enforces a segmentation to have the same topology as the ground truth, i.e.,having the same Betti number. The proposed topology-preserving loss function is differentiable and can be incorporated into end-to-end training of a deep neural network. Our method achieves much better performance on the Betti number error, which directly accounts for the topological correctness. It also performs superior on other topology-relevant metrics, e.g., the Adjusted Rand Index and the Variation of Information, without sacrificing per-pixel accuracy. We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on a broad spectrum of natural and biomedical datasets.

paragraphs: Image segmentation can look accurate at the pixel level while making serious structural mistakes, such as breaking a thin connection. This paper focuses on preserving topology: the connectivity and related structural properties of segmented regions. It adds a training objective that directly addresses errors ordinary pixel accuracy may fail to capture.

The proposed loss is continuous-valued and differentiable, so it can be incorporated into end-to-end neural network training. It enforces agreement between the predicted segmentation and ground truth in terms of Betti numbers, the topological quantities used by the method. This gives learning an explicit structural target alongside the task of assigning labels to individual pixels.

Across natural and biomedical datasets, the method substantially improves Betti number error. It also improves other topology-relevant measures, including Adjusted Rand Index and Variation of Information, without sacrificing per-pixel accuracy. The findings show that emphasizing structural correctness during training can improve the organization of the resulting segmentation while maintaining its reported accuracy at the individual-pixel level.
summary.tldr: A differentiable loss promotes matching segmentation topology to ground truth, improving structural metrics without sacrificing reported pixel accuracy.

title: Topology-Preserving Deep Image Segmentation

abstract: Despite renewed interest in emergent language simulations with neural networks, little is known about the basic properties of the induced code, and how they compare to human language. One fundamental characteristic of the latter, known as Zipf's Law of Abbreviation (ZLA), is that more frequent words are efficiently associated to shorter strings. We study whether the same pattern emerges when two neural networks, a speaker'' and a listener'', are trained to play a signaling game. Surprisingly, we find that networks develop an \emph{anti-efficient} encoding scheme, in which the most frequent inputs are associated to the longest messages, and messages in general are skewed towards the maximum length threshold. This anti-efficient code appears easier to discriminate for the listener, and, unlike in human communication, the speaker does not impose a contrasting least-effort pressure towards brevity. Indeed, when the cost function includes a penalty for longer messages, the resulting message distribution starts respecting ZLA. Our analysis stresses the importance of studying the basic features of emergent communication in a highly controlled setup, to ensure the latter will not strand too far from human language. Moreover, we present a concrete illustration of how different functional pressures can lead to successful communication codes that lack basic properties of human language, thus highlighting the role such pressures play in the latter.

paragraphs: Human languages tend to give shorter words to things people say more often, a pattern called Zipf’s Law of Abbreviation. This paper asks whether neural networks develop the same pattern when they learn to communicate. It studies a controlled signaling game in which one network produces messages and another learns to interpret them.

The observed pattern goes in the opposite direction: frequent inputs receive longer messages, and message lengths tend toward the allowed maximum. The authors suggest that these longer codes are easier for the listener to distinguish. Meanwhile, the speaker has no competing incentive to reduce effort by making its messages brief. Successful communication therefore does not, by itself, reproduce this feature of human language.

Adding a penalty for long messages changes the result: the message distribution starts following the human abbreviation pattern. The finding shows how the pressures built into a learning objective can shape an emergent communication system. It also motivates examining basic properties of learned codes, alongside whether the networks successfully exchange information.
summary.tldr: Neural communicators learn longer messages for frequent inputs unless a length penalty encourages the abbreviation pattern found in human language.

title: Anti-efficient encoding in emergent communication

abstract: In this paper, we introduce various mechanisms to obtain accelerated first-order stochastic optimization algorithms when the objective function is convex or strongly convex. Specifically, we extend the Catalyst approach originally designed for deterministic objectives to the stochastic setting. Given an optimization method with mild convergence guarantees for strongly convex problems, the challenge is to accelerate convergence to a noise-dominated region, and then achieve convergence with an optimal worst-case complexity depending on the noise variance of the gradients. A side contribution of our work is also a generic analysis that can handle inexact proximal operators, providing new insights about the robustness of stochastic algorithms when the proximal operator cannot be exactly computed.

Given an optimization method with mild convergence guarantees for strongly convex problems, the challenge is to accelerate convergence to a noise-dominated region, and then achieve convergence with an optimal worst-case complexity depending on the noise variance of the gradients. A side contribution of our work is also a generic analysis that can handle inexact proximal operators, providing new insights about the robustness of stochastic algorithms when the proximal operator cannot be exactly computed.

paragraphs: Optimization with noisy gradients has two related challenges: making rapid initial progress and continuing to improve once gradient noise becomes the dominant obstacle. This paper develops a general acceleration framework for convex and strongly convex objectives. Its aim is to improve suitable existing optimization methods through reusable mechanisms.

The framework extends Catalyst, an acceleration approach originally developed for deterministic objectives, to stochastic optimization. It starts with a method that has mild convergence guarantees on strongly convex problems. The analysis addresses both accelerated progress toward the region dominated by noise and subsequent convergence with optimal worst-case complexity depending on gradient noise variance.

The paper also provides a general analysis of inexact proximal operators, optimization steps that may themselves be difficult to compute precisely. This helps explain how stochastic methods behave when those steps are only approximated. Together, these contributions address acceleration and robustness to imperfect computation within the stated convex setting, while explicitly accounting for noise in the available gradients.
summary.tldr: The framework extends Catalyst to accelerate stochastic convex optimization while accounting for gradient noise and approximate proximal steps.

title: A Generic Acceleration Framework for Stochastic Composite Optimization

abstract: We develop BatchBALD, a tractable approximation to the mutual information between a batch of points and model parameters, which we use as an acquisition function to select multiple informative points jointly for the task of deep Bayesian active learning. BatchBALD is a greedy linear-time $1 - \nicefrac{1}{e}$-approximate algorithm amenable to dynamic programming and efficient caching. We compare BatchBALD to the commonly used approach for batch data acquisition and find that the current approach acquires similar and redundant points, sometimes performing worse than randomly acquiring data. We finish by showing that, using BatchBALD to consider dependencies within an acquisition batch, we achieve new state of the art performance on standard benchmarks, providing substantial data efficiency improvements in batch acquisition.

paragraphs: BatchBALD addresses how an active learning system should choose several data points together. Selecting points that each appear informative can still produce a redundant batch: multiple points may teach the model much the same thing. The paper reports that the commonly used batch acquisition approach selects similar points and can sometimes perform worse than random acquisition.

The proposed acquisition function approximates the mutual information between an entire batch and the model parameters. In plain terms, it evaluates how much the selected points collectively reveal about the model, accounting for dependencies within the batch. The greedy algorithm has a stated 1 − 1/e approximation guarantee and linear-time behavior, with dynamic programming and caching supporting efficient computation.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and substantial improvements in data efficiency for batch acquisition. The central finding is that considering points jointly can make a labeling batch more useful. Diversity here follows from accounting for shared information, rather than simply treating each point's individual informativeness as enough.
summary.tldr: BatchBALD selects informative batches jointly, reducing redundant acquisitions and improving data efficiency on standard benchmarks.

title: BatchBALD: Efficient and Diverse Batch Acquisition for Deep Bayesian Active Learning

abstract: Recently, a provocative claim was published that number sense spontaneously emerges in a deep neural network trained merely for visual object recognition. This has, if true, far reaching significance to the fields of machine learning and cognitive science alike. In this paper, we prove the above claim to be unfortunately incorrect. The statistical analysis to support the claim is flawed in that the sample set used to identify number-aware neurons is too small, compared to the huge number of neurons in the object recognition network. By this flawed analysis one could mistakenly identify number-sensing neurons in any randomly initialized deep neural networks that are not trained at all. With the above critique we ask the question what if a deep convolutional neural network is carefully trained for numerosity? Our findings are mixed. Even after being trained with number-depicting images, the deep learning approach still has difficulties to acquire the abstract concept of numbers, a cognitive task that preschoolers perform with ease. But on the other hand, we do find some encouraging evidences suggesting that deep neural networks are more robust to distribution shift for small numbers than for large numbers.

paragraphs: The paper examines a claim that number sense emerges spontaneously in a neural network trained only to recognize visual objects. The authors challenge the statistical evidence for that claim. They identify a mismatch between the small sample used to find number-sensitive neurons and the very large number of neurons examined.

According to their analysis, the same flawed procedure can identify apparently number-sensitive neurons in randomly initialized networks that have never been trained. This makes the statistical procedure central to the dispute: finding such neurons under that test does not establish that object-recognition training produced number sense. The authors then investigate networks deliberately trained on images depicting numbers.

Those follow-up findings are mixed. Even with explicit numerosity training, the networks have difficulty acquiring an abstract concept of number. At the same time, the authors find encouraging evidence that the networks handle distribution shifts more robustly for small numbers than for large ones. The paper thus combines a critique of an earlier inference with a qualified account of what targeted training achieves.
summary.tldr: The paper rejects flawed evidence for spontaneously learned number sense and finds mixed results when networks are explicitly trained for numerosity.

title: On Numerosity of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Message passing neural network (MPNN) has recently emerged as a successful framework by achieving state-of-the-art performances on many graph-based learning tasks. MPNN has also recently been extended to multi-relational graphs (each edge is labelled), and hypergraphs (each edge can connect any number of vertices). However, in real-world datasets involving text and knowledge, relationships are much more complex in which hyperedges can be multi-relational, recursive, and ordered. Such structures present several unique challenges because it is not clear how to adapt MPNN to variable-sized hyperedges in them. In this work, we first unify exisiting MPNNs on different structures into G-MPNN (Generalised MPNN) framework. Motivated by real-world datasets, we then propose a novel extension of the framework, MPNN-R (MPNN-Recursive) to handle recursively-structured data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed G-MPNN and MPNN-R.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks learn from relationships among connected entities. Existing extensions support labeled edges and hyperedges, which can connect more than two vertices. The paper focuses on richer structures found in text and knowledge data, where relationships can also be ordered, have different types, and be recursively structured.

These combinations create a challenge for message passing because a hyperedge can have a variable number of participants while carrying additional structure. The authors first introduce G-MPNN, a generalized framework that unifies existing message passing approaches across different structures. They then develop MPNN-R, an extension designed to handle recursive data. This progression connects established architectures to a framework that accommodates more complex relationships.

Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of both G-MPNN and MPNN-R. The contribution is therefore both organizational and methodological: it brings several existing forms of message passing into one account and extends that account to recursive structures. This matters for representing data whose relationships require more information than a simple connection between a pair of entities.
summary.tldr: G-MPNN unifies message passing across graph structures, while MPNN-R extends the framework to recursively structured relationships.

title: Neural Message Passing for Multi-Relational Ordered and Recursive Hypergraphs

abstract: Self-supervised representation learning approaches have recently surpassed their supervised learning counterparts on downstream tasks like object detection and image classification. Somewhat mysteriously the recent gains in performance come from training instance classification models, treating each image and it's augmented versions as samples of a single class. In this work, we first present quantitative experiments to demystify these gains. We demonstrate that approaches like MOCO and PIRL learn occlusion-invariant representations. However, they fail to capture viewpoint and category instance invariance which are crucial components for object recognition. Second, we demonstrate that these approaches obtain further gains from access to a clean object-centric training dataset like Imagenet. Finally, we propose an approach to leverage unstructured videos to learn representations that possess higher viewpoint invariance. Our results show that the learned representations outperform MOCOv2 trained on the same data in terms of invariances encoded and the performance on downstream image classification and semantic segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what contrastive self-supervised image models actually learn to ignore. These models treat an image and its augmented versions as belonging together. The authors examine whether the resulting representations remain stable under changes that matter for recognition, rather than treating strong downstream performance as evidence that all useful invariances have been learned.

Their experiments show that MOCO and PIRL learn representations resistant to occlusion, but fail to capture viewpoint invariance and invariance across different instances of a category. They also find that access to a clean, object-centered dataset such as ImageNet contributes additional performance gains. Thus, the reported success reflects both the learned invariances and properties of the training data.

The authors then propose learning from unstructured videos to obtain stronger viewpoint invariance. Compared with MOCOv2 trained on the same data, their representations perform better in the invariances measured and on downstream image classification and semantic segmentation. These findings connect representation quality to the particular variations the training process exposes.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies gaps in contrastive image invariances and uses unstructured video to improve viewpoint invariance and downstream performance.

title: Demystifying Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning: Invariances, Augmentations and Dataset Biases

abstract: Contrastive self-supervised learning has emerged as a promising approach to unsupervised visual representation learning. In general, these methods learn global (image-level) representations that are invariant to different views (i.e., compositions of data augmentation) of the same image. However, many visual understanding tasks require dense (pixel-level) representations. In this paper, we propose View-Agnostic Dense Representation (VADeR) for unsupervised learning of dense representations. VADeR learns pixelwise representations by forcing local features to remain constant over different viewing conditions. Specifically, this is achieved through pixel-level contrastive learning: matching features (that is, features that describes the same location of the scene on different views) should be close in an embedding space, while non-matching features should be apart. VADeR provides a natural representation for dense prediction tasks and transfers well to downstream tasks. Our method outperforms ImageNet supervised pretraining (and strong unsupervised baselines) in multiple dense prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Many contrastive learning methods produce one representation for an entire image, encouraging it to remain consistent across augmented views. Dense prediction tasks need information at individual pixels instead. VADeR adapts the consistency principle to local visual features, learning representations that remain stable across different viewing conditions.

Its training objective compares features that describe the same scene location in different views. Matching features are pulled together in the embedding space, while features from nonmatching locations are pushed apart. This makes the correspondence between local scene content central to learning, aligning the representation with tasks that require spatially detailed predictions.

The learned features transfer well to downstream dense prediction tasks. The authors report improvements over ImageNet supervised pretraining and strong unsupervised baselines on multiple such tasks. These findings support learning at the spatial level required by the eventual prediction problem. The contribution is a pixelwise contrastive approach that retains view consistency while producing representations suited to detailed visual understanding.
summary.tldr: VADeR learns view-consistent pixel representations through contrastive learning and improves transfer to multiple dense prediction tasks.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Dense Visual Representations

abstract: We study stochastic structured bandits for minimizing regret. The fact that the popular optimistic algorithms do not achieve the asymptotic instance-dependent regret optimality (asymptotic optimality for short) has recently alluded researchers. On the other hand, it is known that one can achieve bounded regret (i.e., does not grow indefinitely with $n$) in certain instances. Unfortunately, existing asymptotically optimal algorithms rely on forced sampling that introduces an $\omega(1)$ term w.r.t. the time horizon $n$ in their regret, failing to adapt to the ``easiness'' of the instance. In this paper, we focus on the finite hypothesis case and ask if one can achieve the asymptotic optimality while enjoying bounded regret whenever possible. We provide a positive answer by introducing a new algorithm called CRush Optimism with Pessimism (CROP) that eliminates optimistic hypotheses by pulling the informative arms indicated by a pessimistic hypothesis. Our finite-time analysis shows that CROP $(i)$ achieves a constant-factor asymptotic optimality and, thanks to the forced-exploration-free design, $(ii)$ adapts to bounded regret, and $(iii)$ its regret bound scales not with $K$ but with an effective number of arms $K_\psi$ that we introduce. We also discuss a problem class where CROP can be exponentially better than existing algorithms in \textit{nonasymptotic} regimes. This problem class also reveals a surprising fact that even a clairvoyant oracle who plays according to the asymptotically optimal arm pull scheme may suffer a linear worst-case regret.

Unfortunately, existing asymptotically optimal algorithms rely on forced sampling that introduces an $\omega(1)$ term w.r.t. the time horizon $n$ in their regret, failing to adapt to the ``easiness'' of the instance. In this paper, we focus on the finite hypothesis case and ask if one can achieve the asymptotic optimality while enjoying bounded regret whenever possible. We provide a positive answer by introducing a new algorithm called CRush Optimism with Pessimism (CROP) that eliminates optimistic hypotheses by pulling the informative arms indicated by a pessimistic hypothesis. Our finite-time analysis shows that CROP $(i)$ achieves a constant-factor asymptotic optimality and, thanks to the forced-exploration-free design, $(ii)$ adapts to bounded regret, and $(iii)$ its regret bound scales not with $K$ but with an effective number of arms $K_\psi$ that we introduce. We also discuss a problem class where CROP can be exponentially better than existing algorithms in \textit{nonasymptotic} regimes. This problem class also reveals a surprising fact that even a clairvoyant oracle who plays according to the asymptotically optimal arm pull scheme may suffer a linear worst-case regret.

paragraphs: In structured bandit problems, a learner chooses among actions while learning about their rewards. This paper asks whether an algorithm can achieve strong long-run regret guarantees while also keeping regret bounded on instances where that is possible. Existing asymptotically optimal methods use forced sampling, which introduces regret that continues growing even on such easier instances.

For a finite set of hypotheses, the authors introduce CROP. It uses a pessimistic hypothesis to identify informative actions whose outcomes can eliminate optimistic hypotheses. This mechanism removes the need for forced exploration. The finite-time analysis establishes asymptotic optimality up to a constant factor, adaptation to bounded regret, and a bound governed by an effective number of actions rather than the total number.

The paper also describes a problem class where CROP can improve exponentially over existing algorithms before the asymptotic regime. In that class, even an oracle following an asymptotically optimal sampling scheme can incur linear worst-case regret. The finding highlights why long-run optimality alone may poorly describe finite-time behavior.
summary.tldr: CROP combines constant-factor asymptotic optimality with bounded-regret adaptation for structured bandits with finitely many hypotheses.

title: Crush Optimism with Pessimism: Structured Bandits Beyond Asymptotic Optimality

abstract: Standard machine learning algorithms typically assume that data is sampled independently from the distribution of interest. In attempts to relax this assumption, fields such as adversarial learning typically assume that data is provided by an adversary, whose sole objective is to fool a learning algorithm. However, in reality, it is often the case that data comes from self-interested agents, with less malicious goals and intentions which lie somewhere between the two settings described above. To tackle this problem, we present a Stackelberg competition model for least squares regression, in which data is provided by agents who wish to achieve specific predictions for their data. Although the resulting optimisation problem is nonconvex, we derive an algorithm which converges globally, outperforming current approaches which only guarantee convergence to local optima. We also provide empirical results on two real-world datasets, the medical personal costs dataset and the red wine dataset, showcasing the performance of our algorithm relative to algorithms which are optimal under adversarial assumptions, outperforming the state of the art.

paragraphs: Training data may come from people or agents who want particular predictions for themselves. Such contributors differ both from independent random samples and from adversaries whose sole goal is to undermine learning. This paper studies that middle ground through a Stackelberg competition model for least-squares regression.

The model explicitly represents data providers as self-interested agents seeking desired predictions. Accounting for that strategic behavior produces a non-convex optimization problem. The authors derive an algorithm with global convergence, improving on approaches whose guarantees stop at local optima. The guarantee concerns the optimization problem arising from this particular model of agent incentives.

Experiments use the medical personal costs and red wine datasets. The authors report improvements over algorithms optimal under adversarial assumptions and over the state of the art in the reported comparisons. These results support matching the learning formulation to contributors' actual objectives: modeling targeted self-interest can lead to a different and more effective solution than treating every strategic data provider as purely malicious.
summary.tldr: A strategic regression model accounts for self-interested data providers and admits a globally convergent algorithm with reported empirical improvements.

title: Optimal Learning from Verified Training Data

abstract: We study the \emph{secure} stochastic convex optimization problem: a learner aims to learn the optimal point of a convex function through sequentially querying a (stochastic) gradient oracle, in the meantime, there exists an adversary who aims to free-ride and infer the learning outcome of the learner from observing the learner's queries. The adversary observes only the points of the queries but not the feedback from the oracle. The goal of the learner is to optimize the accuracy, i.e., obtaining an accurate estimate of the optimal point, while securing her privacy, i.e., making it difficult for the adversary to infer the optimal point. We formally quantify this tradeoff between learner’s accuracy and privacy and characterize the lower and upper bounds on the learner's query complexity as a function of desired levels of accuracy and privacy. For the analysis of lower bounds, we provide a general template based on information theoretical analysis and then tailor the template to several families of problems, including stochastic convex optimization and (noisy) binary search. We also present a generic secure learning protocol that achieves the matching upper bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm can reveal information through the locations it queries, even if its feedback remains private. This paper studies a learner seeking the optimum of a convex function through sequential queries to a stochastic gradient oracle. An adversary sees the query points and tries to infer the learner's result, but cannot observe the oracle's responses.

The learner must balance accurate optimization with making the optimum difficult for that observer to identify. The authors formalize this accuracy–privacy tradeoff through query complexity: how many oracle calls are needed for specified accuracy and privacy levels. They derive lower and upper bounds that describe the cost of satisfying both requirements.

For the lower bounds, the paper develops a general information-theoretic template and applies it to stochastic convex optimization and noisy binary search. It also presents a generic secure learning protocol whose upper bound matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. This establishes nearly matching requirements and achievable performance within the stated observation model.
summary.tldr: The paper nearly characterizes the query cost of accurate optimization when an adversary can observe query locations but not oracle feedback.

title: Optimal Query Complexity of Secure Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: We develop a novel and single-loop variance-reduced algorithm to solve a class of stochastic nonconvex-convex minimax problems involving a nonconvex-linear objective function, which has various applications in different fields such as ma- chine learning and robust optimization. This problem class has several compu- tational challenges due to its nonsmoothness, nonconvexity, nonlinearity, and non-separability of the objective functions. Our approach relies on a new combi- nation of recent ideas, including smoothing and hybrid biased variance-reduced techniques. Our algorithm and its variants can achieve $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2/3})$-convergence rate and the best-known oracle complexity under standard assumptions, where T is the iteration counter. They have several computational advantages compared to exist- ing methods such as simple to implement and less parameter tuning requirements. They can also work with both single sample or mini-batch on derivative estimators, and with constant or diminishing step-sizes. We demonstrate the benefits of our algorithms over existing methods through two numerical examples, including a nonsmooth and nonconvex-non-strongly concave minimax model.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization asks one part of a problem to minimize an objective while another maximizes it. This paper studies a stochastic nonconvex-convex class with a nonconvex-linear objective structure. Such problems can combine nonsmoothness, nonlinearity, and dependencies between variables that make straightforward optimization difficult.

The authors develop a single-loop algorithm that combines smoothing with hybrid biased variance reduction. Smoothing addresses irregularities in the objective, while variance reduction addresses noise in derivative estimates. The algorithm and its variants can use either one sample or a minibatch for those estimates, and they support both constant and diminishing step sizes.

Under standard assumptions, the methods attain a convergence rate of order T to the power of minus two-thirds and the best-known oracle complexity stated in the paper. The authors also emphasize implementation simplicity and reduced parameter-tuning requirements. Two numerical examples demonstrate benefits over existing methods, including a nonsmooth minimax example without strong concavity. These findings concern the studied problem class and its assumptions, rather than arbitrary adversarial optimization.
summary.tldr: A single-loop stochastic minimax algorithm combines smoothing and variance reduction to obtain strong convergence guarantees under standard assumptions.

title: Hybrid Variance-Reduced SGD Algorithms For Minimax Problems with Nonconvex-Linear Function

abstract: Machine learning on tiny IoT devices based on microcontroller units (MCU) is appealing but challenging: the memory of microcontrollers is 2-3 orders of magnitude smaller even than mobile phones. We propose MCUNet, a framework that jointly designs the efficient neural architecture (TinyNAS) and the lightweight inference engine (TinyEngine), enabling ImageNet-scale inference on microcontrollers. TinyNAS adopts a two-stage neural architecture search approach that first optimizes the search space to fit the resource constraints, then specializes the network architecture in the optimized search space. TinyNAS can automatically handle diverse constraints (i.e. device, latency, energy, memory) under low search costs. TinyNAS is co-designed with TinyEngine, a memory-efficient inference library to expand the search space and fit a larger model. TinyEngine adapts the memory scheduling according to the overall network topology rather than layer-wise optimization, reducing the memory usage by 3.4×, and accelerating the inference by 1.7-3.3× compared to TF-Lite Micro [3] and CMSIS-NN [28]. MCUNet is the first to achieves >70% ImageNet top1 accuracy on an off-the-shelf commercial microcontroller, using 3.5× less SRAM and 5.7× less Flash compared to quantized MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18. On visual&audio wake words tasks, MCUNet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and runs 2.4-3.4× faster than Mo- bileNetV2 and ProxylessNAS-based solutions with 3.7-4.1× smaller peak SRAM. Our study suggests that the era of always-on tiny machine learning on IoT devices has arrived.

title: MCUNet: Tiny Deep Learning on IoT Devices

abstract: Learning from Observations (LfO) is a practical reinforcement learning scenario from which many applications can benefit through the reuse of incomplete resources. Compared to conventional imitation learning (IL), LfO is more challenging because of the lack of expert action guidance. In both conventional IL and LfO, distribution matching is at the heart of their foundation. Traditional distribution matching approaches are sample-costly which depend on on-policy transitions for policy learning. Towards sample-efficiency, some off-policy solutions have been proposed, which, however, either lack comprehensive theoretical justifications or depend on the guidance of expert actions. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient LfO approach which enables off-policy optimization in a principled manner. To further accelerate the learning procedure, we regulate the policy update with an inverse action model, which assists distribution matching from the perspective of mode-covering. Extensive empirical results on challenging locomotion tasks indicate that our approach is comparable with state-of-the-art in terms of both sample-efficiency and asymptotic performance.

paragraphs: Learning from observations uses expert behavior without access to the expert's actions. This makes it harder than conventional imitation learning, where actions provide direct guidance. Both settings rely on distribution matching, but traditional approaches require on-policy transitions for learning, making them costly in samples. The paper seeks a principled way to improve efficiency when action labels are unavailable.

The proposed approach enables off-policy optimization, allowing learning to draw on transitions beyond those collected under the current policy. It also uses an inverse action model to regulate policy updates and accelerate learning. This additional guidance supports distribution matching through mode-covering, helping the optimization account for the modes of the behavior distribution being matched.

Extensive experiments on challenging locomotion tasks find the method comparable with state-of-the-art approaches in both sample efficiency and asymptotic performance. The contribution combines an off-policy foundation with a mechanism for guiding policy updates in the absence of expert actions. The reported results support the usefulness of that combination for the evaluated observation-only imitation tasks.
summary.tldr: A principled off-policy imitation method learns without expert actions and uses an inverse action model to support efficient distribution matching.

title: Off-Policy Imitation Learning from Observations

abstract: Team sports is a new application domain for agent modeling with high real-world impact. A fundamental challenge for modeling professional players is their large number (over 1K), which includes many bench players with sparse participation in a game season. The diversity and sparsity of player observations make it difficult to extend previous agent representation models to the sports domain. This paper develops a new approach for agent representations, based on a Markov game model, that is tailored towards applications in professional ice hockey. We introduce a novel player representation via player generation framework where a variational encoder embeds player information with latent variables. The encoder learns a context-specific shared prior to induce a shrinkage effect for the posterior player representations, allowing it to share statistical information across players with different participations. To model the play dynamics in sequential sports data, we design a Variational Recurrent Ladder Agent Encoder (VaRLAE). It learns a contextualized player representation with a hierarchy of latent variables that effectively prevents latent posterior collapse. We validate our player representations in major sports analytics tasks. Our experimental results, based on a large dataset that contains over 4.5M events, show state-of-the-art performance for our VarLAE on facilitating 1) identifying the acting player, 2) estimating expected goals, and 3) predicting the final score difference.

paragraphs: Representing professional hockey players is difficult because there are many players and some participate only sparsely. A model must learn from uneven amounts of experience while accounting for different playing contexts. This paper develops player representations within a Markov game model tailored to sequential ice-hockey data.

A variational encoder represents player information through latent variables. It learns a shared prior that depends on context, drawing individual posterior representations toward shared information through shrinkage. These results support contextualized representations as useful inputs to multiple sports-analysis tasks, while addressing the particular challenge of learning about players with limited observations.
summary.tldr: VaRLAE learns contextual hockey-player representations that share information across uneven participation levels and improve three sports-analytics tasks.

title: Learning Agent Representations for Ice Hockey

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation has attracted appealing academic attentions by transferring knowledge from labeled source domain to unlabeled target domain. However, most existing methods assume the source data are drawn from a single domain, which cannot be successfully applied to explore complementarily transferable knowledge from multiple source domains with large distribution discrepancies. Moreover, they require access to source data during training, which are inefficient and unpractical due to privacy preservation and memory storage. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Confident-Anchor-induced multi-source-free Domain Adaptation (CAiDA) model, which is a pioneer exploration of knowledge adaptation from multiple source domains to the unlabeled target domain without any source data, but with only pre-trained source models. Specifically, a source-specific transferable perception module is proposed to automatically quantify the contributions of the complementary knowledge transferred from multi-source domains to the target domain. To generate pseudo labels for the target domain without access to the source data, we develop a confident-anchor-induced pseudo label generator by constructing a confident anchor group and assigning each unconfident target sample with a semantic-nearest confident anchor. Furthermore, a class-relationship-aware consistency loss is proposed to preserve consistent inter-class relationships by aligning soft confusion matrices across domains. Theoretical analysis answers why multi-source domains are better than a single source domain, and establishes a novel learning bound to show the effectiveness of exploiting multi-source domains. Experiments on several representative datasets illustrate the superiority of our proposed CAiDA model. The code is available at https://github.com/Learning-group123/CAiDA.

paragraphs: CAiDA adapts knowledge from several source domains to an unlabeled target domain using only pretrained source models. The original source data are unavailable during adaptation. This addresses a practical obstacle to combining knowledge across domains when retaining or accessing the underlying datasets is undesirable because of privacy or storage concerns.

The method first estimates how much transferable knowledge each source contributes. It then constructs a group of confident target examples that act as anchors. Less-confident examples receive pseudo labels through their semantically nearest confident anchors, providing training signals without source data or target labels. A further consistency loss aligns soft confusion matrices across domains to preserve relationships among classes.

These components address complementary needs: selecting useful source knowledge, assigning target labels, and maintaining class structure during adaptation. The paper provides theoretical analysis of the benefit of multiple sources and a learning bound supporting their use. Experiments on several representative datasets report stronger performance for CAiDA. The stated evidence supports combining source models through explicit contribution estimates and target-domain anchors in the studied adaptation setting.
summary.tldr: CAiDA combines pretrained source models and confident target examples to adapt to an unlabeled domain without accessing source data.

title: Confident Anchor-Induced Multi-Source Free Domain Adaptation

abstract: We present a novel neural network Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) statistic by identifying a new connection between neural tangent kernel (NTK) and MMD. This connection enables us to develop a computationally efficient and memory-efficient approach to compute the MMD statistic and perform NTK based two-sample tests towards addressing the long-standing challenge of memory and computational complexity of the MMD statistic, which is essential for online implementation to assimilating new samples. Theoretically, such a connection allows us to understand the NTK test statistic properties, such as the Type-I error and testing power for performing the two-sample test, by adapting existing theories for kernel MMD. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed NTK-MMD statistic.

paragraphs: Two-sample testing asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD, supplies a statistic for this task, but its computational and memory demands can make repeated updates difficult. This paper introduces a neural-network MMD statistic through a connection with the neural tangent kernel, or NTK.

That connection enables a computation- and memory-efficient way to calculate the statistic and carry out NTK-based two-sample tests. Efficiency matters particularly when new observations arrive over time and must be incorporated into an online procedure. The method therefore connects neural-network computation to a testing framework whose resource requirements are a longstanding practical concern.

The same connection allows existing kernel-MMD theory to describe the new statistic’s false-positive behavior and ability to detect distribution differences. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution combines a more efficient computational approach with a route to understanding its statistical testing properties.
summary.tldr: Connecting the neural tangent kernel to MMD yields efficient two-sample testing with statistical properties grounded in existing kernel theory.

title: Neural Tangent Kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy

abstract: Mean-Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MF-MARL) is attractive in the applications involving a large population of homogeneous agents, as it exploits the permutation invariance of agents and avoids the curse of many agents. Most existing results only focus on online settings, in which agents can interact with the environment during training. In some applications such as social welfare optimization, however, the interaction during training can be prohibitive or even unethical in the societal systems. To bridge such a gap, we propose a SAFARI (peSsimistic meAn-Field vAlue iteRatIon) algorithm for off-line MF-MARL, which only requires a handful of pre-collected experience data. Theoretically, under a weak coverage assumption that the experience dataset contains enough information about the optimal policy, we prove that for an episodic mean-field MDP with a horizon $H$ and $N$ training trajectories, SAFARI attains a sub-optimality gap of $\mathcal{O}(H^2d_{\rm eff} /\sqrt{N})$, where $d_{\rm eff}$ is the effective dimension of the function class for parameterizing the value function, but independent on the number of agents. Numerical experiments are provided.

paragraphs: Mean-field reinforcement learning uses the interchangeability of homogeneous agents to handle large populations. Much prior work assumes that agents can interact with the environment during training. This paper addresses the offline setting, motivated by applications such as social welfare optimization where experimenting in the actual system can be prohibitive or ethically problematic.

The proposed SAFARI algorithm performs pessimistic mean-field value iteration using pre-collected experience. Its theoretical guarantee relies on a coverage assumption: the dataset must contain enough information about the optimal policy. This condition makes clear what the stored experience needs to support, even though training does not require new interaction with the environment.

For an episodic mean-field decision process with horizon H and N training trajectories, the authors bound the suboptimality gap by O(H^2 d_eff / sqrt(N)). Here d_eff measures the effective dimension of the value-function class. The bound is independent of the number of agents, which is the key scaling benefit for large homogeneous populations. Numerical experiments accompany the theory, while the guarantee links performance to data quantity, horizon, representation complexity, and the stated coverage condition.
summary.tldr: SAFARI learns offline mean-field policies with a suboptimality guarantee independent of agent count, provided the dataset sufficiently covers the optimal policy.

title: Pessimism Meets Invariance: Provably Efficient Offline Mean-Field Multi-Agent RL

abstract: Existing rotated object detectors are mostly inherited from the horizontal detection paradigm, as the latter has evolved into a well-developed area. However, these detectors are difficult to perform prominently in high-precision detection due to the limitation of current regression loss design, especially for objects with large aspect ratios. Taking the perspective that horizontal detection is a special case for rotated object detection, in this paper, we are motivated to change the design of rotation regression loss from induction paradigm to deduction methodology, in terms of the relation between rotation and horizontal detection. We show that one essential challenge is how to modulate the coupled parameters in the rotation regression loss, as such the estimated parameters can influence to each other during the dynamic joint optimization, in an adaptive and synergetic way. Specifically, we first convert the rotated bounding box into a 2-D Gaussian distribution, and then calculate the Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) between the Gaussian distributions as the regression loss. By analyzing the gradient of each parameter, we show that KLD (and its derivatives) can dynamically adjust the parameter gradients according to the characteristics of the object. For instance, it will adjust the importance (gradient weight) of the angle parameter according to the aspect ratio. This mechanism can be vital for high-precision detection as a slight angle error would cause a serious accuracy drop for large aspect ratios objects. More importantly, we have proved that KLD is scale invariant. We further show that the KLD loss can be degenerated into the popular Ln-norm loss for horizontal detection. Experimental results on seven datasets using different detectors show its consistent superiority, and codes are available at https://github.com/yangxue0827/RotationDetection.
originalAbstract: Existing rotated object detectors are mostly inherited from the horizontal detection paradigm, as the latter has evolved into a well-developed area. However, these detectors are difficult to perform prominently in high-precision detection due to the limitation of current regression loss design, especially for objects with large aspect ratios. Taking the perspective that horizontal detection is a special case for rotated object detection, in this paper, we are motivated to change the design of rotation regression loss from induction paradigm to deduction methodology, in terms of the relation between rotation and horizontal detection. We show that one essential challenge is how to modulate the coupled parameters in the rotation regression loss, as such the estimated parameters can influence to each other during the dynamic joint optimization, in an adaptive and synergetic way. Specifically, we first convert the rotated bounding box into a 2-D Gaussian distribution, and then calculate the Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) between the Gaussian distributions as the regression loss. By analyzing the gradient of each parameter, we show that KLD (and its derivatives) can dynamically adjust the parameter gradients according to the characteristics of the object. For instance, it will adjust the importance (gradient weight) of the angle parameter according to the aspect ratio. This mechanism can be vital for high-precision detection as a slight angle error would cause a serious accuracy drop for large aspect ratios objects. More importantly, we have proved that KLD is scale invariant. We further show that the KLD loss can be degenerated into the popular Ln-norm loss for horizontal detection. Experimental results on seven datasets using different detectors show its consistent superiority, and codes are available at https://github.com/yangxue0827/RotationDetection.

paragraphs: Detecting rotated objects requires jointly estimating several interacting box parameters. Loss functions inherited from horizontal detection can struggle with precise localization, especially for long, narrow objects: a small angular error can substantially misalign their boxes. This paper redesigns the regression loss around the geometry of rotated boxes.

The method represents each rotated box as a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution and compares predicted and target distributions using Kullback-Leibler divergence. An analysis of the gradients shows how this loss adjusts parameter updates according to object characteristics. In particular, the importance assigned to angle changes depends on aspect ratio, connecting optimization directly to the sensitivity of the object’s geometry.

The authors prove that the KLD loss is scale invariant and show that it can reduce to a familiar norm-based loss for horizontal detection. This connects the rotated formulation to the horizontal case within the same approach. Experiments across seven datasets and different detectors show consistent superiority. Together, the analysis and results support treating box parameters as a coupled geometric object when seeking high-precision detections.
summary.tldr: Representing rotated boxes as Gaussian distributions yields a scale-invariant KLD loss that adapts parameter gradients to object geometry and improves detection.

title: Learning High-Precision Bounding Box for Rotated Object Detection via Kullback-Leibler Divergence

abstract: Image-level contrastive representation learning has proven to be highly effective as a generic model for transfer learning. Such generality for transfer learning, however, sacrifices specificity if we are interested in a certain downstream task. We argue that this could be sub-optimal and thus advocate a design principle which encourages alignment between the self-supervised pretext task and the downstream task. In this paper, we follow this principle with a pretraining method specifically designed for the task of object detection. We attain alignment in the following three aspects: 1) object-level representations are introduced via selective search bounding boxes as object proposals; 2) the pretraining network architecture incorporates the same dedicated modules used in the detection pipeline (e.g. FPN); 3) the pretraining is equipped with object detection properties such as object-level translation invariance and scale invariance. Our method, called Selective Object COntrastive learning (SoCo), achieves state-of-the-art results for transfer performance on COCO detection using a Mask R-CNN framework. Code is available at https://github.com/hologerry/SoCo.

paragraphs: Self-supervised image pretraining often aims to produce representations useful for many different tasks. This paper argues that such generality can come at the expense of a particular downstream task. For object detection, the authors propose aligning pretraining more closely with the representations, network components, and transformation properties that detection requires.

Their method, Selective Object COntrastive learning, or SoCo, makes this alignment concrete in three ways. It uses bounding boxes produced by selective search to introduce object-level representations. It includes dedicated detection components, such as a feature pyramid network, during pretraining. The authors report state-of-the-art transfer performance on COCO detection with a Mask R-CNN framework. This result supports their design principle in the evaluated detection setting: pretraining can benefit from matching the eventual task at several levels simultaneously. The significance is that the pretraining objective and architecture are treated as parts of the detection pipeline, rather than chosen solely for broad transferability.
summary.tldr: SoCo aligns self-supervised pretraining with object detection through object-level representations, detection modules, and relevant invariances.

title: Aligning Pretraining for Detection via Object-Level Contrastive Learning

abstract: We present a self-supervised learning framework, COCO-LM, that pretrains Language Models by COrrecting and COntrasting corrupted text sequences. Following ELECTRA-style pretraining, COCO-LM employs an auxiliary language model to corrupt text sequences, upon which it constructs two new tasks for pretraining the main model. The first token-level task, Corrective Language Modeling, is to detect and correct tokens replaced by the auxiliary model, in order to better capture token-level semantics. The second sequence-level task, Sequence Contrastive Learning, is to align text sequences originated from the same source input while ensuring uniformity in the representation space. Experiments on GLUE and SQuAD demonstrate that COCO-LM not only outperforms recent state-of-the-art pretrained models in accuracy, but also improves pretraining efficiency. It achieves the MNLI accuracy of ELECTRA with 50% of its pretraining GPU hours. With the same pretraining steps of standard base/large-sized models, COCO-LM outperforms the previous best models by 1+ GLUE average points.

paragraphs: COCO-LM pretrains language models through two complementary tasks built from corrupted text. An auxiliary language model replaces tokens in input sequences, supplying material for the main model to learn from. The framework uses this corruption to train both understanding of individual tokens and representations of whole sequences.

The token-level task asks the model to detect replaced tokens and correct them, linking recognition of a corruption with recovery of the intended content. The sequence-level task brings together representations derived from the same original input while encouraging uniformity across the representation space. Together, the tasks connect local textual distinctions with relationships between complete sequences.

Experiments on GLUE and SQuAD report improvements in accuracy and pretraining efficiency over recent leading models. COCO-LM matches ELECTRA's MNLI accuracy using half its pretraining GPU hours. With the same number of pretraining steps as standard base and large models, it exceeds previous best models by more than one GLUE average point. These results support combining corrective and contrastive learning within one pretraining framework.
summary.tldr: COCO-LM combines token correction with sequence contrastive learning to improve language-model accuracy and pretraining efficiency.

title: COCO-LM: Correcting and Contrasting Text Sequences for Language Model Pretraining

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of policy selection in domains with abundant logged data, but with a restricted interaction budget. Solving this problem would enable safe evaluation and deployment of offline reinforcement learning policies in industry, robotics, and recommendation domains among others. Several off-policy evaluation (OPE) techniques have been proposed to assess the value of policies using only logged data. However, there is still a big gap between the evaluation by OPE and the full online evaluation in the real environment. Yet, large amounts of online interactions are often not possible in practice. To overcome this problem, we introduce active offline policy selection --- a novel sequential decision approach that combines logged data with online interaction to identify the best policy. This approach uses OPE estimates to warm start the online evaluation. Then, in order to utilize the limited environment interactions wisely we decide which policy to evaluate next based on a Bayesian optimization method with a kernel function that represents policy similarity. We use multiple benchmarks with a large number of candidate policies to show that the proposed approach improves upon state-of-the-art OPE estimates and pure online policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Choosing a reinforcement learning policy is difficult when historical interaction data are plentiful but new interactions are expensive or restricted. Off-policy evaluation estimates how candidate policies would perform using existing logs. The paper starts from the observation that these estimates can differ substantially from evaluations carried out in the actual environment.

The proposed approach combines the two sources of evidence in a sequential selection process. It first uses estimates from logged data to initialize online evaluation. It then uses Bayesian optimization to decide which policy should receive the next allocation of scarce environment interactions. A kernel represents similarities between policies, making those relationships part of the selection procedure.

Across multiple benchmarks with many candidate policies, the approach improves on both leading off-policy estimates and evaluation based purely on online interaction. The contribution is a way to direct a limited evaluation budget toward identifying the best policy, while making use of information already present in historical data.
summary.tldr: Active offline policy selection combines logged-data estimates with strategically chosen online evaluations to select policies under a limited interaction budget.

title: Active Offline Policy Selection

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are notorious for making more mistakes for the classes that have substantially fewer samples than the others during training. Such class imbalance is ubiquitous in clinical applications and very crucial to handle because the classes with fewer samples most often correspond to critical cases (e.g., cancer) where misclassifications can have severe consequences.Not to miss such cases, binary classifiers need to be operated at high True Positive Rates (TPRs) by setting a higher threshold, but this comes at the cost of very high False Positive Rates (FPRs) for problems with class imbalance. Existing methods for learning under class imbalance most often do not take this into account. We argue that prediction accuracy should be improved by emphasizing the reduction of FPRs at high TPRs for problems where misclassification of the positive, i.e. critical, class samples are associated with higher cost.To this end, we pose the training of a DNN for binary classification as a constrained optimization problem and introduce a novel constraint that can be used with existing loss functions to enforce maximal area under the ROC curve (AUC) through prioritizing FPR reduction at high TPR. We solve the resulting constrained optimization problem using an Augmented Lagrangian method (ALM).Going beyond binary, we also propose two possible extensions of the proposed constraint for multi-class classification problems.We present experimental results for image-based binary and multi-class classification applications using an in-house medical imaging dataset, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method improves the baselines in majority of the cases by attaining higher accuracy on critical classes while reducing the misclassification rate for the non-critical class samples.

paragraphs: When a critical class has few training examples, overall classification accuracy can hide costly mistakes. Detecting a high proportion of critical cases can also produce many false alarms among noncritical cases. This paper argues that training should directly prioritize reducing false positives while maintaining a high true positive rate, especially when missing positive cases carries greater cost.

The authors formulate binary neural-network training as a constrained optimization problem. Their proposed constraint can be combined with existing loss functions and targets area under the ROC curve while emphasizing the high-true-positive-rate region. They solve the resulting problem using an Augmented Lagrangian method, bringing the desired operating behavior into training. They also propose two extensions of the constraint for multiclass classification.

Experiments cover an in-house medical imaging dataset, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100. In the majority of evaluated cases, the method improves on the baselines by increasing accuracy for critical classes while reducing errors on noncritical samples. The finding supports explicitly training for this balance rather than relying on overall accuracy to reflect performance on rare, consequential cases.
summary.tldr: A constrained training objective prioritizes fewer false alarms at high detection rates for critical classes, improving most evaluated cases.

title: Constrained Optimization to Train Neural Networks on Critical and Under-Represented Classes

abstract: In many sequential decision making applications, the change of decision would bring an additional cost, such as the wear-and-tear cost associated with changing server status. To control the switching cost, we introduce the problem of online convex optimization with continuous switching constraint, where the goal is to achieve a small regret given a budget on the \emph{overall} switching cost. We first investigate the hardness of the problem, and provide a lower bound of order $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ when the switching cost budget $S=\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, and $\Omega(\min\{\frac{T}{S},T\})$ when $S=O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon. The essential idea is to carefully design an adaptive adversary, who can adjust the loss function according to the cumulative switching cost of the player incurred so far based on the orthogonal technique. We then develop a simple gradient-based algorithm which enjoys the minimax optimal regret bound. Finally, we show that, for strongly convex functions, the regret bound can be improved to $O(\log T)$ for $S=\Omega(\log T)$, and $O(\min\{T/\exp(S)+S,T\})$ for $S=O(\log T)$.

paragraphs: Changing decisions can incur costs beyond the loss associated with each decision itself, such as wear from changing server status. This paper studies online convex optimization with a budget on total switching cost. The learner must achieve low regret while respecting that cumulative restriction on how much its decisions change.

The lower bounds reveal two regimes. When switching budget S is at least on the order of the square root of horizon T, the regret lower bound is of square-root-T order. For smaller budgets, it is of order the smaller of T/S and T. The proof uses an adaptive adversary whose losses respond to the learner's accumulated switching cost. A simple gradient-based algorithm achieves minimax-optimal regret.

Stronger curvature improves the achievable guarantees. For strongly convex losses, logarithmic regret is attainable with a switching budget of logarithmic order. Smaller budgets give an upper bound of order the minimum of T/exp(S) + S and T. These results quantify how available switching and loss curvature jointly affect learning performance.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal regret under a total switching budget and shows improved guarantees for strongly convex losses.

title: Online Convex Optimization with Continuous Switching Constraint

abstract: Machine Learning (ML) research has focused on maximizing the accuracy of predictive tasks. ML models, however, are increasingly more complex, resource intensive, and costlier to deploy in resource-constrained environments. These issues are exacerbated for prediction tasks with sequential classification on progressively transitioned stages with “happens-before” relation between them.We argue that it is possible to “unfold” a monolithic single multi-class classifier, typically trained for all stages using all data, into a series of single-stage classifiers. Each single- stage classifier can be cascaded gradually from cheaper to more expensive binary classifiers that are trained using only the necessary data modalities or features required for that stage. UnfoldML is a cost-aware and uncertainty-based dynamic 2D prediction pipeline for multi-stage classification that enables (1) navigation of the accuracy/cost tradeoff space, (2) reducing the spatio-temporal cost of inference by orders of magnitude, and (3) early prediction on proceeding stages. UnfoldML achieves orders of magnitude better cost in clinical settings, while detecting multi- stage disease development in real time. It achieves within 0.1% accuracy from the highest-performing multi-class baseline, while saving close to 20X on spatio- temporal cost of inference and earlier (3.5hrs) disease onset prediction. We also show that UnfoldML generalizes to image classification, where it can predict different level of labels (from coarse to fine) given different level of abstractions of a image, saving close to 5X cost with as little as 0.4% accuracy reduction.
