paragraphs: UnfoldML addresses prediction problems with ordered stages, where one stage precedes another. A single classifier trained across all stages and all available data can be expensive to deploy. The proposed pipeline separates that classifier into stage-specific classifiers, each using the data modalities or features needed for its own prediction.

These findings support allocating prediction effort according to stage and uncertainty in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: UnfoldML combines stage-specific classifier cascades with uncertainty-based decisions to reduce inference costs while preserving accuracy and enabling earlier predictions.

title: UnfoldML: Cost-Aware and Uncertainty-Based Dynamic 2D Prediction for Multi-Stage Classification

abstract: There are multiple scales of abstraction from which we can describe the same image, depending on whether we are focusing on fine-grained details or a more global attribute of the image. In brain mapping, learning to automatically parse images to build representations of both small-scale features (e.g., the presence of cells or blood vessels) and global properties of an image (e.g., which brain region the image comes from) is a crucial and open challenge. However, most existing datasets and benchmarks for neuroanatomy consider only a single downstream task at a time. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new dataset, annotations, and multiple downstream tasks that provide diverse ways to readout information about brain structure and architecture from the same image. Our multi-task neuroimaging benchmark (MTNeuro) is built on volumetric, micrometer-resolution X-ray microtomography images spanning a large thalamocortical section of mouse brain, encompassing multiple cortical and subcortical regions. We generated a number of different prediction challenges and evaluated several supervised and self-supervised models for brain-region prediction and pixel-level semantic segmentation of microstructures. Our experiments not only highlight the rich heterogeneity of this dataset, but also provide insights into how self-supervised approaches can be used to learn representations that capture multiple attributes of a single image and perform well on a variety of downstream tasks. Datasets, code, and pre-trained baseline models are provided at: https://mtneuro.github.io/.

Its experiments highlight the dataset's structural diversity and provide evidence about how self-supervised representations can capture multiple image attributes and support varied downstream tasks. The released data, code, and pretrained baseline models provide a common foundation for studying representation quality across levels of abstraction in brain imaging.
summary.tldr: MTNeuro tests whether brain-image representations capture both fine microstructures and broader regional information using multiple tasks on shared mouse-brain images.

title: MTNeuro: A Benchmark for Evaluating Representations of Brain Structure Across Multiple Levels of Abstraction

abstract: AI-for-science approaches have been applied to solve scientific problems (e.g., nuclear fusion, ecology, genomics, meteorology) and have achieved highly promising results. Spatial precipitation downscaling is one of the most important meteorological problem and urgently requires the participation of AI. However, the lack of a well-organized and annotated large-scale dataset hinders the training and verification of more effective and advancing deep-learning models for precipitation downscaling. To alleviate these obstacles, we present the first large-scale spatial precipitation downscaling dataset named RainNet, which contains more than 62,400 pairs of high-quality low/high-resolution precipitation maps for over 17 years, ready to help the evolution of deep learning models in precipitation downscaling. Specifically, the precipitation maps carefully collected in RainNet cover various meteorological phenomena (e.g., hurricane, squall), which is of great help to improve the model generalization ability. In addition, the map pairs in RainNet are organized in the form of image sequences (720 maps per month or 1 map/hour), showing complex physical properties, e.g., temporal misalignment, temporal sparse, and fluid properties. Furthermore, two deep-learning-oriented metrics are specifically introduced to evaluate or verify the comprehensive performance of the trained model (e.g., prediction maps reconstruction accuracy). To illustrate the applications of RainNet, 14 state-of-the-art models, including deep models and traditional approaches, are evaluated. To fully explore potential downscaling solutions, we propose an implicit physical estimation benchmark framework to learn the above characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate the value of RainNet in training and evaluating downscaling models. Our dataset is available at https://neuralchen.github.io/RainNet/.

RainNet addresses this need with more than 62,400 low- and high-resolution map pairs covering over 17 years, providing a large organized resource for developing downscaling methods.

The maps include varied weather phenomena, such as hurricanes and squalls, and are arranged as image sequences with hourly maps. This organization exposes challenges associated with time and physical behavior, including temporal misalignment, temporal sparsity, and fluid properties. The dataset therefore supports studying precipitation as an evolving process rather than only as separate images.

The paper introduces two evaluation metrics and compares 14 models spanning deep-learning and traditional approaches. It also proposes an implicit physical estimation benchmark framework intended to learn the dataset's relevant characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate RainNet's value for training and evaluating downscaling models. Its contribution combines data, evaluation tools, and a modeling framework around the specific demands of precipitation reconstruction.
summary.tldr: RainNet provides paired precipitation maps, evaluation metrics, and benchmarks for learning to reconstruct rainfall at higher spatial resolution.

title: RainNet: A Large-Scale Imagery Dataset and Benchmark for Spatial Precipitation Downscaling

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection aims to identify OOD data based on representations extracted from well-trained deep models. However, existing methods largely ignore the reprogramming property of deep models and thus may not fully unleash their intrinsic strength: without modifying parameters of a well-trained deep model, we can reprogram this model for a new purpose via data-level manipulation (e.g., adding a specific feature perturbation). This property motivates us to reprogram a classification model to excel at OOD detection (a new task), and thus we propose a general methodology named watermarking in this paper. Specifically, we learn a unified pattern that is superimposed onto features of original data, and the model's detection capability is largely boosted after watermarking. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of watermarking, demonstrating the significance of the reprogramming property of deep models in OOD detection.

However, existing methods largely ignore the reprogramming property of deep models and thus may not fully unleash their intrinsic strength: without modifying parameters of a well-trained deep model, we can reprogram this model for a new purpose via data-level manipulation (e.g., adding a specific feature perturbation). This property motivates us to reprogram a classification model to excel at OOD detection (a new task), and thus we propose a general methodology named watermarking in this paper. Specifically, we learn a unified pattern that is superimposed onto features of original data, and the model's detection capability is largely boosted after watermarking. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of watermarking, demonstrating the significance of the reprogramming property of deep models in OOD detection.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection seeks to recognize data outside the distribution a model is expected to handle. Existing methods often use representations from an already trained deep model. This paper explores another property of those models: manipulating data can reprogram their behavior for a new purpose without changing their learned parameters.

The proposed method, called watermarking, learns a single shared pattern and superimposes it on the features of the original data. The pattern is designed to make a classification model more effective at out-of-distribution detection. Learning therefore takes place in the added pattern, while the well-trained model's parameters remain fixed.

The authors report that watermarking substantially boosts detection capability, with extensive experiments supporting its effectiveness. The finding suggests that a classifier's usefulness for detection depends partly on how data are presented to it, not only on its existing representations. The paper's contribution is a general method for exploiting that reprogramming property through a learned, unified feature perturbation.
summary.tldr: A learned shared watermark improves out-of-distribution detection by reprogramming a classifier through its data while keeping model parameters fixed.

title: Watermarking for Out-of-distribution Detection

abstract: The workhorse of machine learning is stochastic gradient descent.To access stochastic gradients, it is common to consider iteratively input/output pairs of a training dataset.Interestingly, it appears that one does not need full supervision to access stochastic gradients, which is the main motivation of this paper.After formalizing the "active labeling" problem, which focuses on active learning with partial supervision, we provide a streaming technique that provably minimizes the ratio of generalization error over the number of samples.We illustrate our technique in depth for robust regression.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent usually learns from examples paired with complete target outputs. This paper asks whether obtaining a useful learning update really requires that much supervision. Its starting observation is that stochastic gradients can be accessed without fully supervising every example, opening a different way to think about what information a learning algorithm should request.

The authors formalize this setting as active labeling, an active learning problem involving partial supervision. The focus is on obtaining information that supports gradient updates rather than automatically treating a complete input-output pair as the basic unit of training. They develop a streaming technique and prove that it minimizes the ratio of generalization error to the number of samples in their formulation.

Robust regression provides the paper's detailed illustration of the technique. The significance is the connection between the supervision collected and the updates needed for learning: incomplete target information can still support a principled optimization procedure. The stated guarantee concerns the specified error-to-sample ratio, so its meaning should remain tied to that objective.
summary.tldr: Active labeling uses partial supervision to obtain stochastic gradients through a streaming method with a guarantee on its error-to-sample ratio.

title: Active Labeling: Streaming Stochastic Gradients

abstract: We present radiance field propagation (RFP), a novel approach to segmenting objects in 3D during reconstruction given only unlabeled multi-view images of a scene. RFP is derived from emerging neural radiance field-based techniques, which jointly encodes semantics with appearance and geometry. The core of our method is a novel propagation strategy for individual objects' radiance fields with a bidirectional photometric loss, enabling an unsupervised partitioning of a scene into salient or meaningful regions corresponding to different object instances. To better handle complex scenes with multiple objects and occlusions, we further propose an iterative expectation-maximization algorithm to refine object masks. To the best of our knowledge, RFP is the first unsupervised approach for tackling 3D scene object segmentation for neural radiance field (NeRF) without any supervision, annotations, or other cues such as 3D bounding boxes and prior knowledge of object class. Experiments demonstrate that RFP achieves feasible segmentation results that are more accurate than previous unsupervised image/scene segmentation approaches, and are comparable to existing supervised NeRF-based methods. The segmented object representations enable individual 3D object editing operations. Codes and datasets will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Radiance field propagation, or RFP, separates a reconstructed 3D scene into individual objects using only unlabeled images from multiple viewpoints. It builds on neural radiance field techniques that jointly represent appearance, geometry, and semantics. The goal is to identify meaningful object regions during reconstruction without annotations, bounding boxes, or prior knowledge of object classes.

The core method propagates individual objects' radiance fields using a bidirectional photometric loss. This enables an unsupervised partition of the scene into object instances. To handle multiple objects and occlusion more effectively, the authors add an iterative expectation-maximization procedure that refines the object masks. The approach therefore combines propagation with repeated refinement of the scene's object assignments.

Experiments produce feasible segmentations that are more accurate than previous unsupervised image or scene segmentation approaches and comparable to existing supervised NeRF-based methods. The resulting separate object representations also enable editing individual 3D objects. These findings demonstrate that multi-view image information can support object separation and reconstruction together without the additional supervision excluded by the method.
summary.tldr: RFP uses unlabeled multi-view images to reconstruct and segment individual 3D objects through radiance-field propagation and mask refinement.

title: Unsupervised Multi-View Object Segmentation Using Radiance Field Propagation

abstract: Deploying TinyML models on low-cost IoT hardware is very challenging, due to limited device memory capacity. Neural processing unit (NPU) hardware address the memory challenge by using model compression to exploit weight quantization and sparsity to fit more parameters in the same footprint. However, designing compressible neural networks (NNs) is challenging, as it expands the design space across which we must make balanced trade-offs. This paper demonstrates Unified DNAS for Compressible (UDC) NNs, which explores a large search space to generate state-of-the-art compressible NNs for NPU. ImageNet results show UDC networks are up to 3.35x smaller (iso-accuracy) or 6.25% more accurate (iso-model size) than previous work.

paragraphs: TinyML models must fit into the limited memory of low-cost connected devices. Neural processing units can use compressed weights to fit more parameters into a given footprint, exploiting quantization and sparsity. Designing a network for this setting therefore involves balancing accuracy with how effectively its parameters can be stored.

The paper introduces Unified DNAS for Compressible networks, or UDC, to explore a large network-design space for NPU deployment. Compression expands that space because network choices must be considered alongside the opportunities offered by quantized and sparse weights. UDC searches for compressible models suited to those constraints, making the compressed model footprint a central consideration in network design.

On ImageNet, the resulting networks are reported to be up to 3.35 times smaller than previous work at the same accuracy, or 6.25% more accurate at the same model size. These comparisons describe two ways to use the improved trade-off: save memory while preserving accuracy, or improve accuracy within a fixed footprint. The findings support searching directly for compressible architectures when device memory is the binding deployment constraint.
summary.tldr: UDC searches for compressible NPU networks, reporting smaller ImageNet models at matched accuracy or higher accuracy at matched size.

title: UDC: Unified DNAS for Compressible TinyML Models for Neural Processing Units

abstract: Network Architecture Search (NAS) methods have recently gathered much attention. They design networks with better performance and use a much shorter search time compared to traditional manual tuning. Despite their efficiency in model deployments, most NAS algorithms target a single task on a fixed hardware system. However, real-life few-shot learning environments often cover a great number of tasks ($T$) and deployments on a wide variety of hardware platforms ($H$). The combinatorial search complexity $T \times H$ creates a fundamental search efficiency challenge if one naively applies existing NAS methods to these scenarios. To overcome this issue, we show, for the first time, how to rapidly adapt model architectures to new tasks in a \emph{many-task many-hardware} few-shot learning setup by integrating Model Agnostic Meta Learning (MAML) into the NAS flow. The proposed NAS method (H-Meta-NAS) is hardware-aware and performs optimisation in the MAML framework. MetaNAS shows a Pareto dominance compared to a variety of NAS and manual baselines in popular few-shot learning benchmarks with various hardware platforms and constraints. In particular, on the 5-way 1-shot Mini-ImageNet classification task, the proposed method outperforms the best manual baseline by a large margin ($5.21\%$ in accuracy) using $60\%$ less computation.

paragraphs: Architecture search often designs a network for one task and one hardware platform. In few-shot learning, however, many tasks may need deployment across many different devices. Running a separate search for every combination creates a task-count times hardware-count scaling problem. This paper targets that repeated search burden.

The proposed H-Meta-NAS method integrates Model Agnostic Meta Learning into hardware-aware architecture search. Its goal is to adapt architectures rapidly to new tasks while accounting for deployment constraints. Meta-learning provides the framework for adaptation across tasks, and hardware awareness makes the target platform part of the optimization rather than a consideration added after architecture selection.

On popular few-shot benchmarks with several hardware platforms and constraints, the authors report Pareto dominance over a variety of searched and manually designed baselines. On the five-way, one-shot Mini-ImageNet task, they report an accuracy advantage of 5.21% over the best manual baseline while using 60% less computation. These findings support adapting architectures across task and hardware combinations as a way to improve both predictive performance and computational requirements.
summary.tldr: H-Meta-NAS combines meta-learning with hardware-aware architecture search to adapt networks across few-shot tasks and deployment platforms.

title: Rapid Model Architecture Adaption for Meta-Learning

abstract: For deep reinforcement learning (RL) from pixels, learning effective state representations is crucial for achieving high performance. However, in practice, limited experience and high-dimensional inputs prevent effective representation learning. To address this, motivated by the success of mask-based modeling in other research fields, we introduce mask-based reconstruction to promote state representation learning in RL. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective self-supervised method, Mask-based Latent Reconstruction (MLR), to predict complete state representations in the latent space from the observations with spatially and temporally masked pixels. MLR enables better use of context information when learning state representations to make them more informative, which facilitates the training of RL agents. Extensive experiments show that our MLR significantly improves the sample efficiency in RL and outperforms the state-of-the-art sample-efficient RL methods on multiple continuous and discrete control benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/Mask-based-Latent-Reconstruction.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from pixels requires an agent to turn large visual observations into useful representations of its state. Limited experience makes that representation-learning problem difficult. This paper introduces an additional self-supervised task intended to extract more useful information from the observations already available to the agent.

Mask-based Latent Reconstruction hides pixels across both space and time and asks the model to predict the complete state representation. The prediction takes place in the latent representation space. Recovering that representation from incomplete observations encourages the model to use contextual information, making the learned state description more informative for reinforcement learning.

Experiments across multiple continuous and discrete control benchmarks report significant improvements in sample efficiency and performance beyond the compared state-of-the-art sample-efficient methods. These findings indicate that the reconstruction task helps agents make better use of limited experience in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a simple auxiliary learning method that connects masked observation modeling directly to the internal representations used to train control agents.
summary.tldr: Predicting complete latent states from spatially and temporally masked observations improves sample efficiency in pixel-based reinforcement learning.

title: Mask-based Latent Reconstruction for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The prototypical network is a prototype classifier based on meta-learning and is widely used for few-shot learning because it classifies unseen examples by constructing class-specific prototypes without adjusting hyper-parameters during meta-testing.Interestingly, recent research has attracted a lot of attention, showing that training a new linear classifier, which does not use a meta-learning algorithm, performs comparably with the prototypical network.However, the training of a new linear classifier requires the retraining of the classifier every time a new class appears.In this paper, we analyze how a prototype classifier works equally well without training a new linear classifier or meta-learning.We experimentally find that directly using the feature vectors, which is extracted by using standard pre-trained models to construct a prototype classifier in meta-testing, does not perform as well as the prototypical network and training new linear classifiers on the feature vectors of pre-trained models.Thus, we derive a novel generalization bound for a prototypical classifier and show that the transformation of a feature vector can improve the performance of prototype classifiers.We experimentally investigate several normalization methods for minimizing the derived bound and find that the same performance can be obtained by using the L2 normalization and minimizing the ratio of the within-class variance to the between-class variance without training a new classifier or meta-learning.

paragraphs: A prototype classifier represents each class through a class-specific reference built from examples. This is attractive for recognizing new classes from little data because it avoids fitting a new classifier each time. The paper asks whether this convenience can be retained without the meta-learning procedure used by prototypical networks.

Simply constructing prototypes from the features of a standard pretrained model does not work as well in the authors’ experiments. They therefore derive a generalization bound to understand how transforming those features could improve classification. The analysis motivates examining normalization methods and the relationship between variation within a class and separation between classes.

Experimentally, L2 normalization and reducing the ratio of within-class variance to between-class variance achieve performance comparable to the alternatives discussed, without meta-learning or training a new classifier. The finding makes feature preparation central to the comparison: the usefulness of a simple prototype classifier depends on how its feature space is organized, not just on the availability of pretrained features.
summary.tldr: Careful feature normalization lets prototype classifiers match the studied alternatives without meta-learning or fitting new classifiers.

title: A Closer Look at Prototype Classifier for Few-shot Image Classification

abstract: The aim of weakly supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS) is to learn semantic segmentation without using dense annotations. WSSS has been intensively studied for 2D images and 3D point clouds. However, the existing WSSS studies have focused on a single domain, i.e. 2D or 3D, even when multi-domain data is available. In this paper, we propose a novel joint 2D-3D WSSS framework taking advantage of WSSS in different domains, using classification labels only. Via projection, we leverage the 2D class activation map as self-supervision to enhance the 3D semantic perception. Conversely, we exploit the similarity matrix of point cloud features for training the image classifier to achieve more precise 2D segmentation. In both directions, we devise a confidence-based scoring method to reduce the effect of inaccurate self-supervision. With extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments, we verify that the proposed joint WSSS framework effectively transfers the benefit of each domain to the other domain, and the resulting semantic segmentation performance is remarkably improved in both 2D and 3D domains. On the ScanNetV2 benchmark, our framework significantly outperforms the prior WSSS approaches, suggesting a new research direction for WSSS.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to individual image pixels or points in a three-dimensional scene. Dense labels for this task are costly, so weakly supervised methods learn from less detailed annotations. This paper uses classification labels alone while jointly learning from images and point clouds, allowing the two domains to help each other.

Information moves in both directions. Image class activation maps indicate regions associated with a category, and projection turns these maps into self-supervision for the point-cloud model. In the reverse direction, similarities among point-cloud features help train the image classifier toward more precise segmentation. Confidence-based scores reduce the influence of inaccurate self-generated supervision in both transfers.

The experiments report improvements in both image and point-cloud segmentation, with substantial gains over prior weakly supervised approaches on ScanNetV2. Quantitative and qualitative results support the claim that useful information transfers in both directions. The approach matters because it treats available two-dimensional and three-dimensional observations as complementary training signals, rather than learning each segmentation problem independently from the same limited level of human annotation.
summary.tldr: A joint framework lets images and point clouds supervise each other, improving both forms of semantic segmentation using classification labels alone.

title: Joint Learning of 2D-3D Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Extensive efforts have been made to understand and improve the fairness of machine learning models based on observational metrics, especially in high-stakes domains such as medical insurance, education, and hiring decisions. However, there is a lack of certified fairness considering the end-to-end performance of an ML model. In this paper, we first formulate the certified fairness of an ML model trained on a given data distribution as an optimization problem based on the model performance loss bound on a fairness constrained distribution, which is within bounded distributional distance with the training distribution. We then propose a general fairness certification framework and instantiate it for both sensitive shifting and general shifting scenarios. In particular, we propose to solve the optimization problem by decomposing the original data distribution into analytical subpopulations and proving the convexity of the subproblems to solve them. We evaluate our certified fairness on six real-world datasets and show that our certification is tight in the sensitive shifting scenario and provides non-trivial certification under general shifting. Our framework is flexible to integrate additional non-skewness constraints and we show that it provides even tighter certification under different real-world scenarios. We also compare our certified fairness bound with adapted existing distributional robustness bounds on Gaussian data and demonstrate that our method is significantly tighter.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to certify model performance under distribution changes constrained by fairness requirements. It formulates certification as an optimization problem: bound the model's loss on distributions that satisfy those requirements and remain within a bounded distance of the training distribution. The certificate therefore depends on an explicitly restricted set of possible shifts.

The proposed framework handles both sensitive shifting and more general shifting scenarios. Its main computational strategy divides the original distribution into subpopulations that can be analyzed separately. The authors prove convexity of the resulting subproblems, making this decomposition a mathematical route to solving the certification problem.

Across six real-world datasets, the authors report tight certificates for sensitive shifting and non-trivial certificates for general shifting. Adding non-skewness constraints can tighten the bounds further. Comparisons on Gaussian data also produce substantially tighter bounds than adapted distributional robustness methods. These results show how structured assumptions about distribution changes can yield informative fairness-related performance guarantees.
summary.tldr: Subpopulation decomposition enables performance certificates over nearby distributions subject to fairness constraints.

title: Certifying Some Distributional Fairness with Subpopulation Decomposition

abstract: During training, models can exploit spurious correlations as shortcuts, resulting in poor generalization performance when shortcuts do not persist. In this work, assuming access to a representation based on domain knowledge (i.e., known concepts) that is invariant to shortcuts, we aim to learn robust and accurate models from biased training data. In contrast to previous work, we do not rely solely on known concepts, but allow the model to also learn unknown concepts. We propose two approaches for mitigating shortcuts that incorporate domain knowledge, while accounting for potentially important yet unknown concepts. The first approach is two-staged. After fitting a model using known concepts, it accounts for the residual using unknown concepts. While flexible, we show that this approach is vulnerable when shortcuts are correlated with the unknown concepts. This limitation is addressed by our second approach that extends a recently proposed regularization penalty. Applied to two real-world datasets, we demonstrate that both approaches can successfully mitigate shortcut learning.

paragraphs: Models can learn shortcuts from correlations that happen to hold in training data but disappear elsewhere. This paper seeks to reduce that behavior using domain knowledge while still allowing models to discover useful concepts beyond what experts already know. It assumes access to a representation of known concepts that is invariant to the shortcuts.

The first proposed approach learns in two stages. It initially fits a model using known concepts, then uses unknown concepts to explain the remaining residual. This makes room for additional predictive information without requiring the known concepts to explain everything. However, the authors show that this flexibility leaves the method vulnerable when shortcuts correlate with the unknown concepts.

The second approach extends an existing regularization penalty to address that vulnerability while continuing to account for potentially important unknown concepts. On two real-world datasets, both approaches successfully mitigate shortcut learning. The work highlights a practical tension: domain knowledge can guide robust prediction, but models also need a way to incorporate useful information outside that knowledge.
summary.tldr: Two methods combine shortcut-invariant known concepts with learned unknown concepts to reduce reliance on spurious correlations.

title: Learning Concept Credible Models for Mitigating Shortcuts

abstract: Learning set functions becomes increasingly important in many applications like product recommendation and compound selection in AI-aided drug discovery. The majority of existing works study methodologies of set function learning under the function value oracle, which, however, requires expensive supervision signals. This renders it impractical for applications with only weak supervisions under the Optimal Subset (OS) oracle, the study of which is surprisingly overlooked. In this work, we present a principled yet practical maximum likelihood learning framework, termed as EquiVSet, that simultaneously meets the following desiderata of learning neural set functions under the OS oracle: i) permutation invariance of the set mass function being modeled; ii) permission of varying ground set; iii) minimum prior and iv) scalability. The main components of our framework involve: an energy-based treatment of the set mass function, DeepSet-style architectures to handle permutation invariance, mean-field variational inference, and its amortized variants. Thanks to the delicate combination of these advanced architectures, empirical studies on three real-world applications (including Amazon product recommendation, set anomaly detection, and compound selection for virtual screening) demonstrate that EquiVSet outperforms the baselines by a large margin.

paragraphs: Learning a set function means learning how to evaluate a collection of items together. Many approaches assume access to numerical function values, which can be expensive to obtain. This paper studies weaker supervision from an optimal-subset oracle: information about which subset is preferred, rather than direct evaluations of the set function.

The proposed framework, EquiVSet, uses maximum likelihood learning and an energy-based probability model over sets. DeepSet-style architectures ensure that changing the order of the same items does not change their modeled probability. Mean-field variational inference and amortized variants support practical learning. The framework is designed to handle changing ground sets, require minimal prior assumptions, and remain scalable.

Experiments cover Amazon product recommendation, set anomaly detection, and compound selection for virtual screening. The authors report large improvements over the evaluated baselines. The broader contribution is a way to learn useful neural set models when supervision identifies good subsets but does not supply costly numerical scores, while respecting the unordered nature of sets and variation in the available items.
summary.tldr: EquiVSet learns neural set functions from preferred-subset supervision while handling unordered items and changing candidate sets.

title: Learning Neural Set Functions Under the Optimal Subset Oracle

abstract: Action recognition has improved dramatically with massive-scale video datasets. Yet, these datasets are accompanied with issues related to curation cost, privacy, ethics, bias, and copyright. Compared to that, only minor efforts have been devoted toward exploring the potential of synthetic video data. In this work, as a stepping stone towards addressing these shortcomings, we study the transferability of video representations learned solely from synthetically-generated video clips, instead of real data. We propose SynAPT, a novel benchmark for action recognition based on a combination of existing synthetic datasets, in which a model is pre-trained on synthetic videos rendered by various graphics simulators, and then transferred to a set of downstream action recognition datasets, containing different categories than the synthetic data. We provide an extensive baseline analysis on SynAPT revealing that the simulation-to-real gap is minor for datasets with low object and scene bias, where models pre-trained with synthetic data even outperform their real data counterparts. We posit that the gap between real and synthetic action representations can be attributed to contextual bias and static objects related to the action, instead of the temporal dynamics of the action itself. The SynAPT benchmark is available at https://github.com/mintjohnkim/SynAPT.

Yet, these datasets are accompanied with issues related to curation cost, privacy, ethics, bias, and copyright. Compared to that, only minor efforts have been devoted toward exploring the potential of synthetic video data. In this work, as a stepping stone towards addressing these shortcomings, we study the transferability of video representations learned solely from synthetically-generated video clips, instead of real data. We propose SynAPT, a novel benchmark for action recognition based on a combination of existing synthetic datasets, in which a model is pre-trained on synthetic videos rendered by various graphics simulators, and then transferred to a set of downstream action recognition datasets, containing different categories than the synthetic data. We provide an extensive baseline analysis on SynAPT revealing that the simulation-to-real gap is minor for datasets with low object and scene bias, where models pre-trained with synthetic data even outperform their real data counterparts. We posit that the gap between real and synthetic action representations can be attributed to contextual bias and static objects related to the action, instead of the temporal dynamics of the action itself. The SynAPT benchmark is available at https://github.com/mintjohnkim/SynAPT.

paragraphs: Large real-video datasets have advanced action recognition, but collecting them brings costs and concerns involving privacy, bias, ethics, and copyright. This paper investigates synthetic videos as a source of representation learning. Its central question is how well features learned entirely from simulated clips transfer to recognizing actions in downstream datasets.

The authors introduce SynAPT, a benchmark assembled from existing synthetic datasets rendered with different graphics simulators. Models are pretrained on those videos and then transferred to action-recognition datasets whose categories differ from the synthetic training categories. This setup examines whether simulated experience produces representations useful beyond the particular actions present during pretraining.

The baseline analysis finds a small simulation-to-real gap on datasets with low object and scene bias; there, synthetic pretraining can even outperform real-video pretraining. The authors propose that contextual cues and static objects associated with actions explain the remaining gap more than action dynamics do. This is an interpretation of the results, suggesting that transferability depends partly on which visual cues downstream datasets reward.
summary.tldr: SynAPT shows that synthetic-video pretraining transfers well when downstream action datasets have low object and scene bias.

title: How Transferable are Video Representations Based on Synthetic Data?

abstract: Temporal networks are widely used as abstract graph representations for real-world dynamic systems. Indeed, recognizing the network evolution states is crucial in understanding and analyzing temporal networks. For instance, social networks will generate the clustering and formation of tightly-knit groups or communities over time, relying on the triadic closure theory. However, the existing methods often struggle to account for the time-varying nature of these network structures, hindering their performance when applied to networks with complex evolution states. To mitigate this problem, we propose a novel framework called ESSEN, an Evolution StateS awarE Network, to measure temporal network evolution using von Neumann entropy and thermodynamic temperature. The developed framework utilizes a von Neumann entropy aware attention mechanism and network evolution state contrastive learning in the graph encoding. In addition, it employs a unique decoder the so-called Mixture of Thermodynamic Experts (MoTE) for decoding. ESSEN extracts local and global network evolution information using thermodynamic features and adaptively recognizes the network evolution states. Moreover, the proposed method is evaluated on link prediction tasks under both transductive and inductive settings, with the corresponding results demonstrating its effectiveness compared to various state-of-the-art baselines.

The paper argues that existing methods struggle with this changing structure, particularly when a network exhibits complex evolution states.

ESSEN represents network evolution using von Neumann entropy and thermodynamic temperature. Together, these components extract local and global information about network change and adaptively recognize its evolution states.

Link prediction provides a practical test of whether the learned evolution information helps anticipate connections. The contribution is a framework that makes structural change an explicit part of graph encoding and decoding, using thermodynamic features to inform both stages.
summary.tldr: ESSEN uses entropy and thermodynamic features to represent changing network structure and improve temporal link prediction.

title: ESSEN: Improving Evolution State Estimation for Temporal Networks using Von Neumann Entropy

abstract: A vital and rapidly growing application, remote sensing offers vast yet sparsely labeled, spatially aligned multimodal data; this makes self-supervised learning algorithms invaluable. We present CROMA: a framework that combines contrastive and reconstruction self-supervised objectives to learn rich unimodal and multimodal representations. Our method separately encodes masked-out multispectral optical and synthetic aperture radar samples—aligned in space and time—and performs cross-modal contrastive learning. Another encoder fuses these sensors, producing joint multimodal encodings that are used to predict the masked patches via a lightweight decoder. We show that these objectives are complementary when leveraged on spatially aligned multimodal data. We also introduce X- and 2D-ALiBi, which spatially biases our cross- and self-attention matrices. These strategies improve representations and allow our models to effectively extrapolate to images up to $17.6\times$ larger at test-time. CROMA outperforms the current SoTA multispectral model, evaluated on: four classification benchmarks—finetuning (avg.$\uparrow$ 1.8%), linear (avg.$\uparrow$ 2.4%) and nonlinear (avg.$\uparrow$ 1.4%) probing, $k$NN classification (avg.$\uparrow$ 3.5%), and $K$-means clustering (avg.$\uparrow$ 8.4%); and three segmentation benchmarks (avg.$\uparrow$ 6.4%). CROMA’s rich, optionally multimodal representations can be widely leveraged across remote sensing applications.

paragraphs: Remote sensing provides abundant imagery from different sensors but relatively few labels. CROMA learns representations from optical and radar observations aligned in both location and time. Its training combines two tasks: bringing corresponding sensor representations into agreement and reconstructing image patches that have been hidden.

Separate encoders process the partially masked optical and radar inputs for cross-modal contrastive learning. Another encoder combines the sensor information, and a lightweight decoder uses that joint representation to predict missing patches. The authors show that these objectives complement each other for spatially aligned multimodal data, producing representations usable with individual sensors or combined inputs.

Evaluations report improvements over the compared leading multispectral model across classification, probing, clustering, and segmentation. The findings indicate that the learned features support multiple downstream uses, rather than gains being confined to a single evaluation procedure.
summary.tldr: CROMA combines radar–optical contrastive learning and masked reconstruction to learn versatile remote-sensing representations.

title: CROMA: Remote Sensing Representations with Contrastive Radar-Optical Masked Autoencoders

abstract: In recent years, many researchers have proposed new models for synaptic plasticity in the brain based on principles of machine learning. The central motivation has been the development of learning algorithms that are able to learn difficult tasks while qualifying as "biologically plausible". However, the concept of a biologically plausible learning algorithm is only heuristically defined as an algorithm that is potentially implementable by biological neural networks. Further, claims that neural circuits could implement any given algorithm typically rest on an amorphous concept of "locality" (both in space and time). As a result, it is unclear what many proposed local learning algorithms actually predict biologically, and which of these are consequently good candidates for experimental investigation. Here, we address this lack of clarity by proposing formal and operational definitions of locality. Specifically, we define different classes of locality, each of which makes clear what quantities cannot be included in a learning rule if an algorithm is to qualify as local with respect to a given (biological) constraint. We subsequently use this framework to distill testable predictions from various classes of biologically plausible synaptic plasticity models that are robust to arbitrary choices about neural network architecture. Therefore, our framework can be used to guide claims of biological plausibility and to identify potential means of experimentally falsifying a proposed learning algorithm for the brain.

paragraphs: Researchers often propose brain-learning algorithms inspired by machine learning and describe them as biologically plausible. Such claims frequently depend on whether a synapse could access the information its update rule requires. The paper argues that informal uses of locality in space and time leave those requirements unclear, making biological predictions difficult to assess.

The authors introduce formal, operational definitions covering different classes of locality. Each class specifies which quantities a learning rule cannot use if it is to satisfy a particular biological constraint. This turns a broad plausibility label into explicit restrictions on the information available to the proposed learning mechanism.

The framework is then used to derive testable predictions from classes of synaptic plasticity models. These predictions remain robust to arbitrary choices of neural network architecture, helping separate claims about learning rules from incidental modeling choices. summary.tldr: The paper formalizes locality constraints on synaptic learning rules so biological plausibility claims yield testable predictions.

title: Formalizing locality for normative synaptic plasticity models

abstract: Policy evaluation via Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is at the core of many MC Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms (e.g., policy gradient methods). In this context, the designer of the learning system specifies an interaction budget that the agent usually spends by collecting trajectories of *fixed length* within a simulator. However, is this data collection strategy the best option? To answer this question, in this paper, we consider as quality index the variance of an unbiased policy return estimator that uses trajectories of different lengths, i.e., *truncated*. We first derive a closed-form expression of this variance that clearly shows the sub-optimality of the fixed-length trajectory schedule. Furthermore, it suggests that adaptive data collection strategies that spend the available budget sequentially might be able to allocate a larger portion of transitions in timesteps in which more accurate sampling is required to reduce the variance of the final estimate. Building on these findings, we present an *adaptive* algorithm called **R**obust and **I**terative **D**ata collection strategy **O**ptimization (RIDO). The main intuition behind RIDO is to split the available interaction budget into mini-batches. At each round, the agent determines the most convenient schedule of trajectories that minimizes an empirical and robust estimate of the estimator's variance. After discussing the theoretical properties of our method, we conclude by assessing its performance across multiple domains. Our results show that RIDO can adapt its trajectory schedule toward timesteps where more sampling is required to increase the quality of the final estimation.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo policy evaluation estimates a policy’s return using simulated trajectories. With a fixed interaction budget, a common choice is to collect trajectories of equal length. This paper asks whether that schedule uses the budget effectively, measuring quality through the variance of an unbiased return estimator that permits different trajectory lengths.

The authors derive a closed-form variance expression that exposes the suboptimality of fixed-length scheduling under their criterion. It also motivates spending more samples at time steps where additional information would most improve precision. Their algorithm, RIDO, divides the interaction budget into mini-batches and updates the trajectory schedule round by round.

At each round, RIDO chooses a schedule to minimize an empirical, robust estimate of the return estimator’s variance. The paper discusses theoretical properties and evaluates the method across several domains. Results show that RIDO can redirect sampling toward time steps needing greater attention and improve final estimation quality. The contribution concerns allocating evaluation data effectively, with unbiasedness and variance providing the central statistical criteria.
summary.tldr: RIDO adaptively varies simulation trajectory lengths to spend a fixed interaction budget where it can reduce policy-return estimation variance.

title: Truncating Trajectories in Monte Carlo Policy Evaluation: an Adaptive Approach

abstract: Modeling complex dynamical systems poses significant challenges, with traditional methods struggling to work on a variety of systems and scale to high-dimensional dynamics. In response, we present DynaDojo, a novel benchmarking platform designed for data-driven dynamical system identification. DynaDojo provides diagnostics on three ways an algorithm’s performance scales: across the number of training samples, the complexity of a dynamical system, and a target error to achieve. Furthermore, DynaDojo enables studying out-of-distribution generalization (by providing unique test conditions for each system) and active learning (by supporting closed-loop control). Through its user-friendly and easily extensible API, DynaDojo accommodates a wide range of user-defined \texttt{Algorithms}, \texttt{Systems}, and \texttt{Challenges} (evaluation metrics). The platform also prioritizes resource-efficient training with parallel processing strategies for running on a cluster. To showcase its utility, in DynaDojo 0.9, we include implementations of 7 baseline algorithms and 20 dynamical systems, along with several demos exhibiting insights researchers can glean using our platform. This work aspires to make DynaDojo a unifying benchmarking platform for system identification, paralleling the role of OpenAI’s Gym in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: DynaDojo is a benchmarking platform for learning dynamical systems from data. The problem is broader than achieving good predictions on one system: researchers also need to understand how an algorithm behaves as the learning problem grows or becomes more demanding. The platform makes these scaling questions explicit parts of evaluation.

Its diagnostics examine performance in relation to training-sample count, system complexity, and the target error. It also supplies distinct test conditions for studying generalization beyond the training distribution. Support for closed-loop control enables active-learning studies, where the learning process can influence the system from which it gathers information.

An extensible interface lets researchers supply algorithms, dynamical systems, and evaluation challenges. Parallel processing supports resource-efficient experiments on clusters. The described release includes seven baseline algorithms, twenty systems, and demonstrations of insights the platform can provide. Its contribution is shared experimental infrastructure for comparing system-identification methods along meaningful dimensions. Becoming a unifying benchmark is the project's aspiration, rather than an established outcome of the reported demonstrations.
summary.tldr: DynaDojo benchmarks how dynamical-system learning methods scale with data, system complexity, and desired accuracy.

title: DynaDojo: An Extensible Platform for Benchmarking Scaling in Dynamical System Identification

abstract: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRS) actively elicit user preferences to generate adaptive recommendations. Mainstream reinforcement learning-based CRS solutions heavily rely on handcrafted reward functions, which may not be aligned with user intent in CRS tasks. Therefore, the design of task-specific rewards is critical to facilitate CRS policy learning, which remains largely under-explored in the literature. In this work, we propose a novel approach to address this challenge by learning intrinsic rewards from interactions with users. Specifically, we formulate intrinsic reward learning as a multi-objective bi-level optimization problem. The inner level optimizes the CRS policy augmented by the learned intrinsic rewards, while the outer level drives the intrinsic rewards to optimize two CRS-specific objectives: maximizing the success rate and minimizing the number of turns to reach a successful recommendation}in conversations. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on three public CRS benchmarks. The results show that our algorithm significantly improves CRS performance by exploiting informative learned intrinsic rewards.

paragraphs: Conversational recommenders ask questions to uncover preferences and adapt their suggestions. Reinforcement learning can guide these interactions, but its behavior depends on the rewards used during training. Handcrafted rewards may not align well with the task or the user's intent, motivating a method that learns useful reward signals from interactions.

The paper formulates reward learning as a two-level optimization problem. At the inner level, the conversational policy is trained with additional learned intrinsic rewards. At the outer level, those rewards are adjusted toward two goals: increasing the rate of successful recommendations and reducing the number of conversational turns needed to achieve success.

This arrangement makes reward design responsive to the outcomes the recommender is intended to achieve. The rewards influence how the policy learns, while success and conversational length guide how the rewards themselves change. Experiments on three public benchmarks report significant performance improvements from informative learned rewards, supporting the usefulness of optimizing these task-specific training signals alongside the conversational policy.
summary.tldr: Learning intrinsic rewards through two-level optimization improves conversational recommendation by targeting successful suggestions and shorter successful conversations.

title: Multi-Objective Intrinsic Reward Learning for Conversational Recommender Systems

abstract: Length generalization, the ability to generalize from small training context sizes to larger ones, is a critical challenge in the development of Transformer-based language models. Positional encoding (PE) has been identified as a major factor influencing length generalization, but the exact impact of different PE schemes on extrapolation in downstream tasks remains unclear. In this paper, we conduct a systematic empirical study comparing the length generalization performance of decoder-only Transformers with five different position encoding approaches including Absolute Position Embedding (APE), T5's Relative PE, ALiBi, and Rotary, in addition to Transformers without positional encoding (NoPE). Our evaluation encompasses a battery of reasoning and mathematical tasks. Our findings reveal that the most commonly used positional encoding methods, such as ALiBi, Rotary, and APE, are not well suited for length generalization in downstream tasks. More importantly, NoPE outperforms other explicit positional encoding methods while requiring no additional computation. We theoretically demonstrate that NoPE can represent both absolute and relative PEs, but when trained with SGD, it mostly resembles T5's relative PE attention patterns. Finally, we find that scratchpad is not always helpful to solve length generalization and its format highly impacts the model's performance. Overall, our work suggests that explicit position embeddings are not essential for decoder-only Transformers to generalize well to longer sequences.

paragraphs: Length generalization asks whether a model trained on shorter sequences can handle longer ones. This paper systematically compares five positional approaches in decoder-only Transformers: absolute embeddings, T5 relative encoding, ALiBi, rotary encoding, and no explicit positional encoding. The evaluation uses a collection of reasoning and mathematical tasks.

In those experiments, common choices including absolute embeddings, ALiBi, and rotary encoding perform poorly at length generalization. Models without explicit positional encoding outperform the explicit alternatives while requiring no additional computation. The authors also prove that such models can represent both absolute and relative positional encodings, showing that omitting an explicit encoding does not eliminate that representational capability.

When trained with stochastic gradient descent, the models without positional encoding mostly develop attention patterns resembling T5's relative encoding. The study further finds that scratchpads do not always help, and their format strongly affects performance. Together, the results suggest that explicit positional embeddings are not essential for good length generalization in decoder-only Transformers, while highlighting the importance of task and representation choices.
summary.tldr: Across tested reasoning and math tasks, decoder-only Transformers without explicit positional encoding generalize to longer sequences better than the compared alternatives.

title: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers

abstract: In this study, we propose a novel deep spatio-temporal point process model, Deep Kernel Mixture Point Processes (DKMPP), that incorporates multimodal covariate information. DKMPP is an enhanced version of Deep Mixture Point Processes (DMPP), which uses a more flexible deep kernel to model complex relationships between events and covariate data, improving the model's expressiveness. To address the intractable training procedure of DKMPP due to the non-integrable deep kernel, we utilize an integration-free method based on score matching, and further improve efficiency by adopting a scalable denoising score matching method. Our experiments demonstrate that DKMPP and its corresponding score-based estimators outperform baseline models, showcasing the advantages of incorporating covariate information, utilizing a deep kernel, and employing score-based estimators.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Deep Kernel Mixture Point Processes, or DKMPP, for modeling events across space and time while incorporating multimodal covariate information. Covariates provide additional information associated with the events. The model extends Deep Mixture Point Processes with a more flexible deep kernel to represent complex relationships between that information and event occurrence.

The added flexibility creates a training obstacle: the deep kernel is non-integrable, making the training procedure intractable. The authors address this with score matching, which supplies an integration-free training approach. They further improve efficiency through a scalable denoising score matching method, connecting the richer model to an estimator that can train it.

Experiments show that DKMPP and its score-based estimators outperform the baseline models considered. The reported findings support three aspects of the design: incorporating covariates, using a deep kernel, and adopting score-based estimation. The contribution therefore concerns both model expressiveness and the computational method needed to make that expressiveness usable in training.
summary.tldr: DKMPP models spatial-temporal events with multimodal covariates and uses score matching to train its otherwise intractable deep kernel.

title: Integration-free Training for Spatio-temporal Multimodal Covariate Deep Kernel Point Processes

abstract: Influence functions (IF) have been seen as a technique for explaining model predictions through the lens of the training data. Their utility is assumed to be in identifying training examples "responsible" for a prediction so that, for example, correcting a prediction is possible by intervening on those examples (removing or editing them) and retraining the model. However, recent empirical studies have shown that the existing methods of estimating IF predict the leave-one-out-and-retrain effect poorly. In order to understand the mismatch between the theoretical promise and the practical results, we analyse five assumptions made by IF methods which are problematic for modern-scale deep neural networks and which concern convexity, numeric stability, training trajectory and parameter divergence. This allows us to clarify what can be expected theoretically from IF. We show that while most assumptions can be addressed successfully, the parameter divergence poses a clear limitation on the predictive power of IF: influence fades over training time even with deterministic training. We illustrate this theoretical result with BERT and ResNet models.Another conclusion from the theoretical analysis is that IF are still useful for model debugging and correcting even though some of the assumptions made in prior work do not hold: using natural language processing and computer vision tasks, we verify that mis-predictions can be successfully corrected by taking only a few fine-tuning steps on influential examples.

paragraphs: Influence functions are used to connect model predictions to training examples that may have shaped them. A common expectation is that they predict what will happen if an example is removed or edited and the model is retrained. Recent empirical results have challenged that expectation, motivating this paper's analysis of the gap between theory and practice.

The authors examine five assumptions involving convexity, numerical stability, training trajectories, and parameter divergence. They find that most can be addressed successfully, but divergence in model parameters imposes a clear limit on predictive power. Influence fades over training time even when training is deterministic. Experiments with BERT and ResNet illustrate this theoretical result.

The analysis also identifies a useful role for influence functions despite those limits. On language and vision tasks, the authors correct mispredictions using only a few fine-tuning steps on influential examples. The findings distinguish predicting the outcome of removal and retraining from guiding targeted model correction: limitations on the former do not eliminate practical value for debugging.
summary.tldr: Parameter divergence limits influence functions' retraining predictions, but influential examples can still guide effective model correction.

title: Theoretical and Practical Perspectives on what Influence Functions Do

abstract: Convolutions encode equivariance symmetries into neural networks leading to better generalisation performance. However, symmetries provide fixed hard constraints on the functions a network can represent, need to be specified in advance, and can not be adapted. Our goal is to allow flexible symmetry constraints that can automatically be learned from data using gradients. Learning symmetry and associated weight connectivity structures from scratch is difficult for two reasons. First, it requires efficient and flexible parameterisations of layer-wise equivariances. Secondly, symmetries act as constraints and are therefore not encouraged by training losses measuring data fit. To overcome these challenges, we improve parameterisations of soft equivariance and learn the amount of equivariance in layers by optimising the marginal likelihood, estimated using differentiable Laplace approximations. The objective balances data fit and model complexity enabling layer-wise symmetry discovery in deep networks. We demonstrate the ability to automatically learn layer-wise equivariances on image classification tasks, achieving equivalent or improved performance over baselines with hard-coded symmetry.

However, symmetries provide fixed hard constraints on the functions a network can represent, need to be specified in advance, and can not be adapted. Our goal is to allow flexible symmetry constraints that can automatically be learned from data using gradients. Learning symmetry and associated weight connectivity structures from scratch is difficult for two reasons. First, it requires efficient and flexible parameterisations of layer-wise equivariances. Secondly, symmetries act as constraints and are therefore not encouraged by training losses measuring data fit. To overcome these challenges, we improve parameterisations of soft equivariance and learn the amount of equivariance in layers by optimising the marginal likelihood, estimated using differentiable Laplace approximations. The objective balances data fit and model complexity enabling layer-wise symmetry discovery in deep networks. We demonstrate the ability to automatically learn layer-wise equivariances on image classification tasks, achieving equivalent or improved performance over baselines with hard-coded symmetry.

Convolutions build such constraints into the architecture, but those choices are fixed in advance. This paper asks whether a network can instead learn how much symmetry to use in each layer directly from data.

The authors address two obstacles: representing flexible layer-level equivariance efficiently, and choosing a learning objective that actually rewards useful constraints. They improve parameterizations of soft equivariance and optimize marginal likelihood using differentiable Laplace approximations. This objective balances agreement with the data against model complexity, giving symmetry a role that a data-fit loss alone does not encourage.

The result supports adapting architectural constraints to the task through gradient-based learning. title: Learning Layer-wise Equivariances Automatically using Gradients

abstract: Fictitious Play (FP) is a simple and natural dynamic for repeated play with many applications in game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning. It was introduced by Brown and its convergence properties for two-player zero-sum games was established later by Robinson. Potential games [Monderer and Shapley 1996] is another class of games which exhibit the FP property [Monderer and Shapley 1996], i.e., FP dynamics converges to a Nash equilibrium if all agents follows it. Nevertheless, except for two-player zero-sum games and for specific instances of payoff matrices [Abernethy et. al. 2021] or for adversarial tie-breaking rules [Daskalakis and Pan, 2014], the \textit{convergence rate} of FP is unknown. In this work, we focus on the rate of convergence of FP when applied to potential games and more specifically identical payoff games. We prove that FP can take exponential time (in the number of strategies) to reach a Nash equilibrium, even if the game is restricted to \textit{two agents}. To prove this, we recursively construct a two-player coordination game with a unique Nash equilibrium. Moreover, every approximate Nash equilibrium in the constructed game must be close to the pure Nash equilibrium in $\ell_1$-distance.

It establishes that slow instances exist, rather than claiming exponential behavior for every potential game.
summary.tldr: Fictitious play can take exponential time to reach equilibrium even in two-player coordination games with identical payoffs and a unique equilibrium.

title: Exponential Lower Bounds for Fictitious Play in Potential Games

abstract: Selecting a suitable pretraining dataset is crucial for both general-domain (e.g., GPT-3) and domain-specific (e.g., Codex) language models (LMs). We formalize this problem as selecting a subset of a large raw unlabeled dataset to match a desired target distribution given unlabeled target samples. Due to the scale and dimensionality of the raw text data, existing methods use simple heuristics or require human experts to manually curate data. Instead, we extend the classic importance resampling approach used in low-dimensions for LM data selection. We propose Data Selection with Importance Resampling (DSIR), an efficient and scalable framework that estimates importance weights in a reduced feature space for tractability and selects data with importance resampling according to these weights. We instantiate the DSIR framework with hashed n-gram features for efficiency, enabling the selection of 100M documents from the full Pile dataset in 4.5 hours. To measure whether hashed n-gram features preserve the aspects of the data that are relevant to the target, we define KL reduction, a data metric that measures the proximity between the selected pretraining data and the target on some feature space. Across 8 data selection methods (including expert selection), KL reduction on hashed n-gram features highly correlates with average downstream accuracy (r=0.82). When selecting data for continued pretraining on a specific domain, DSIR performs comparably to expert curation across 8 target distributions. When pretraining general-domain models (target is Wikipedia and books), DSIR improves over random selection and heuristic filtering baselines by 2--2.5% on the GLUE benchmark.

title: Data Selection for Language Models via Importance Resampling

abstract: One-shot channel simulation is a fundamental data compression problem concerned with encoding a single sample from a target distribution $Q$ using a coding distribution $P$ using as few bits as possible on average. Algorithms that solve this problem find applications in neural data compression and differential privacy and can serve as a more efficient and natural alternative to quantization-based methods. Unfortunately, existing solutions are too slow or have limited applicability, preventing their widespread adaptation. In this paper, we conclusively solve one-shot channel simulation for one-dimensional problems where the target-proposal density ratio is unimodal by describing an algorithm with optimal runtime. We achieve this by constructing a rejection sampling procedure equivalent to greedily searching over the points of a Poisson process. Hence, we call our algorithm greedy Poisson rejection sampling (GPRS) and analyze the correctness and time complexity of several of its variants. Finally, we empirically verify our theorems, demonstrating that GPRS significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art method, A* coding.

paragraphs: One-shot channel simulation asks how to encode a single sample from a target distribution using a coding distribution while keeping the average message short. It has applications in neural compression and differential privacy. The paper addresses the computational obstacles that have made existing solutions too slow or too restricted for wider use.

The proposed algorithm, greedy Poisson rejection sampling, connects rejection sampling with a greedy search over points of a Poisson process. This connection provides the basis for several algorithm variants whose correctness and running time the authors analyze. The central optimal-runtime result applies to one-dimensional problems where the ratio of target density to proposal density is unimodal, meaning it has a single mode.

Experiments verify the theoretical results and show substantial performance improvements over A* coding, the comparison method identified in the abstract. The significance is a computationally optimal solution within the stated one-dimensional, unimodal-ratio setting. The paper pairs that guarantee with empirical evidence that the construction can outperform an existing channel-simulation algorithm in practice.
summary.tldr: Greedy Poisson rejection sampling achieves optimal runtime for one-dimensional channel simulation with a unimodal target-to-proposal density ratio.

title: Greedy Poisson Rejection Sampling

abstract: The problem of designing learners that provide guarantees that their predictions are provably correct is of increasing importance in machine learning. However, learning theoretic guarantees have only been considered in very specific settings. In this work, we consider the design and analysis of reliable learners in challenging test-time environments as encountered in modern machine learning problems: namely adversarial test-time attacks (in several variations) and natural distribution shifts. In this work, we provide a reliable learner with provably optimal guarantees in such settings. We discuss computationally feasible implementations of the learner and further show that our algorithm achieves strong positive performance guarantees on several natural examples: for example, linear separators under log-concave distributions or smooth boundary classifiers under smooth probability distributions.

paragraphs: This paper studies learners whose predictions come with provable correctness guarantees when test conditions are challenging. It considers several forms of adversarial test-time attack as well as natural distribution shifts. The motivation is that earlier learning-theoretic guarantees address only specific settings, leaving a need for reliability analyses that cover these changing test environments.

The authors develop a reliable learner and prove that its guarantees are optimal in the settings they consider. They also discuss computationally feasible implementations. Together, these contributions address both the strength of the correctness guarantees and how the proposed learner could be implemented, rather than treating reliability solely as an abstract existence question.

Positive performance guarantees are established for several structured examples, including linear separators under log-concave distributions and classifiers with smooth boundaries under smooth probability distributions. These examples make the theory concrete by connecting the learner's guarantees to specified classifier and distribution families. The result expands the theoretical treatment of reliable prediction under adversarial changes and natural shifts within the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a reliable learner with provably optimal guarantees for studied adversarial attacks and natural distribution shifts.

title: Reliable learning in challenging environments

abstract: We investigate the potential of learning visual representations using synthetic images generated by text-to-image models. This is a natural question in the light of the excellent performance of such models in generating high-quality images. We consider specifically the Stable Diffusion, one of the leading open source text-to-image models. We show that (1) when the generative model is properly configured, training self-supervised methods on synthetic images can match or beat the real image counterpart;(2) by treating the multiple images generated from the same text prompt as positives for each other, we develop a multi-positive contrastive learning method, which we call StableRep. With solely synthetic images, the representations learned by StableRep surpass the performance of representations learned by SimCLR and CLIP using the same set of text prompts and corresponding real images, on large scale datasets. When we further add language supervision, \name~trained with 20M synthetic images (10M captions) achieves better accuracy than CLIP trained with 50M real images (50M captions).
