paragraphs: People often find it easier to compare relative similarity than to assign an absolute similarity score. Yet different comparisons may reflect different attributes, such as shape or color. This paper studies triplet judgments in which the attribute behind each comparison is unknown, a situation that can arise when many people contribute judgments through crowdsourcing.

The proposed Multiview Triplet Embedding algorithm produces several low-dimensional maps, each corresponding to a hidden attribute. Multiple maps allow the method to represent different bases for comparison within the same collection of objects. The aim is to uncover the attributes reflected in the judgments without being told which attribute generated each triplet.

The method can help assess how many attributes contributed to the data and how difficult a distance-comparison task is. It can also identify objects that admit multiple interpretations relative to other objects. These uses make the embedding an instrument for examining the comparison process itself, as well as a representation of object similarity. The abstract presents these as capabilities of the method without claiming that every ambiguous judgment can be uniquely resolved.
summary.tldr: Multiview Triplet Embedding learns separate similarity maps for hidden attributes underlying unlabeled relative comparisons.

title: Multiview Triplet Embedding: Learning Attributes in Multiple Maps

abstract: Computational results demonstrate that posterior sampling for reinforcement learning (PSRL) dramatically outperforms existing algorithms driven by optimism, such as UCRL2. We provide insight into the extent of this performance boost and the phenomenon that drives it. We leverage this insight to establish an $\tilde{O}(H\sqrt{SAT})$ Bayesian regret bound for PSRL in finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes. This improves upon the best previous Bayesian regret bound of $\tilde{O}(H S \sqrt{AT})$ for any reinforcement learning algorithm. Our theoretical results are supported by extensive empirical evaluation.
originalAbstract: Computational results demonstrate that posterior sampling for reinforcement learning (PSRL) dramatically outperforms existing algorithms driven by optimism, such as UCRL2. We provide insight into the extent of this performance boost and the phenomenon that drives it. We leverage this insight to establish an $\tilde{O}(H\sqrt{SAT})$ Bayesian regret bound for PSRL in finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes. This improves upon the best previous Bayesian regret bound of $\tilde{O}(H S \sqrt{AT})$ for any reinforcement learning algorithm. Our theoretical results are supported by extensive empirical evaluation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why posterior sampling for reinforcement learning performs much better in computational results than existing optimism-driven algorithms such as UCRL2. Its goal is both to assess the size of this advantage and to understand the phenomenon responsible for it. This connects observed algorithm behavior with a theoretical account of learning performance.

Using that insight, the authors prove a Bayesian regret bound of order H√(SAT), up to logarithmic factors, for finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes. The previous best bound described in the abstract has order HS√(AT), also up to logarithmic factors. The improvement changes the dependence on S from linear to square-root while retaining the other displayed factors.

Extensive empirical evaluation supports the theoretical results. The contribution combines an improved Bayesian regret guarantee with evidence about the performance gap motivating the study. Its theoretical setting is specifically finite-horizon episodic decision processes, and the strong empirical comparison concerns the evaluated algorithms. Together, these results provide support for posterior sampling from both analysis and computation.
summary.tldr: The paper explains posterior sampling's empirical advantage and proves an improved Bayesian regret bound for finite-horizon episodic reinforcement learning.

title: Why is Posterior Sampling Better than Optimism for Reinforcement Learning?

abstract: Aerodynamic shape optimization has many industrial applications. Existing methods, however, are so computationally demanding that typical engineering practices are to either simply try a limited number of hand-designed shapes or restrict oneself to shapes that can be parameterized using only few degrees of freedom. In this work, we introduce a new way to optimize complex shapes fast and accurately. To this end, we train Geodesic Convolutional Neural Networks to emulate a fluidynamics simulator. The key to making this approach practical is remeshing the original shape using a poly-cube map, which makes it possible to perform the computations on GPUs instead of CPUs. The neural net is then used to formulate an objective function that is differentiable with respect to the shape parameters, which can then be optimized using a gradient-based technique. This outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 5 to 20% for standard problems and, even more importantly, our approach applies to cases that previous methods cannot handle.

paragraphs: Aerodynamic shape optimization can demand so much computation that engineers explore only a few hand-designed candidates or restrict shapes to a small number of adjustable parameters. This paper proposes a learned alternative that supports optimization of more complex shapes. The main idea is to train a Geodesic Convolutional Neural Network to emulate a fluid dynamics simulator.

A practical ingredient is remeshing the original shape using a poly-cube map. This representation makes the relevant computations suitable for GPUs instead of CPUs. The trained network then supplies an objective that is differentiable with respect to shape parameters, allowing a gradient-based method to determine how those parameters should change.

The approach connects simulation approximation directly to the optimization process: the learned model both evaluates shapes and enables gradients for improving them. The authors report improvements of 5–20% over state-of-the-art methods on standard problems. They also state that the approach handles cases previous methods cannot address, extending the range of shapes that can be optimized.
summary.tldr: A GPU-compatible neural surrogate for fluid simulation enables gradient-based optimization of complex aerodynamic shapes.

title: Geodesic Convolutional Shape Optimization

abstract: For reliable transmission across a noisy communication channel, classical results from information theory show that it is asymptotically optimal to separate out the source and channel coding processes. However, this decomposition can fall short in the finite bit-length regime, as it requires non-trivial tuning of hand-crafted codes and assumes infinite computational power for decoding. In this work, we propose to jointly learn the encoding and decoding processes using a new discrete variational autoencoder model. By adding noise into the latent codes to simulate the channel during training, we learn to both compress and error-correct given a fixed bit-length and computational budget. We obtain codes that are not only competitive against several separation schemes, but also learn useful robust representations of the data for downstream tasks such as classification. Finally, inference amortization yields an extremely fast neural decoder, almost an order of magnitude faster compared to standard decoding methods based on iterative belief propagation.

paragraphs: Communication systems need to compress information and protect it against transmission noise. Classical information theory supports separating these jobs in an asymptotic setting. This paper focuses on finite bit lengths and limited computation, where separate coding schemes can require substantial tuning and decoding can be costly.

The authors jointly learn encoding and decoding with a discrete variational autoencoder. During training, noise is added to the latent codes to simulate the communication channel. This exposes the model to transmission errors while it learns a representation, allowing compression and error correction to be shaped together under fixed bit-length and computational budgets.

The learned codes are competitive with several separation schemes and also provide robust representations useful for downstream classification. The neural decoder uses amortized inference, replacing repeated decoding work with a learned inference procedure. The authors report decoding almost an order of magnitude faster than standard iterative belief-propagation methods. The results support joint learning as a practical option when transmission length and decoding resources are constrained.
summary.tldr: A discrete variational autoencoder jointly learns compression and error correction under fixed budgets, producing competitive codes and fast neural decoding.

title: Neural Joint Source-Channel Coding

abstract: In this work, we study the Submodular Cost Submodular Cover problem, which is to minimize the submodular cost required to ensure that the submodular benefit function exceeds a given threshold. Existing approximation ratios for the greedy algorithm assume a value oracle to the benefit function. However, access to a value oracle is not a realistic assumption for many applications of this problem, where the benefit function is difficult to compute. We present two incomparable approximation ratios for this problem with an approximate value oracle and demonstrate that the ratios take on empirically relevant values through a case study with the Influence Threshold problem in online social networks.
originalAbstract: In this work, we study the Submodular Cost Submodular Cover problem, which is to minimize the submodular cost required to ensure that the submodular benefit function exceeds a given threshold. Existing approximation ratios for the greedy algorithm assume a value oracle to the benefit function. However, access to a value oracle is not a realistic assumption for many applications of this problem, where the benefit function is difficult to compute. We present two incomparable approximation ratios for this problem with an approximate value oracle and demonstrate that the ratios take on empirically relevant values through a case study with the Influence Threshold problem in online social networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies a selection problem in which both cost and benefit are submodular set functions. The objective is to obtain benefit above a specified threshold while minimizing cost. Because these quantities depend on the selected collection, evaluating a candidate solution requires access to the benefit function.

Existing approximation guarantees for the greedy algorithm assume an exact value oracle: a way to obtain the benefit of a set precisely. The authors focus on applications where that assumption is unrealistic because benefit is difficult to compute. They derive two approximation ratios for the setting where only approximate benefit evaluations are available, bringing evaluation uncertainty into the performance analysis.

The two ratios are incomparable, meaning neither provides the stronger guarantee in every case. A case study on the Influence Threshold problem in online social networks shows that the ratios can take empirically relevant values. The contribution therefore extends the theoretical treatment of the problem to imperfect benefit estimates and demonstrates the relevance of those bounds in a concrete application.
summary.tldr: Two incomparable approximation guarantees address submodular covering when benefit values are available only approximately.

title: Submodular Cost Submodular Cover with an Approximate Oracle

abstract: Most existing notions of algorithmic fairness are one-shot: they ensure some form of allocative equality at the time of decision making, but do not account for the adverse impact of the algorithmic decisions today on the long-term welfare and prosperity of certain segments of the population. We take a broader perspective on algorithmic fairness. We propose an effort-based measure of fairness and present a data-driven framework for characterizing the long-term impact of algorithmic policies on reshaping the underlying population. Motivated by the psychological literature on social learning and the economic literature on equality of opportunity, we propose a micro-scale model of how individuals may respond to decision-making algorithms. We employ existing measures of segregation from sociology and economics to quantify the resulting macro- scale population-level change. Importantly, we observe that different models may shift the group- conditional distribution of qualifications in different directions. Our findings raise a number of important questions regarding the formalization of fairness for decision-making models.

paragraphs: A decision system can satisfy an equality criterion at the moment it allocates opportunities while still influencing how a population changes afterward. This paper studies that longer-term perspective on fairness. It asks how people’s responses to algorithmic decisions can reshape qualifications and group differences over time.

The authors propose an effort-based fairness measure and a data-driven framework for analyzing population change. A model of individual responses draws on social learning and equality of opportunity. Existing segregation measures from sociology and economics then quantify the population-level consequences. This connects a description of individual adaptation to a way of assessing changes across groups.

The findings indicate that different decision-making models may move group-conditional qualification distributions in different directions. Thus, an assessment based only on current allocations can miss consequences produced through later responses. The framework makes those modeled consequences part of the fairness discussion, while the paper’s conclusion raises questions about how fairness should be formalized when policies help change the populations they evaluate.
summary.tldr: An effort-based fairness framework models how responses to algorithmic decisions can reshape group qualifications and population segregation over time.

title: On the Long-term Impact of Algorithmic Decision Policies: Effort Unfairness and Feature Segregation through Social Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning in multi-agent scenarios is important for real-world applications but presents challenges beyond those seen in single-agent settings. We present an actor-critic algorithm that trains decentralized policies in multi-agent settings, using centrally computed critics that share an attention mechanism which selects relevant information for each agent at every timestep. This attention mechanism enables more effective and scalable learning in complex multi-agent environments, when compared to recent approaches. Our approach is applicable not only to cooperative settings with shared rewards, but also individualized reward settings, including adversarial settings, as well as settings that do not provide global states, and it makes no assumptions about the action spaces of the agents. As such, it is flexible enough to be applied to most multi-agent learning problems.

We present an actor-critic algorithm that trains decentralized policies in multi-agent settings, using centrally computed critics that share an attention mechanism which selects relevant information for each agent at every timestep. This attention mechanism enables more effective and scalable learning in complex multi-agent environments, when compared to recent approaches. Our approach is applicable not only to cooperative settings with shared rewards, but also individualized reward settings, including adversarial settings, as well as settings that do not provide global states, and it makes no assumptions about the action spaces of the agents. paragraphs: When several agents learn together, the information relevant to one agent can depend on what the others are doing. This paper introduces an actor-critic algorithm that trains decentralized policies with centrally computed critics. The policies govern agents’ behavior, while the critics provide evaluations used during learning.

The critics share an attention mechanism that selects relevant information separately for each agent at every timestep. This lets the training process adapt its focus as interactions change. The authors report that this selective use of information supports more effective and scalable learning in complex multi-agent environments compared with recent approaches.

The framework accommodates several different relationships between agents: they may share rewards, receive individual rewards, or operate adversarially. It also applies when no global state is supplied and imposes no assumptions on agents’ action spaces. These properties broaden its applicability beyond a single cooperative setup. The main contribution is a flexible way to coordinate training information while still learning decentralized policies.
summary.tldr: Attention-based centralized critics help train decentralized agents by selecting relevant information for each agent at each timestep.

title: Actor-Attention-Critic for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Policy gradient methods ignore the potential value of adjusting environment variables: unobservable state features that are randomly determined by the environment in a physical setting, but are controllable in a simulator. This can lead to slow learning, or convergence to suboptimal policies, if the environment variable has a large impact on the transition dynamics. In this paper, we present fingerprint policy optimisation (FPO), which finds a policy that is optimal in expectation across the distribution of environment variables. The central idea is to use Bayesian optimisation (BO) to actively select the distribution of the environment variable that maximises the improvement generated by each iteration of the policy gradient method. To make this BO practical, we contribute two easy-to-compute low-dimensional fingerprints of the current policy. Our experiments show that FPO can efficiently learn policies that are robust to significant rare events, which are unlikely to be observable under random sampling, but are key to learning good policies.

paragraphs: Fingerprint policy optimisation uses control over a simulator's environment variables to improve policy learning. These variables represent unobserved state features that are randomly determined in a physical setting but can be adjusted in simulation. When they strongly affect dynamics, ordinary sampling can lead to slow learning or suboptimal policies.

The method uses Bayesian optimisation to choose the distribution of an environment variable that maximizes the improvement produced by each policy-gradient iteration. To make that selection practical, the authors introduce two inexpensive, low-dimensional descriptions, or fingerprints, of the current policy. These fingerprints support adapting the training distribution as the policy changes.

The overall objective is a policy that is optimal in expectation across the environment-variable distribution. Experiments show efficient learning of policies robust to significant rare events that random sampling is unlikely to reveal. The result highlights the usefulness of actively choosing simulated training conditions: rare conditions can matter greatly for learning a good policy even when they seldom appear through ordinary sampling.
summary.tldr: Fingerprint policy optimisation actively selects simulated environment distributions to improve policy learning and robustness to important rare events.

title: Fingerprint Policy Optimisation for Robust Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep networks have achieved impressive performance in various domains, but their applications are largely limited by the prohibitive computational overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, namely collaborative channel pruning (CCP), to reduce the computational overhead with negligible performance degradation. The joint impact of pruned/preserved channels on the loss function is quantitatively analyzed, and such interchannel dependency is exploited to determine which channels to be pruned. The channel selection problem is then reformulated as a constrained 0-1 quadratic optimization problem, and the Hessian matrix, which is essential in constructing the above optimization, can be efficiently approximated. Empirical evaluation on two benchmark data sets indicates that our proposed CCP algorithm achieves higher classification accuracy with similar computational complexity than other stateof-the-art channel pruning algorithms

paragraphs: Collaborative channel pruning addresses the computational cost of deep networks by deciding which channels to remove together. The central concern is that a channel's usefulness depends on other channels. A pruning decision therefore needs to account for the combined effect of what is removed and what remains, rather than treating every channel as an independent choice.

The method quantitatively analyzes how these joint decisions affect the loss function. It expresses channel selection as a constrained binary quadratic optimization problem: each channel receives a keep-or-remove decision, and the objective captures interactions between decisions. Constructing this problem requires a Hessian matrix, for which the authors provide an efficient approximation.

Experiments on two benchmark datasets report higher classification accuracy than other leading channel-pruning methods at similar computational complexity. The stated outcome supports using interchannel dependencies to reduce overhead with negligible performance degradation. The contribution is both a selection criterion based on joint effects and a practical way to obtain the curvature information that criterion needs.
summary.tldr: Collaborative channel pruning accounts for interactions among channels to reduce computation while preserving classification accuracy.

title: Collaborative Channel Pruning for Deep Networks

abstract: In recommender systems, usually the ratings of a user to most items are missing and a critical problem is that the missing ratings are often missing not at random (MNAR) in reality. It is widely acknowledged that MNAR ratings make it difficult to accurately predict the ratings and unbiasedly estimate the performance of rating prediction. Recent approaches use imputed errors to recover the prediction errors for missing ratings, or weight observed ratings with the propensities of being observed. These approaches can still be severely biased in performance estimation or suffer from the variance of the propensities. To overcome these limitations, we first propose an estimator that integrates the imputed errors and propensities in a doubly robust way to obtain unbiased performance estimation and alleviate the effect of the propensity variance. To achieve good performance guarantees, based on this estimator, we propose joint learning of rating prediction and error imputation, which outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches on four real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Recommendation data usually contain only a small portion of all possible user ratings. The missing entries often follow a selective pattern rather than disappearing at random. This makes both rating prediction and performance evaluation difficult: observed ratings may give a distorted picture of how a recommender would perform across all user–item pairs.

The paper combines two ways of addressing this distortion. One estimates prediction errors for missing ratings; the other weights observed ratings according to their chances of being observed. Used separately, these approaches can suffer from substantial evaluation bias or variability associated with those observation probabilities. The proposed estimator integrates both sources of information in a doubly robust construction.

The estimator is designed to provide unbiased performance estimation while alleviating the effect of propensity variance. The authors then use it to jointly learn rating predictions and error imputations, connecting the evaluation correction to model training. Their method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches on four real-world datasets, supporting the practical value of learning these components together.
summary.tldr: A doubly robust estimator combines missing-error estimates with observation propensities to improve recommendation learning and performance evaluation.

title: Doubly Robust Joint Learning for Recommendation on Data Missing Not at Random

abstract: We consider an agent that is assigned with a temporal logic task in an environment whose semantic representation is only partially known. We represent the semantics of the environment with a set of state properties, called \emph{atomic propositions} over which, the agent holds a probabilistic belief and updates it as new sensory measurements arrive. The goal is to design a joint perception and planning strategy for the agent that realizes the task with high probability. We develop a planning strategy that takes the semantic uncertainties into account and by doing so provides probabilistic guarantees on the task success. Furthermore, as new data arrive, the belief over the atomic propositions evolves and, subsequently, the planning strategy adapts accordingly. We evaluate the proposed method on various finite-horizon tasks in planar navigation settings where the empirical results show that the proposed method provides reliable task performance that also improves as the knowledge about the environment enhances.

paragraphs: An agent may need to complete a formally specified task before it fully understands what different parts of its environment mean. This paper studies tasks expressed in temporal logic when relevant state properties are only partially known. The agent represents uncertainty about those properties, called atomic propositions, through probabilistic beliefs.

The proposed strategy combines perception and planning so that decisions account for semantic uncertainty. As new sensory measurements arrive, the agent updates its beliefs and adapts its plan accordingly. The planning method also provides probabilistic guarantees on task success, connecting the uncertainty representation to the likelihood of satisfying the assigned task.

The authors evaluate the approach on finite-horizon tasks in planar navigation environments. Their empirical results show reliable task performance and improvement as knowledge of the environment increases. The finding supports planning that explicitly tracks uncertain meaning: additional observations can change both what the agent believes about its surroundings and how it acts to complete the task.
summary.tldr: The method adapts perception and planning to uncertain environmental properties, providing probabilistic task guarantees and improved navigation performance as knowledge grows.

title: Task-Oriented Active Perception and Planning in Environments with Partially Known Semantics

abstract: Human observers can learn to recognize new categories of images from a handful of examples, yet doing so with artificial ones remains an open challenge. We hypothesize that data-efficient recognition is enabled by representations which make the variability in natural signals more predictable. We therefore revisit and improve Contrastive Predictive Coding, an unsupervised objective for learning such representations. This new implementation produces features which support state-of-the-art linear classification accuracy on the ImageNet dataset. When used as input for non-linear classification with deep neural networks, this representation allows us to use 2-5x less labels than classifiers trained directly on image pixels. Finally, this unsupervised representation substantially improves transfer learning to object detection on the PASCAL VOC dataset, surpassing fully supervised pre-trained ImageNet classifiers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how unsupervised representation learning can reduce the number of labels needed for image recognition. Its motivating hypothesis is that recognition becomes more data-efficient when representations make variation in natural signals easier to predict. The authors revisit Contrastive Predictive Coding and improve its implementation to learn features guided by this objective.

The learned features support state-of-the-art linear classification accuracy on ImageNet in the reported evaluation. The authors also feed these representations into deep nonlinear classifiers. In that setting, classifiers need two to five times fewer labels than classifiers trained directly from image pixels, showing that the representation remains useful beyond a simple linear prediction stage.

The evaluation extends to object detection on PASCAL VOC, where the unsupervised representation substantially improves transfer and surpasses fully supervised ImageNet-pretrained classifiers. Together, the results support the practical value of learning predictive structure before training a labeled recognition model. They provide evidence for the motivating hypothesis through classification efficiency and transfer performance, without establishing it as a universal explanation of recognition.
summary.tldr: Improved Contrastive Predictive Coding learns image features that reduce label requirements and improve transfer to object detection in the reported evaluations.

title: Data-Efficient Image Recognition with Contrastive Predictive Coding

abstract: Reinforcement learning is typically concerned with learning control policies tailored to a particular agent. We investigate whether there exists a single global policy that can generalize to control a wide variety of agent morphologies – ones in which even dimensionality of state and action spaces changes. We propose to express this global policy as a collection of identical modular neural networks, dubbed as Shared Modular Policies (SMP), that correspond to each of the agent’s actuators. Every module is only responsible for controlling its corresponding actuator and receives information from only its local sensors. In addition, messages are passed between modules, propagating information between distant modules. We show that a single modular policy can successfully generate locomotion behaviors for several planar agents with different skeletal structures such as monopod hoppers, quadrupeds, bipeds, and generalize to variants not seen during training – a process that would normally require training and manual hyperparameter tuning for each morphology. We observe that a wide variety of drastically diverse locomotion styles across morphologies as well as centralized coordination emerges via message passing between decentralized modules purely from the reinforcement learning objective. Videos and code at https://huangwl18.github.io/modular-rl/

paragraphs: A control policy is usually trained for one agent’s body, with a particular number of sensors and actuators. This paper investigates whether one policy can control agents with different skeletal structures, even when their state and action spaces have different dimensions. Its solution expresses control through repeated local modules.

Shared Modular Policies assign an identical neural-network module to each actuator. Each module controls its own actuator using local sensory information, while messages exchanged among modules carry information across the body. This arrangement combines local control with a communication mechanism capable of supporting coordination between distant parts of an agent.

The authors demonstrate locomotion for several planar morphologies, including monopod hoppers, quadrupeds, and bipeds, and transfer to variants absent from training. They observe diverse locomotion styles and centralized coordination emerging through messages between decentralized modules, driven solely by the reinforcement-learning objective. The results show that one shared modular policy can handle the evaluated range of bodies without separately training and manually tuning a policy for each morphology.
summary.tldr: Identical actuator-level controllers communicate to form one shared policy that controls multiple body shapes and generalizes to unseen variants.

title: One Policy to Control Them All: Shared Modular Policies for Agent-Agnostic Control

abstract: The remarkable recent advances in object-centric generative world models raise a few questions. First, while many of the recent achievements are indispensable for making a general and versatile world model, it is quite unclear how these ingredients can be integrated into a unified framework. Second, despite using generative objectives, abilities for object detection and tracking are mainly investigated, leaving the crucial ability of temporal imagination largely under question. Third, a few key abilities for more faithful temporal imagination such as multimodal uncertainty and situation-awareness are missing. In this paper, we introduce Generative Structured World Models (G-SWM). The G-SWM achieves the versatile world modeling not only by unifying the key properties of previous models in a principled framework but also by achieving two crucial new abilities, multimodal uncertainty and situation-awareness. Our thorough investigation on the temporal generation ability in comparison to the previous models demonstrates that G-SWM achieves the versatility with the best or comparable performance for all experiment settings including a few complex settings that have not been tested before. https://sites.google.com/view/gswm

paragraphs: Object-centric world models represent a scene in terms of its constituent objects. The paper argues that much evaluation has emphasized detecting and tracking those objects, leaving a different capability less understood: generating plausible developments over time. It also asks how useful ingredients from earlier models can be combined into a unified framework.

Generative Structured World Models, or G-SWM, bring those ingredients together and add two capabilities emphasized by the authors: multimodal uncertainty and situation-awareness. Multimodal uncertainty allows temporal imagination to represent distinct possible outcomes. Situation-awareness makes the surrounding circumstances part of that capability. These properties matter when generating a scene’s future requires more than continuing a single, context-independent trajectory.

The authors investigate temporal generation directly and compare G-SWM with previous models across multiple experimental settings. They report best or comparable performance throughout, including some complex settings that had not previously been tested. The finding supports the model’s versatility across those evaluations while making temporal imagination itself a central target for assessing object-centric generative models.
summary.tldr: G-SWM combines object-centric modeling capabilities with multimodal uncertainty and situation-awareness to improve the generation of possible futures.

title: Improving Generative Imagination in Object-Centric World Models

abstract: Recent advances in maximizing mutual information (MI) between the source and target have demonstrated its effectiveness in text generation. However, previous works paid little attention to modeling the backward network of MI (i.e., dependency from the target to the source), which is crucial to the tightness of the variational information maximization lower bound. In this paper, we propose Adversarial Mutual Information (AMI): a text generation framework which is formed as a novel saddle point (min-max) optimization aiming to identify joint interactions between the source and target. Within this framework, the forward and backward networks are able to iteratively promote or demote each other’s generated instances by comparing the real and synthetic data distributions. We also develop a latent noise sampling strategy that leverages random variations at the high-level semantic space to enhance the long term dependency in the generation process. Extensive experiments based on different text generation tasks demonstrate that the proposed AMI framework can significantly outperform several strong baselines, and we also show that AMI has potential to lead to a tighter lower bound of maximum mutual information for the variational information maximization problem.

In this paper, we propose Adversarial Mutual Information (AMI): a text generation framework which is formed as a novel saddle point (min-max) optimization aiming to identify joint interactions between the source and target. Within this framework, the forward and backward networks are able to iteratively promote or demote each other’s generated instances by comparing the real and synthetic data distributions. paragraphs: Mutual information measures dependence between source text and generated target text. Methods that maximize it rely partly on a backward network, which models the source given the target. This paper argues that this backward direction deserves more attention because its quality affects how tightly the training objective bounds the mutual information being sought.

Adversarial Mutual Information organizes training as a min-max problem involving both forward and backward networks. By comparing real and generated data distributions, these networks can iteratively favor or discourage instances produced by each other. This makes their interaction part of the learning mechanism. The paper also introduces sampling of latent noise in a high-level semantic space to strengthen long-range dependencies during generation.

Across different text generation tasks, experiments show that the framework can significantly outperform several strong baselines. The authors also present evidence that it has the potential to tighten the variational lower bound used for mutual information maximization. That latter finding is a possibility supported by the work, rather than a guarantee that every trained model obtains a tighter bound.
summary.tldr: Adversarial training of forward and backward text models improves generation in experiments and may tighten a mutual-information lower bound.

title: Adversarial Mutual Information for Text Generation

abstract: We evaluate a wide range of ImageNet models with five trained human labelers. In our year-long experiment, trained humans first annotated 40,000 images from the ImageNet and ImageNetV2 test sets with multi-class labels to enable a semantically coherent evaluation. Then we measured the classification accuracy of the five trained humans on the full task with 1,000 classes. Only the latest models from 2020 are on par with our best human labeler, and human accuracy on the 590 object classes is still 4% and 10% higher than the best model on ImageNet and ImageNetV2, respectively. Moreover, humans achieve the same accuracy on ImageNet and ImageNetV2, while all models see a consistent accuracy drop. Overall, our results show that there is still substantial room for improvement on ImageNet and direct accuracy comparisons between humans and machines may overstate machine performance.

paragraphs: This paper revisits what it means for an image classifier to match human accuracy on ImageNet. Five trained human labelers are compared with a wide range of models. To make the evaluation semantically coherent, humans first annotate 40,000 images from ImageNet and ImageNetV2 with multiple class labels. The study then measures human performance on the full 1,000-class task.

Only the latest models from 2020 match the best human labeler in this evaluation. Looking specifically at 590 object classes reveals a larger remaining gap: human accuracy is reported as 4% higher on ImageNet and 10% higher on ImageNetV2 than the best model. Thus, the overall comparison can conceal meaningful differences within the task.

The comparison across datasets adds another distinction. Humans achieve the same accuracy on ImageNet and ImageNetV2, whereas every evaluated model experiences an accuracy drop. Together, these findings show substantial remaining room for improvement and support the authors’ warning that direct headline comparisons between human and machine accuracy may overstate machine performance.
summary.tldr: A trained-human evaluation finds remaining ImageNet performance gaps and greater human consistency across ImageNet and ImageNetV2.

title: Evaluating Machine Accuracy on ImageNet

abstract: Many popular reinforcement learning problems (e.g., navigation in a maze, some Atari games, mountain car) are instances of the episodic setting under its stochastic shortest path (SSP) formulation, where an agent has to achieve a goal state while minimizing the cumulative cost. Despite the popularity of this setting, the exploration-exploitation dilemma has been sparsely studied in general SSP problems, with most of the theoretical literature focusing on different problems (i.e., fixed-horizon and infinite-horizon) or making the restrictive loop-free SSP assumption (i.e., no state can be visited twice during an episode). In this paper, we study the general SSP problem with no assumption on its dynamics (some policies may actually never reach the goal). We introduce UC-SSP, the first no-regret algorithm in this setting, and prove a regret bound scaling as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}( D S \sqrt{ A D K})$ after $K$ episodes for any unknown SSP with $S$ states, $A$ actions, positive costs and SSP-diameter $D$, defined as the smallest expected hitting time from any starting state to the goal. We achieve this result by crafting a novel stopping rule, such that UC-SSP may interrupt the current policy if it is taking too long to achieve the goal and switch to alternative policies that are designed to rapidly terminate the episode.

paragraphs: In stochastic shortest-path reinforcement learning, an agent must reach a goal while minimizing accumulated cost. Episodes need not have a predetermined length, and a poor policy may never reach the goal. This makes exploration difficult: gathering information can leave the agent following an unproductive policy indefinitely.

The paper introduces UC-SSP for this general setting without requiring loop-free dynamics. Its key mechanism is a stopping rule that can interrupt a policy when reaching the goal takes too long. The algorithm then switches to alternative policies designed to bring the episode to an end quickly.

For unknown problems with positive costs and SSP-diameter D, the authors prove a regret bound scaling as D times S times the square root of A times D times K, up to logarithmic factors. Here S counts states, A actions, and K episodes; D describes the smallest expected goal-reaching time from any starting state. The bound establishes no-regret learning under these conditions while allowing repeated state visits and policies that fail to terminate.
summary.tldr: UC-SSP achieves a no-regret guarantee for positive-cost stochastic shortest-path problems by interrupting policies that take too long to reach the goal.

title: No-Regret Exploration in Goal-Oriented Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Optimally solving decentralized partially observable Markov decision processes under either full or no information sharing received significant attention in recent years. However, little is known about how partial information sharing affects existing theory and algorithms. This paper addresses this question for a team of two agents, with one-sided information sharing—\ie both agents have imperfect information about the state of the world, but only one has access to what the other sees and does. From the perspective of a central planner, we show that the original problem can be reformulated into an equivalent information-state Markov decision process and solved as such. Besides, we prove that the optimal value function exhibits a specific form of uniform continuity. We also present a heuristic search algorithm utilizing this property and providing the first results for this family of problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies cooperative decision-making by two agents who both have incomplete information about the world. Their information is asymmetric: one agent can access the other's observations and actions, while the reverse does not hold. This sits between the more commonly studied cases of full sharing and no sharing.

From a central planner's perspective, the authors reformulate the decentralized problem as an equivalent information-state Markov decision process. The equivalence allows the original planning task to be solved through that representation. The contribution depends on the specified two-agent, one-sided-sharing structure, which gives the planner a way to organize the relevant information.

The authors also prove a particular form of uniform continuity for the optimal value function. They use that regularity property in a heuristic search algorithm and present initial results for this problem family. The work therefore connects the structure of partial information sharing to both a mathematical reformulation and a search procedure, showing how the information pattern can guide the design of an optimal-planning approach.
summary.tldr: Two-agent planning with one-sided information sharing can be reformulated as an equivalent information-state MDP and addressed with a continuity-guided search algorithm.

title: Optimally Solving Two-Agent Decentralized POMDPs Under One-Sided Information Sharing

abstract: While successful in many fields, deep neural networks (DNNs) still suffer from some open problems such as bad local minima and unsatisfactory generalization performance. In this work, we propose a novel architecture called Maximum-and-Concatenation Networks (MCN) to try eliminating bad local minima and improving generalization ability as well. Remarkably, we prove that MCN has a very nice property; that is, every local minimum of an (l+1)-layer MCN can be better than, at least as good as, the global minima of the network consisting of its first l layers. In other words, by increasing the network depth, MCN can autonomously improve its local minima’s goodness, what is more, it is easy to plug MCN into an existing deep model to make it also have this property. Finally, under mild conditions, we show that MCN can approximate certain continuous function arbitrarily well with high efficiency; that is, the covering number of MCN is much smaller than most existing DNNs such as deep ReLU. Based on this, we further provide a tight generalization bound to guarantee the inference ability of MCN when dealing with testing samples.

paragraphs: Maximum-and-Concatenation Networks, or MCNs, are designed to improve the quality of local minima and support generalization. The paper focuses on an architectural property relating a deeper network to the network formed by its initial layers. This makes depth part of the theoretical argument about optimization quality.

The authors prove that every local minimum of an MCN with one additional layer is at least as good as the global minima of the network consisting of its preceding layers. This is a comparison across depths, rather than a statement that all local minima of a fixed network are globally optimal. They also describe incorporating MCN into existing deep models to give them this property.

Under mild conditions, MCNs can approximate certain continuous functions arbitrarily well with high efficiency. The authors connect this to a covering number smaller than that of many existing networks, including deep ReLU models, and derive a tight generalization bound. The contribution links an architectural design to guarantees about optimization, approximation, and prediction on unseen samples.
summary.tldr: MCNs guarantee that local minima after adding a layer are no worse than the preceding network's global minima, alongside approximation and generalization results.

title: Maximum-and-Concatenation Networks

abstract: Domain adaptation aims to correct the classifiers when faced with distribution shift between source (training) and target (test) domains. State-of-the-art domain adaptation methods make use of deep networks to extract domain-invariant representations. However, existing methods assume that all the instances in the source domain are correctly labeled; while in reality, it is unsurprising that we may obtain a source domain with noisy labels. In this paper, we are the first to comprehensively investigate how label noise could adversely affect existing domain adaptation methods in various scenarios. Further, we theoretically prove that there exists a method that can essentially reduce the side-effect of noisy source labels in domain adaptation. Specifically, focusing on the generalized target shift scenario, where both label distribution $P_Y$ and the class-conditional distribution $P_{X|Y}$ can change, we discover that the denoising Conditional Invariant Component (DCIC) framework can provably ensures (1) extracting invariant representations given examples with noisy labels in the source domain and unlabeled examples in the target domain and (2) estimating the label distribution in the target domain with no bias. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.
originalAbstract: Domain adaptation aims to correct the classifiers when faced with distribution shift between source (training) and target (test) domains. State-of-the-art domain adaptation methods make use of deep networks to extract domain-invariant representations. However, existing methods assume that all the instances in the source domain are correctly labeled; while in reality, it is unsurprising that we may obtain a source domain with noisy labels. In this paper, we are the first to comprehensively investigate how label noise could adversely affect existing domain adaptation methods in various scenarios. Further, we theoretically prove that there exists a method that can essentially reduce the side-effect of noisy source labels in domain adaptation. Specifically, focusing on the generalized target shift scenario, where both label distribution $P_Y$ and the class-conditional distribution $P_{X|Y}$ can change, we discover that the denoising Conditional Invariant Component (DCIC) framework can provably ensures (1) extracting invariant representations given examples with noisy labels in the source domain and unlabeled examples in the target domain and (2) estimating the label distribution in the target domain with no bias. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation adjusts a classifier when its training and test data follow different distributions. Methods that learn domain-invariant representations commonly assume the source labels are correct. This paper investigates what happens when that assumption fails, examining how noisy source labels can harm adaptation methods across different scenarios.

The proposed denoising Conditional Invariant Component framework, or DCIC, focuses on generalized target shift. In this setting, both class frequencies and the distribution of inputs within each class may change between domains. The framework uses noisy labeled source examples together with unlabeled target examples, addressing label corruption and distribution change within the same adaptation problem.

The authors establish theoretical guarantees for extracting invariant representations and estimating target-domain class frequencies without bias in the setting they analyze. They also prove the existence of a method that can substantially reduce the adverse effect of noisy source labels. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support DCIC’s effectiveness, connecting the theoretical treatment of label noise to observed adaptation improvements.
summary.tldr: DCIC addresses noisy source labels under generalized target shift, with guarantees for invariant representations and unbiased target class-frequency estimation.

title: Label-Noise Robust Domain Adaptation

abstract: Multi-agent evaluation aims at the assessment of an agent’s strategy on the basis of interaction with others. Typically, existing methods such as $\alpha$-rank and its approximation still require to exhaustively compare all pairs of joint strategies for an accurate ranking, which in practice is computationally expensive. In this paper, we aim to reduce the number of pairwise comparisons in recovering a satisfying ranking for $n$ strategies in two-player meta-games, by exploring the fact that agents with similar skills may achieve similar payoffs against others. Two situations are considered: the first one is when we can obtain the true payoffs; the other one is when we can only access noisy payoff. Based on these formulations, we leverage low-rank matrix completion and design two novel algorithms for noise-free and noisy evaluations respectively. For both of these settings, we theorize that $O(nr \log n)$ ($n$ is the number of agents and $r$ is the rank of the payoff matrix) payoff entries are required to achieve sufficiently well strategy evaluation performance. Empirical results on evaluating the strategies in three synthetic games and twelve real world games demonstrate that strategy evaluation from a few entries can lead to comparable performance to algorithms with full knowledge of the payoff matrix.

summary.tldr: Low-rank payoff matrix completion enables alpha-rank-style strategy evaluation from a limited set of exact or noisy comparisons.

title: Estimating $α$-Rank from A Few Entries with Low Rank Matrix Completion

abstract: We introduce Deep Adaptive Design (DAD), a method for amortizing the cost of adaptive Bayesian experimental design that allows experiments to be run in real-time. Traditional sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design approaches require substantial computation at each stage of the experiment. This makes them unsuitable for most real-world applications, where decisions must typically be made quickly. DAD addresses this restriction by learning an amortized design network upfront and then using this to rapidly run (multiple) adaptive experiments at deployment time. This network represents a design policy which takes as input the data from previous steps, and outputs the next design using a single forward pass; these design decisions can be made in milliseconds during the live experiment. To train the network, we introduce contrastive information bounds that are suitable objectives for the sequential setting, and propose a customized network architecture that exploits key symmetries. We demonstrate that DAD successfully amortizes the process of experimental design, outperforming alternative strategies on a number of problems.

Bayesian approaches can make this process computationally demanding because they perform substantial optimization at each stage. Deep Adaptive Design addresses the resulting timing problem by moving much of that computation into training performed before the live experiment.

This allows decisions to be made in milliseconds during deployment and lets the trained network support multiple adaptive experiments. Training uses newly introduced contrastive information bounds suited to sequential decisions, together with an architecture that exploits relevant symmetries.

The experiments show that this upfront learning successfully amortizes the design process and outperforms alternative strategies on several problems. The practical significance is that experiment-specific adaptation remains possible during deployment without repeating the original expensive design computation at every step. The learned policy provides the connection between prior computation and rapid responses to newly observed data.
summary.tldr: Deep Adaptive Design trains experimental-design policies upfront so that adaptive decisions can be made in milliseconds during live experiments.

title: Deep Adaptive Design: Amortizing Sequential Bayesian Experimental Design

abstract: Methods that infer causal dependence from observational data are central to many areas of science, including medicine, economics, and the social sciences. A variety of theoretical properties of these methods have been proven, but empirical evaluation remains a challenge, largely due to the lack of observational data sets for which treatment effect is known. We describe and analyze observational sampling from randomized controlled trials (OSRCT), a method for evaluating causal inference methods using data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs). This method can be used to create constructed observational data sets with corresponding unbiased estimates of treatment effect, substantially increasing the number of data sets available for evaluating causal inference methods. We show that, in expectation, OSRCT creates data sets that are equivalent to those produced by randomly sampling from empirical data sets in which all potential outcomes are available. We then perform a large-scale evaluation of seven causal inference methods over 37 data sets, drawn from RCTs, as well as simulators, real-world computational systems, and observational data sets augmented with a synthetic response variable. We find notable performance differences when comparing across data from different sources, demonstrating the importance of using data from a variety of sources when evaluating any causal inference method.

paragraphs: Evaluating causal inference methods is difficult because observational datasets rarely come with known treatment effects. Without a trustworthy reference, it is hard to judge whether a method has recovered a causal relationship accurately. This paper studies observational sampling from randomized controlled trials, or OSRCT, as a way to construct useful evaluation datasets.

OSRCT creates observational datasets from trial data while retaining corresponding unbiased estimates of treatment effects. The authors show that, in expectation, the constructed datasets are equivalent to those obtained by random sampling from empirical datasets containing all potential outcomes. This supplies a theoretical connection between available experimental data and a richer evaluation setting that would otherwise be difficult to obtain.

The empirical study compares seven causal inference methods across 37 datasets from trials, simulators, real computational systems, and observational data with synthetic responses. Performance differs noticeably across these sources. Those differences support evaluating causal methods on varied kinds of data: conclusions drawn from one source may not reflect how methods compare on another.
summary.tldr: Sampling observational datasets from randomized trials expands causal inference evaluation, and comparisons across data sources reveal consequential performance differences.

title: How and Why to Use Experimental Data to Evaluate Methods for Observational Causal Inference

abstract: Back-propagation through time (BPTT) has been widely used for training Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). BPTT updates RNN parameters on an instance by back-propagating the error in time over the entire sequence length, and as a result, leads to poor trainability due to the well-known gradient explosion/decay phenomena. While a number of prior works have proposed to mitigate vanishing/explosion effect through careful RNN architecture design, these RNN variants still train with BPTT. We propose a novel forward-propagation algorithm, FPTT, where at each time, for an instance, we update RNN parameters by optimizing an instantaneous risk function. Our proposed risk is a regularization penalty at time $t$ that evolves dynamically based on previously observed losses, and allows for RNN parameter updates to converge to a stationary solution of the empirical RNN objective. We consider both sequence-to-sequence as well as terminal loss problems. Empirically FPTT outperforms BPTT on a number of well-known benchmark tasks, thus enabling architectures like LSTMs to solve long range dependencies problems.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks are commonly trained by propagating errors backward through a sequence. Over long sequences, gradients can grow excessively or shrink, making learning difficult. This paper changes the training procedure itself through forward propagation through time, or FPTT, rather than addressing the problem only through network architecture.

FPTT updates network parameters at each time step by optimizing an instantaneous risk function. Its regularization penalty evolves using losses observed earlier in the sequence, allowing earlier learning signals to affect the current update. The proposed construction allows parameter updates to converge to a stationary solution of the empirical recurrent-network objective.

The authors consider both sequence-to-sequence problems and problems where loss is supplied at the end. Experiments show FPTT outperforming back-propagation through time on several established benchmarks, including enabling LSTM architectures to handle long-range dependencies. The theoretical destination is a stationary solution, rather than a claimed global optimum, while the benchmark results provide empirical evidence for the training procedure's usefulness.
summary.tldr: FPTT trains recurrent networks through sequential updates with a dynamic regularizer, supporting stationary convergence and improved benchmark performance.

title: Training Recurrent Neural Networks via Forward Propagation Through Time

abstract: The current best practice for computing optimal transport (OT) is via entropy regularization and Sinkhorn iterations. This algorithm runs in quadratic time as it requires the full pairwise cost matrix, which is prohibitively expensive for large sets of objects. In this work we propose two effective log-linear time approximations of the cost matrix: First, a sparse approximation based on locality sensitive hashing (LSH) and, second, a Nystr{ö}m approximation with LSH-based sparse corrections, which we call locally corrected Nystr{ö}m (LCN). These approximations enable general log-linear time algorithms for entropy-regularized OT that perform well even for the complex, high-dimensional spaces common in deep learning. We analyse these approximations theoretically and evaluate them experimentally both directly and end-to-end as a component for real-world applications. Using our approximations for unsupervised word embedding alignment enables us to speed up a state-of-the-art method by a factor of 3 while also improving the accuracy by 3.1 percentage points without any additional model changes. For graph distance regression we propose the graph transport network (GTN), which combines graph neural networks (GNNs) with enhanced Sinkhorn. GTN outcompetes previous models by 48% and still scales log-linearly in the number of nodes.

This paper replaces that costly matrix with approximations that support log-linear computation, targeting large collections of objects in the high-dimensional spaces used by deep learning.

The second combines a Nyström approximation with sparse corrections based on that hashing scheme; the authors call it locally corrected Nyström. The authors report a 48% improvement over previous models while retaining log-linear scaling in node count. These application results show that the computational savings can accompany stronger task performance.
summary.tldr: Two cost-matrix approximations enable log-linear entropy-regularized optimal transport and improve reported word-alignment and graph-distance results.

title: Scalable Optimal Transport in High Dimensions for Graph Distances, Embedding Alignment, and More

abstract: Measuring contributions is a classical problem in cooperative game theory where the Shapley value is the most well-known solution concept. In this paper, we establish the convergence property of the Shapley value in parametric Bayesian learning games where players perform a Bayesian inference using their combined data, and the posterior-prior KL divergence is used as the characteristic function. We show that for any two players, under some regularity conditions, their difference in Shapley value converges in probability to the difference in Shapley value of a limiting game whose characteristic function is proportional to the log-determinant of the joint Fisher information. As an application, we present an online collaborative learning framework that is asymptotically Shapley-fair. Our result enables this to be achieved without any costly computations of posterior-prior KL divergences. Only a consistent estimator of the Fisher information is needed. The effectiveness of our framework is demonstrated with experiments using real-world data.

This paper studies Shapley values in parametric Bayesian learning games. A coalition’s value is measured by the divergence between its posterior and prior distributions, so credit reflects the information gained through combined data.

The main theorem concerns differences in credit between pairs of players. Under regularity conditions, these differences converge in probability to the corresponding Shapley-value differences in a limiting game. That game uses a value function proportional to the log-determinant of joint Fisher information. The result replaces a difficult information-gain calculation with an asymptotic description built from Fisher information.

The authors use this relationship to construct an online collaborative learning framework that is asymptotically Shapley-fair. It avoids expensive posterior-prior divergence computations and instead needs a consistent estimator of Fisher information. Experiments with real-world data demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The convergence statement is specifically about pairwise Shapley-value differences under the stated conditions, and the fairness property is asymptotic, preserving the distinction between limiting behavior and exact fairness at every stage.
summary.tldr: Under regularity conditions, Shapley-value differences in Bayesian learning approach a Fisher-information-based limit, enabling asymptotically fair collaboration.

title: On the Convergence of the Shapley Value in Parametric Bayesian Learning Games

abstract: Generalizing causal knowledge across environments is a common challenge shared across many of the data-driven disciplines, including AI and ML. Experiments are usually performed in one environment (e.g., in a lab, on Earth, in a training ground), almost invariably, with the intent of being used elsewhere (e.g., outside the lab, on Mars, in the real world), in an environment that is related but somewhat different than the original one, where certain conditions and mechanisms are likely to change. This generalization task has been studied in the causal inference literature under the rubric of transportability (Pearl and Bareinboim, 2011). While most transportability works focused on generalizing associational and interventional distributions, the generalization of counterfactual distributions has not been formally studied. In this paper, we investigate the transportability of counterfactuals from an arbitrary combination of observational and experimental distributions coming from disparate domains. Specifically, we introduce a sufficient and necessary graphical condition and develop an efficient, sound, and complete algorithm for transporting counterfactual quantities across domains in nonparametric settings. Failure of the algorithm implies the impossibility of generalizing the target counterfactual from the available data without further assumptions.

paragraphs: Causal knowledge is often collected in one environment and used in another where some conditions or mechanisms differ. This paper studies that transfer for counterfactual quantities: questions about what would have happened under alternative circumstances. Such questions go beyond describing observed associations or the results of interventions.

The authors consider an arbitrary combination of observational and experimental distributions from different domains. They introduce a graphical condition that is both necessary and sufficient for transporting the target counterfactual within their nonparametric setting. They also develop an efficient algorithm that is sound and complete, tying the graphical characterization to a procedure for obtaining transportable quantities.

Completeness gives algorithmic failure a substantive meaning. Within the stated framework, failure means that the available data cannot determine the target counterfactual without additional assumptions. The contribution therefore addresses both sides of transfer: how to generalize counterfactual knowledge when the information supports it, and how to recognize when that information is insufficient.
summary.tldr: A necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion and complete algorithm determine when counterfactual quantities can be transported across environments.

title: Counterfactual Transportability: A Formal Approach

abstract: We study methods for estimating model uncertainty for neural networks (NNs) in regression. To isolate the effect of model uncertainty, we focus on a noiseless setting with scarce training data. We introduce five important desiderata regarding model uncertainty that any method should satisfy. However, we find that established benchmarks often fail to reliably capture some of these desiderata, even those that are required by Bayesian theory. To address this, we introduce a new approach for capturing model uncertainty for NNs, which we call Neural Optimization-based Model Uncertainty (NOMU). The main idea of NOMU is to design a network architecture consisting of two connected sub-NNs, one for model prediction and one for model uncertainty, and to train it using a carefully-designed loss function. Importantly, our design enforces that NOMU satisfies our five desiderata. Due to its modular architecture, NOMU can provide model uncertainty for any given (previously trained) NN if given access to its training data. We evaluate NOMU in various regressions tasks and noiseless Bayesian optimization (BO) with costly evaluations. In regression, NOMU performs at least as well as state-of-the-art methods. In BO, NOMU even outperforms all considered benchmarks.

This paper studies that uncertainty with scarce, noiseless training data, isolating uncertainty about the model from observation noise. The authors identify five desired properties and find that established benchmark methods do not reliably capture some of them, including properties required by Bayesian theory.

NOMU uses two connected neural subnetworks: one predicts the target, and the other represents model uncertainty. A specially designed training loss works with this architecture to enforce the five proposed properties. These results support the architecture’s usefulness in the studied scarce-data, noiseless setting, where uncertainty estimates can guide decisions about costly evaluations.
summary.tldr: NOMU couples prediction and uncertainty subnetworks to enforce five uncertainty properties and performs strongly in scarce-data, noiseless evaluations.

title: NOMU: Neural Optimization-based Model Uncertainty

abstract: Stochastic high dimensional bandit problems with low dimensional structures are useful in different applications such as online advertising and drug discovery. In this work, we propose a simple unified algorithm for such problems and present a general analysis framework for the regret upper bound of our algorithm. We show that under some mild unified assumptions, our algorithm can be applied to different high-dimensional bandit problems. Our framework utilizes the low dimensional structure to guide the parameter estimation in the problem, therefore our algorithm achieves the comparable regret bounds in the LASSO bandit as a sanity check, as well as novel bounds that depend logarithmically on dimensions in the low-rank matrix bandit, the group sparse matrix bandit, and in a new problem: the multi-agent LASSO bandit.

Our framework utilizes the low dimensional structure to guide the parameter estimation in the problem, therefore our algorithm achieves the comparable regret bounds in the LASSO bandit as a sanity check, as well as novel bounds that depend logarithmically on dimensions in the low-rank matrix bandit, the group sparse matrix bandit, and in a new problem: the multi-agent LASSO bandit.

paragraphs: High-dimensional bandit problems involve repeatedly choosing actions while learning which choices yield good rewards. Although the unknown parameters may have many coordinates, useful structure can make the underlying problem much smaller. This paper develops a unified algorithm for stochastic bandit problems with such low-dimensional structure, motivated by applications including online advertising and drug discovery.

The central idea is to use that structure to guide parameter estimation. Rather than analyzing each structured problem entirely separately, the authors provide a general framework for bounding regret, the cost of making decisions while learning. Under a shared set of assumptions described as mild, the same algorithm and analysis apply across several high-dimensional settings.

For the LASSO bandit, the framework recovers comparable regret bounds as a check on its behavior. It also produces new bounds with logarithmic dependence on dimension for low-rank matrix bandits, group sparse matrix bandits, and a newly introduced multi-agent LASSO bandit. These results show how one analytical approach can capture benefits from several different forms of low-dimensional structure.
summary.tldr: A unified bandit algorithm exploits low-dimensional structure to obtain regret guarantees across several high-dimensional settings.

title: A Simple Unified Framework for High Dimensional Bandit Problems

abstract: Tabular datasets with low-sample-size or many variables are prevalent in biomedicine. Practitioners in this domain prefer linear or tree-based models over neural networks since the latter are harder to interpret and tend to overfit when applied to tabular datasets. To address these neural networks’ shortcomings, we propose an intrinsically interpretable network for heterogeneous biomedical data. We design a locally sparse neural network where the local sparsity is learned to identify the subset of most relevant features for each sample. This sample-specific sparsity is predicted via a gating network, which is trained in tandem with the prediction network. By forcing the model to select a subset of the most informative features for each sample, we reduce model overfitting in low-sample-size data and obtain an interpretable model. We demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art models when applied to synthetic or real-world biomedical datasets using extensive experiments. Furthermore, the proposed framework dramatically outperforms existing schemes when evaluating its interpretability capabilities. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our model to two important biomedical tasks: survival analysis and marker gene identification.

paragraphs: Biomedical tables often contain few samples or many variables, conditions that make neural-network overfitting a concern. Interpretability is another reason practitioners may favor linear or tree-based models. This paper proposes a neural network that addresses both issues by learning which features are most relevant separately for each sample.

A gating network selects a sparse subset of features, and a prediction network uses the resulting sample-specific information. The two networks train together. Because different samples can receive different subsets, the model’s sparsity is local rather than a single feature selection applied uniformly to the dataset. The authors use this restriction to reduce overfitting and make the model’s selected inputs interpretable.

Experiments on synthetic and real biomedical datasets report better predictive performance than state-of-the-art models and substantially stronger interpretability evaluations than existing schemes. The paper also demonstrates the framework on survival analysis and marker gene identification. These applications illustrate how selecting relevant variables per sample can support both prediction and examination of which measured features the model uses.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained gating network selects relevant features for each biomedical sample, improving interpretability and reducing overfitting in the reported experiments.

title: Locally Sparse Neural Networks for Tabular Biomedical Data

abstract: Modern machine learning models deployed in the wild can encounter both covariate and semantic shifts, giving rise to the problems of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization and OOD detection respectively. While both problems have received significant research attention lately, they have been pursued independently. This may not be surprising, since the two tasks have seemingly conflicting goals. This paper provides a new unified approach that is capable of simultaneously generalizing to covariate shifts while robustly detecting semantic shifts. We propose a margin-based learning framework that exploits freely available unlabeled data in the wild that captures the environmental test-time OOD distributions under both covariate and semantic shifts. We show both empirically and theoretically that the proposed margin constraint is the key to achieving both OOD generalization and detection. Extensive experiments show the superiority of our framework, outperforming competitive baselines that specialize in either OOD generalization or OOD detection. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/deeplearning-wisc/scone.
