paragraphs: A deployed model can encounter unfamiliar inputs for different reasons. Covariate shifts change the input distribution and call for continued generalization, while semantic shifts introduce changes that call for out-of-distribution detection. These goals can appear to conflict: the model must remain useful under some changes while recognizing other changes as outside its intended prediction setting.

The paper proposes one margin-based learning framework for both tasks. It uses freely available unlabeled data from the deployment environment that captures test-time distributions involving both kinds of shift. A margin constraint is the central mechanism for reconciling the two objectives. The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that this constraint is key to achieving generalization and detection together.

Experiments show the framework outperforming competitive methods specialized in either task. The stated finding is that a unified treatment can improve both capabilities in the evaluated settings, rather than requiring two independently designed solutions. Its use of environmental data is integral to the approach: the unlabeled examples supply information about the kinds of distribution changes the model will encounter.
summary.tldr: A margin-based framework uses unlabeled environmental data to jointly improve generalization under covariate shifts and detection of semantic shifts.

title: Feed Two Birds with One Scone: Exploiting Wild Data for Both Out-of-Distribution Generalization and Detection

abstract: Models trained on one set of domains often suffer performance drops on unseen domains, e.g., when wildlife monitoring models are deployed in new camera locations. In this work, we study principles for designing data augmentations for out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. In particular, we focus on real-world scenarios in which some domain-dependent features are robust, i.e., some features that vary across domains are predictive OOD. For example, in the wildlife monitoring application above, image backgrounds vary across camera locations but indicate habitat type, which helps predict the species of photographed animals. Motivated by theoretical analysis on a linear setting, we propose targeted augmentations, which selectively randomize spurious domain-dependent features while preserving robust ones. We prove that targeted augmentations improve OOD performance, allowing models to generalize better with fewer domains. In contrast, existing approaches such as generic augmentations, which fail to randomize domain-dependent features, and domain-invariant augmentations, which randomize all domain-dependent features, both perform poorly OOD. In experiments on three real-world datasets, we show that targeted augmentations set new states-of-the-art for OOD performance by 3.2-15.2%.

A theoretical analysis in a linear setting motivates this selective treatment. Within the studied analysis, they prove improved out-of-domain performance and better generalization with fewer domains. The key is to distinguish which changing features carry reliable information.

Both perform poorly out of domain in the comparison described. Experiments on three real-world datasets report improvements over the previous state of the art of 3.2–15.2%. These findings support designing augmentations around the predictive role of features, rather than treating all variation across environments alike.
summary.tldr: Selectively randomizing spurious features while preserving useful domain-dependent information improves generalization to unseen domains.

title: Out-of-Domain Robustness via Targeted Augmentations

abstract: Characterizing the remarkable generalization properties of over-parameterized neural networks remains an open problem. A growing body of recent literature shows that the bias of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and architecture choice implicitly leads to better generalization. In this paper, we show on the contrary that, independently of architecture, SGD can itself be the cause of poor generalization if one does not ensure good initialization. Specifically, we prove that any differentiably parameterized model, trained under gradient flow, obeys a weak spectral bias law which states that sufficiently high frequencies train arbitrarily slowly. This implies that very high frequencies present at initialization will remain after training, and hamper generalization. Further, we empirically test the developed theoretical insights using practical, deep networks. Finally, we contrast our framework with that supplied by the flat-minima conjecture and show that Fourier analysis grants a more reliable framework for understanding the generalization of neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether a network’s starting point can undermine generalization even when its architecture and training procedure otherwise seem favorable. It challenges the idea that the implicit tendencies of stochastic gradient descent necessarily produce useful solutions. The authors argue that a poor initialization can leave harmful structure in the learned function that training removes too slowly.

Their main theorem concerns any differentiably parameterized model trained under gradient flow. It establishes a weak spectral bias: sufficiently high-frequency components learn arbitrarily slowly. In functional terms, these components correspond to very rapid variation. If such variation is present at initialization, it can persist through training and interfere with generalization.

The authors test their theoretical insights empirically using practical deep networks. They also compare their perspective with the flat-minima conjecture and argue that Fourier analysis provides a more reliable framework for understanding generalization. The central lesson is that initialization affects which unwanted components training can realistically change, with the broad formal statement specifically established in the gradient-flow setting.
summary.tldr: A gradient-flow analysis shows how high-frequency structure introduced at initialization can persist during training and harm generalization.

title: How much does Initialization Affect Generalization?

abstract: Efficiently capturing the long-range patterns in sequential data sources salient to a given task—such as classification and generative modeling—poses a fundamental challenge. Popular approaches in the space tradeoff between the memory burden of brute-force enumeration and comparison, as in transformers, the computational burden of complicated sequential dependencies, as in recurrent neural networks, or the parameter burden of convolutional networks with many or large filters. We instead take inspiration from wavelet-based multiresolution analysis to define a new building block for sequence modeling, which we call a MultiresLayer. The key component of our model is the multiresolution convolution, capturing multiscale trends in the input sequence. Our MultiresConv can be implemented with shared filters across a dilated causal convolution tree. Thus it garners the computational advantages of convolutional networks and the principled theoretical motivation of wavelet decompositions. Our MultiresLayer is straightforward to implement, requires significantly fewer parameters, and maintains at most a $O(N \log N)$ memory footprint for a length $N$ sequence. Yet, by stacking such layers, our model yields state-of-the-art performance on a number of sequence classification and autoregressive density estimation tasks using CIFAR-10, ListOps, and PTB-XL datasets.

paragraphs: Sequence models need to capture relevant patterns across long distances without excessive memory, computation, or parameter costs. This paper introduces MultiresLayer, a building block inspired by wavelet-based multiresolution analysis. Its central idea is to capture trends at several scales within the same sequence, rather than relying on a large collection of independent convolution filters.

The core MultiresConv operation uses shared filters arranged in a tree of dilated causal convolutions. This construction combines convolutional computation with the theoretical motivation of wavelet decompositions. The layer requires significantly fewer parameters and has a memory footprint bounded by O(N log N) for a sequence of length N.

Stacking these layers produces state-of-the-art results on several sequence-classification and autoregressive density-estimation tasks involving CIFAR-10, ListOps, and PTB-XL. These findings show that the proposed multiscale structure can support strong predictive performance alongside its resource advantages. The contribution is a reusable sequence-modeling component whose design links scale-sensitive representations to efficient convolutional operations.
summary.tldr: MultiresLayer uses shared multiscale convolutions to model long sequences efficiently while achieving strong results on several sequence tasks.

title: Sequence Modeling with Multiresolution Convolutional Memory

abstract: Misalignment between model predictions and intended usage can be detrimental for the deployment of computer vision models. The issue is exacerbated when the task involves complex structured outputs, as it becomes harder to design procedures which address this misalignment. In natural language processing, this is often addressed using reinforcement learning techniques that align models with a task reward. We adopt this approach and show its surprising effectiveness to improve generic models pretrained to imitate example outputs across multiple computer vision tasks, such as object detection, panoptic segmentation, colorization and image captioning. We believe this approach has the potential to be widely useful for better aligning models with a diverse range of computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: A computer-vision model can learn to imitate example outputs while still producing predictions poorly aligned with how it will be used. The paper focuses on this mismatch, especially for tasks with complex structured outputs. In those settings, designing a training procedure that captures the intended use becomes more difficult.

The authors adopt a reinforcement-learning approach used in natural-language processing: tuning a pretrained model against a task reward. The starting models have already learned to imitate examples. Reward-based tuning adds an objective tied to the task, creating a direct mechanism for improving alignment between predictions and the purpose they are meant to serve.

The paper demonstrates improvements across object detection, panoptic segmentation, colorization, and image captioning. This range is the main evidence for the approach's usefulness beyond a single vision problem. The authors suggest that task-reward tuning could be broadly useful for computer vision, while the demonstrated finding is its effectiveness across the particular tasks they study.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement-learning-based task-reward tuning improves pretrained models across several computer-vision tasks.

title: Tuning Computer Vision Models With Task Rewards

abstract: The number of parameters in large transformers has been observed to grow exponentially. Despite notable performance improvements, concerns have been raised that such a growing model size will run out of data in the near future. As manifested in the neural scaling law, modern learning backbones are not data-efficient. To maintain the utility of the model capacity, training data should be increased proportionally. In this paper, we study the neural scaling law under the previously overlooked data scarcity regime, focusing on the more challenging situation where we need to train a gigantic model with a disproportionately limited supply of available training data. We find that the existing power laws underestimate the data inefficiency of large transformers. Their performance will drop significantly if the training set is insufficient. Fortunately, we discover another blessing - such a data-inefficient scaling law can be restored through a model reusing approach that warm-starts the training of a large model by initializing it using smaller models. Our empirical study shows that model reusing can effectively reproduce the power law under the data scarcity regime. When progressively applying model reusing to expand the model size, we also observe consistent performance improvement in large transformers. We release our code at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/Data-Efficient-Scaling.

paragraphs: Increasing a transformer’s size does not automatically make good use of a limited training dataset. This paper studies the data-scarce regime, where a very large model must learn from disproportionately little data. The authors find that existing scaling power laws underestimate the severity of this problem: performance can decline substantially when training data is insufficient.

Their proposed remedy is model reuse. Instead of beginning the larger model’s training without this prior foundation, they initialize it using smaller models. This warm start changes how the larger model makes use of the available data. The approach addresses the relationship between model capacity and data supply through initialization rather than assuming that enough additional data will become available.

Empirically, model reuse restores the observed power-law behavior under the studied data scarcity conditions. The authors also report consistent performance improvements when repeatedly applying reuse to expand model size. These findings suggest that how a model is initialized can materially affect scaling behavior when data, rather than model capacity, is the limiting resource.
summary.tldr: Initializing large transformers from smaller models improves their empirical scaling behavior when training data is scarce.

title: Data Efficient Neural Scaling Law via Model Reusing

abstract: Operator learning for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) is rapidly emerging as a promising approach for surrogate modeling of intricate systems. Transformers with the self-attention mechanism—a powerful tool originally designed for natural language processing—have recently been adapted for operator learning. However, they confront challenges, including high computational demands and limited interpretability. This raises a critical question: Is there a more efficient attention mechanism for Transformer-based operator learning? This paper proposes the Position-induced Transformer (PiT), built on an innovative position-attention mechanism, which demonstrates significant advantages over the classical self-attention in operator learning. Position-attention draws inspiration from numerical methods for PDEs. Different from self-attention, position-attention is induced by only the spatial interrelations of sampling positions for input functions of the operators, and does not rely on the input function values themselves, thereby greatly boosting efficiency. PiT exhibits superior performance over current state-of-the-art neural operators in a variety of complex operator learning tasks across diverse PDE benchmarks. Additionally, PiT possesses an enhanced discretization convergence feature, compared to the widely-used Fourier neural operator.

paragraphs: Operator learning builds models of mappings between functions, offering surrogate models for systems described by partial differential equations. Transformers have been adapted to this setting, but their self-attention can be computationally demanding and difficult to interpret. This paper asks whether a more suitable attention mechanism can exploit the spatial structure already present in these problems.

The Position-induced Transformer uses attention determined only by spatial relationships among the locations where input functions are sampled. Unlike conventional self-attention, this attention mechanism does not depend on the function values at those locations. Inspired by numerical PDE methods, it makes sampling geometry the basis for attention and substantially improves efficiency.

Across diverse PDE benchmarks, PiT outperforms leading neural operators on the evaluated operator-learning tasks. It also exhibits improved discretization convergence compared with the Fourier neural operator, addressing how the model behaves as the sampling discretization changes. These findings show that spatial relationships can provide a powerful basis for attention in this setting, alongside the practical benefit of reducing the computation associated with value-dependent attention.
summary.tldr: PiT uses sampling positions to determine attention, improving efficiency and performance on PDE operator-learning benchmarks.

title: Positional Knowledge is All You Need: Position-induced Transformer (PiT) for Operator Learning

abstract: We provide generalization bounds for matrix completion with Schatten $p$ quasi-norm constraints, which is equivalent to deep matrix factorization with Frobenius constraints. In the uniform sampling regime, the sample complexity scales like $\widetilde{O}\left( rn\right)$ where $n$ is the size of the matrix and $r$ is a constraint of the same order as the ground truth rank in the isotropic case. In the distribution-free setting, the bounds scale as $\widetilde{O}\left(r^{1-\frac{p}{2}}n^{1+\frac{p}{2}}\right)$, which reduces to the familiar $\sqrt{r}n^{\frac{3}{2}}$ for $p=1$. Furthermore, we provide an analogue of the weighted trace norm for this setting which brings the sample complexity down to $\widetilde{O}(nr)$ in all cases. We then present a non-linear model, Functionally Rescaled Matrix Completion (FRMC) which applies a single trainable function from $\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ to each entry of a latent matrix, and prove that this adds only negligible terms of the overall sample complexity, whilst experiments demonstrate that this simple model improvement already leads to significant gains on real data. We also provide extensions of our results to various neural architectures, thereby providing the first comprehensive uniform convergence PAC analysis of neural network matrix completion.

paragraphs: Matrix completion predicts missing entries from observed ones. This paper studies how much data such prediction needs under Schatten p quasi-norm constraints, which correspond to Frobenius constraints on a deep matrix factorization. The analysis connects these model restrictions to guarantees about performance beyond the observed entries.

Under uniform sampling, the sample complexity is approximately proportional to rn, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here n measures matrix size, and r is comparable to the true rank in the isotropic case. Without assumptions on the sampling distribution, the bound depends more strongly on n and p. A proposed analogue of the weighted trace norm restores the approximately nr rate across the cases considered.

They prove that this nonlinear addition contributes only negligible extra sample-complexity terms, while experiments show substantial gains on real data. Extensions to other neural architectures broaden the generalization analysis beyond this particular model.
summary.tldr: The paper proves matrix-completion generalization bounds and shows that a shared nonlinear rescaling can improve predictions with negligible added sample complexity.

title: Generalization Analysis of Deep Non-linear Matrix Completion

abstract: Federated representation learning (FRL) is a popular personalized federated learning (FL) framework where clients work together to train a common representation while retaining their personalized heads. Existing studies, however, largely focus on the over-parameterized regime. In this paper, we make the initial efforts to investigate FRL in the under-parameterized regime, where the FL model is insufficient to express the variations in all ground-truth models. We propose a novel FRL algorithm FLUTE, and theoretically characterize its sample complexity and convergence rate for linear models in the under-parameterized regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first FRL algorithm with provable performance guarantees in this regime. FLUTE features a data-independent random initialization and a carefully designed objective function that aids the distillation of subspace spanned by the global optimal representation from the misaligned local representations. On the technical side, we bridge low-rank matrix approximation techniques with the FL analysis, which may be of broad interest. We also extend FLUTE beyond linear representations. Experimental results demonstrate that FLUTE outperforms state-of-the-art FRL solutions in both synthetic and real-world tasks.

This paper studies the under-parameterized case: the shared model lacks enough expressive capacity to capture all variation among the ground-truth client models. That makes choosing what information the common representation should retain especially important.

The proposed algorithm, FLUTE, starts from a data-independent random initialization and uses a carefully designed objective. The objective helps recover the subspace of the globally optimal representation from local representations that do not align. The analysis connects this federated learning problem with low-rank matrix approximation, providing a mathematical route to understanding the shared structure.

summary.tldr: FLUTE learns shared federated representations under limited model capacity, with guarantees for linear models and favorable synthetic and real-world results.

title: Federated Representation Learning in the Under-Parameterized Regime

abstract: Generative models for structure-based drug design (SBDD) have shown promising results in recent years. Existing works mainly focus on how to generate molecules with higher binding affinity, ignoring the feasibility prerequisites for generated 3D poses and resulting in false positives. We conduct thorough studies on key factors of ill-conformational problems when applying autoregressive methods and diffusion to SBDD, including mode collapse and hybrid continuous-discrete space. In this paper, we introduce MolCRAFT, the first SBDD model that operates in the continuous parameter space, together with a novel noise reduced sampling strategy. Empirical results show that our model consistently achieves superior performance in binding affinity with more stable 3D structure, demonstrating our ability to accurately model interatomic interactions. To our best knowledge, MolCRAFT is the first to achieve reference-level Vina Scores (-6.59 kcal/mol) with comparable molecular size, outperforming other strong baselines by a wide margin (-0.84 kcal/mol). Code is available at https://github.com/AlgoMole/MolCRAFT.

paragraphs: Structure-based molecular generation seeks molecules that bind well to a target, but favorable binding scores are less useful when the generated three-dimensional pose is infeasible. The paper investigates why autoregressive and diffusion approaches can produce problematic conformations. Its analysis examines mode collapse and the difficulty of combining continuous and discrete spaces.

MolCRAFT moves the generation process into a continuous parameter space and introduces a sampling strategy designed to reduce noise. This approach addresses the representation and sampling choices underlying molecular geometry. The aim is to generate molecules that combine strong binding affinity with more stable three-dimensional structures, accounting for the interactions between atoms.

Empirical results report improvements in both binding affinity and structural stability. MolCRAFT reaches a reference-level Vina score of −6.59 kcal/mol at comparable molecular size, with a reported −0.84 kcal/mol margin over strong baselines. These results support the proposed representation and sampling strategy for generating promising molecular poses, with the stated evidence centered on computational binding scores and generated structures.
summary.tldr: MolCRAFT generates molecules in continuous parameter space to improve both binding scores and the stability of generated three-dimensional structures.

title: MolCRAFT: Structure-Based Drug Design in Continuous Parameter Space

abstract: An important issue with Large Language Models (LLMs) is their undesired ability to generate toxic language. In this work, we show that the neurons responsible for toxicity can be determined by their power to discriminate toxic sentences, and that toxic language can be mitigated by reducing their activation levels proportionally to this power. We propose AUROC adaptation (AurA), an intervention that can be applied to any pre-trained LLM to mitigate toxicity. As the intervention is proportional to the ability of each neuron to discriminate toxic content, it is free of any model-dependent hyperparameters. We show that AurA can achieve up to $2.2\times$ reduction in toxicity with only a $0.72$ perplexity increase. We also show that AurA is effective with models of different scale (from 1.5B to 40B parameters), and its effectiveness in mitigating toxic language, while preserving common-sense zero-shot abilities, holds across all scales. AurA can be combined with pre-prompting strategies, boosting its average mitigation potential from $1.28\times$ to $2.35\times$. Moreover, AurA can counteract adversarial pre-prompts that maliciously elicit toxic content, making it an effective method for deploying safer and less toxic models.

Moreover, AurA can counteract adversarial pre-prompts that maliciously elicit toxic content, making it an effective method for deploying safer and less toxic models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses toxic language generation by intervening on a pretrained model’s internal neuron activations. The authors identify relevant neurons through their ability to distinguish toxic sentences. Their method, AUROC adaptation or AurA, reduces each neuron’s activation in proportion to that discriminative ability, avoiding model-dependent hyperparameters.

The reported evaluation finds toxicity reductions of up to 2.2 times with a perplexity increase of 0.72. Across tested models ranging from 1.5 billion to 40 billion parameters, AurA mitigates toxicity while preserving common-sense zero-shot abilities. These results assess both the desired behavioral change and the retention of useful capabilities across model scales.

AurA can also be combined with prompting strategies: the authors report that this increases its average mitigation potential from 1.28 times to 2.35 times. It additionally counters adversarial prompts intended to elicit toxic output. The contribution links a measurable property of individual neurons to a proportional intervention, offering an internal mechanism that can complement prompt-based approaches to toxicity reduction.
summary.tldr: AurA reduces toxic generation by proportionally suppressing neurons that distinguish toxic content, with benefits across the tested model scales.

title: Whispering Experts: Neural Interventions for Toxicity Mitigation in Language Models

abstract: We study an online contextual dynamic pricing problem, where customers decide whether to purchase a product based on its features and price. We introduce a novel approach to modeling a customer’s expected demand by incorporating feature-based price elasticity, which can be equivalently represented as a valuation with heteroscedastic noise. To solve the problem, we propose a computationally efficient algorithm called "Pricing with Perturbation (PwP)", which enjoys an $O(\sqrt{dT\log T})$ regret while allowing arbitrary adversarial input context sequences. We also prove a matching lower bound at $\Omega(\sqrt{dT})$ to show the optimality regarding $d$ and $T$ (up to $\log T$ factors). Our results shed light on the relationship between contextual elasticity and heteroscedastic valuation, providing insights for effective and practical pricing strategies.

The authors show that this can equivalently be expressed through customer valuations whose noise has feature-dependent variability, known as heteroscedasticity.

They develop a computationally efficient algorithm called Pricing with Perturbation. Its regret bound is O(√(dT log T)), where d and T describe contextual dimension and the time horizon. Regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall against the pricing benchmark. The result permits arbitrary adversarial sequences of input contexts, rather than requiring a benign ordering of feature information.

A lower bound of Ω(√(dT)) shows that the upper bound has optimal dependence on d and T up to logarithmic factors. This provides a theoretical benchmark for the algorithm’s efficiency in learning to price. The broader contribution connects two descriptions of demand uncertainty and uses that connection to obtain a pricing method with near-matching performance bounds.
summary.tldr: Pricing with Perturbation handles feature-dependent price sensitivity with regret optimal in dimension and horizon up to logarithmic factors.

title: Pricing with Contextual Elasticity and Heteroscedastic Valuation

abstract: Various human-designed prompt engineering techniques have been proposed to improve problem solvers based on Large Language Models (LLMs), yielding many disparate code bases. We unify these approaches by describing LLM-based agents as computational graphs. The nodes implement functions to process multimodal data or query LLMs, and the edges describe the information flow between operations. Graphs can be recursively combined into larger composite graphs representing hierarchies of inter-agent collaboration (where edges connect operations of different agents). Our novel automatic graph optimizers (1) refine node-level LLM prompts (node optimization) and (2) improve agent orchestration by changing graph connectivity (edge optimization). Experiments demonstrate that our framework can be used to efficiently develop, integrate, and automatically improve various LLM agents. Our code is public.

The framework introduces two forms of automatic optimization: changing the prompts used at individual nodes and changing graph connections to improve how agents coordinate. These address both local instructions and the broader organization of computation.

Experiments demonstrate that this representation supports efficient development, integration, and automatic improvement of different language agents. The approach matters because prompt quality and collaboration structure become parts of the same optimizable system. Developers can express an agent, compose it with others, and improve the resulting workflow within a shared abstraction rather than rebuilding each arrangement as a separate implementation.
summary.tldr: GPTSwarm models language agents as composable graphs and automatically improves both their prompts and their information flow.

title: GPTSwarm: Language Agents as Optimizable Graphs

abstract: We explore the single-spiked covariance model within the context of sparse principal component analysis (PCA), which aims to recover a sparse unit vector from noisy samples. From an information-theoretic perspective, $O(k \log p)$ observations are sufficient to recover a $k$-sparse $p$-dimensional vector $\mathbf{v}$. However, existing polynomial-time methods require at least $O(k^2)$ samples for successful recovery, highlighting a significant gap in sample efficiency. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel thresholding-based algorithm that requires only $\Omega(k \log p)$ samples, provided the signal strength $\lambda = \Omega(||\mathbf{v}||_\infty^{-1})$. We also propose a two-stage nonconvex algorithm that further enhances estimation performance. This approach integrates our thresholding algorithm with truncated power iteration, achieving the minimax optimal rate of statistical error under the desired sample complexity. Numerical experiments validate the superior performance of our algorithms in terms of estimation accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks a direction with relatively few nonzero coordinates from noisy observations. This paper studies the single-spiked covariance model, where the target is a sparse unit vector. It addresses a gap between the roughly k log p observations sufficient from an information-theoretic perspective and the at-least-quadratic dependence on sparsity reported for existing polynomial-time methods.

The proposed thresholding algorithm works with a sample requirement on the k log p scale under an explicit signal-strength condition. Specifically, lambda must be at least on the order of the reciprocal of the vector’s largest absolute coordinate. This qualification is central: the improved sample requirement is established with that signal assumption, rather than as an unconditional resolution of the gap.

A second algorithm combines the thresholding procedure with truncated power iteration in a two-stage nonconvex method. It achieves the minimax-optimal statistical error rate under the stated sample complexity. Numerical experiments also report advantages in estimation accuracy and computational efficiency, complementing the theoretical guarantees for this covariance model.
summary.tldr: Under a stated signal-strength condition, thresholding and a two-stage refinement improve sparse PCA sample efficiency and achieve optimal statistical error.

title: Fast and Provable Algorithms for Sparse PCA with Improved Sample Complexity

abstract: Recent advances in deep learning rely heavily on massive datasets, leading to substantial storage and training costs. Dataset pruning aims to alleviate this demand by discarding redundant examples. However, many existing methods require training a model with a full dataset over a large number of epochs before being able to prune the dataset, which ironically makes the pruning process more expensive than just training the model on the entire dataset. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Difficulty and Uncertainty-Aware Lightweight (DUAL) score, which aims to identify important samples from the early training stage by considering both example difficulty and prediction uncertainty. To address a catastrophic accuracy drop at an extreme pruning ratio, we further propose a pruning ratio-adaptive sampling using Beta distribution. Experiments on various datasets and learning scenarios such as image classification with label noise and image corruption, and model architecture generalization demonstrate the superiority of our method over previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches. Specifically, on ImageNet-1k, our method reduces the time cost for pruning to 66% compared to previous methods while achieving a SOTA 60% test accuracy at a 90% pruning ratio. On CIFAR datasets, the time cost is reduced to just 15% while maintaining SOTA performance.

paragraphs: Dataset pruning reduces training and storage demands by removing redundant examples. However, identifying which examples to keep can itself require extensive training on the full dataset. The paper targets this overhead by scoring useful samples early enough for pruning to offer a more practical computational benefit.

Its DUAL score combines example difficulty with prediction uncertainty during early training. The method also uses sampling based on a Beta distribution that adapts to the pruning ratio. This additional component addresses severe accuracy losses when an extremely large fraction of the dataset is removed.

Experiments cover image classification, noisy labels, image corruption, and generalization across model architectures. On ImageNet-1k, pruning takes 66% of the time required by previous methods, with a reported state-of-the-art 60% test accuracy after removing 90% of the data. On CIFAR datasets, pruning time falls to 15% while retaining state-of-the-art performance. These findings connect early sample assessment with both lower selection costs and useful accuracy under aggressive pruning.
summary.tldr: DUAL uses early example difficulty and prediction uncertainty to reduce dataset-pruning costs while preserving strong accuracy.

title: Lightweight Dataset Pruning without Full Training via Example Difficulty and Prediction Uncertainty

abstract: Distributional Compositional Generalization (DCG) refers to the ability to tackle tasks from new distributions by leveraging the knowledge of concepts learned from supporting distributions. In this work, we aim to explore the statistical mechanisms of DCG, which have been largely overlooked in previous studies. By statistically formulating the problem, this paper seeks to address two key research questions: 1) Can a method to one DCG problem be applicable to another? 2) What statistical properties can indicate a learning algorithm’s capacity for knowledge composition in DCG tasks? To address the first question, an invariant measure is proposed to provide a dimension where all different methods converge. This measure underscores the critical role of data in enabling improvements without trade-offs. As for the second question, we reveal that by decoupling the impacts of insufficient data and knowledge composition, the ability of the learning algorithm to compose knowledge relies on the compatibility and sensitivity between the learning algorithm and the composition rule. In summary, the statistical analysis of the generalization mechanisms provided in this paper deepens our understanding of compositional generalization, offering a complementary evidence on the importance of data in DCG task.

paragraphs: Distributional compositional generalization concerns solving tasks from new distributions by combining concepts learned from supporting distributions. This paper studies the statistical mechanisms behind that ability. It asks whether a method for one such problem can apply to another, and which statistical properties reveal an algorithm's capacity to compose knowledge.

For the first question, the authors propose an invariant measure that provides a common dimension for comparing different methods. Their analysis highlights the role of data in enabling improvements without trade-offs. The measure supplies a shared statistical perspective on approaches that might otherwise be studied separately for their particular compositional tasks.

For the second question, the analysis separates the effect of insufficient data from the effect of knowledge composition itself. After making that distinction, it connects compositional ability to compatibility and sensitivity between the learning algorithm and the composition rule. This helps clarify why evaluating composition requires considering both available data and the relationship between the learner and the way knowledge must be combined.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a statistical account of compositional generalization that separates data scarcity from algorithm–composition compatibility.

title: On the Statistical Mechanisms of Distributional Compositional Generalization

abstract: Transfer reinforcement learning aims to derive a near-optimal policy for a target environment with limited data by leveraging abundant data from related source domains. However, it faces two key challenges: the lack of performance guarantees for the transferred policy, which can lead to undesired actions, and the risk of negative transfer when multiple source domains are involved. We propose a novel framework based on the pessimism principle, which constructs and optimizes a conservative estimation of the target domain’s performance. Our framework effectively addresses the two challenges by providing an optimized lower bound on target performance, ensuring safe and reliable decisions, and by exhibiting monotonic improvement with respect to the quality of the source domains, thereby avoiding negative transfer. We construct two types of conservative estimations, rigorously characterize their effectiveness, and develop efficient distributed algorithms with convergence guarantees. Our framework provides a theoretically sound and practically robust solution for transfer learning in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Transfer reinforcement learning uses data from related environments to help choose a policy for a target environment with limited data. Two problems arise: a transferred policy may lack a target-performance guarantee, and using several source environments can cause negative transfer. This paper develops a framework that addresses both through conservative estimates of target performance.

The framework follows the pessimism principle by constructing and optimizing a lower bound on how a policy will perform in the target domain. This provides a performance-based foundation for the transferred decision. The authors also establish monotonic improvement with source-domain quality, which is the property their framework uses to avoid negative transfer.

The paper constructs two forms of conservative estimation, theoretically characterizes their effectiveness, and develops efficient distributed algorithms with convergence guarantees. Its contribution connects the transfer objective, the protection against negative transfer, and the optimization procedure within one framework. The stated guarantees concern the framework’s target-performance bounds and source-quality behavior, giving theoretical support to its proposed transfer strategy.
summary.tldr: This transfer reinforcement learning framework optimizes conservative target-performance bounds and establishes improvement with source-domain quality.

title: Pessimism Principle Can Be Effective: Towards a Framework for Zero-Shot Transfer Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite the impressive capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in vision-language tasks, they are prone to hallucinations in real-world scenarios. This paper investigates the hallucination phenomenon in MLLMs from the perspective of modality conflict. Unlike existing works focusing on the conflicts between model responses and inputs, we study the inherent conflicts in inputs from different modalities that place MLLMs in a dilemma and directly lead to hallucinations. We formally define the modality conflict and construct a dataset named Multimodal Modality Conflict (MMMC) to simulate this phenomenon in vision-language tasks. Three methods based on prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning are proposed to alleviate the hallucination caused by modality conflict. Extensive experiments are conducted on the MMMC dataset to analyze the merits and demerits of these methods. Our results show that the reinforcement learning method achieves the best performance in mitigating the hallucination under modality conflict, while the supervised fine-tuning method shows promising and stable performance. Our work sheds light on the unnoticed modality conflict that leads to hallucinations and provides more insights into the robustness of MLLMs.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may receive conflicting information from different input modalities. This paper investigates how those conflicts can lead to hallucinations. Its focus is on inconsistency already present within the inputs, creating a dilemma for the model before it produces a response, rather than only on discrepancies between a response and its evidence.

The authors formally define modality conflict and construct the Multimodal Modality Conflict dataset to simulate it in vision-language tasks. They then propose three ways to reduce the resulting hallucinations: prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Evaluating these approaches on a shared dataset allows the study to examine their respective strengths and weaknesses.

Reinforcement learning performs best at mitigating hallucinations under modality conflict in the reported experiments. Supervised fine-tuning also delivers promising, stable performance. These findings identify input disagreement as a useful target for robustness research and provide comparative evidence about ways to address it. The ranking concerns the conflict setting evaluated on this dataset, rather than establishing one method as best for every source of hallucination.
summary.tldr: A new dataset and three mitigation approaches expose modality conflict as a hallucination source, with reinforcement learning performing best in the reported evaluation.

title: Robust Multimodal Large Language Models Against Modality Conflict

abstract: Modern LLMs show mastery over an ever-growing range of skills, as well as the ability to compose them flexibly. However, extending model capabilities to new skills in a scalable manner is an open problem: fine-tuning and parameter-efficient variants risk catastrophic forgetting, while context-based approaches have limited expressiveness and are constrained by the model’s effective context. We explore skill neologisms–soft tokens integrated in the model’s vocabulary and optimized to improve capabilities over a specific skill–as a way to selectively acquire new skills without weight updates. We first observe that pretrained LLMs already exhibit tokens associated with procedural knowledge. We then show on a controlled synthetic task that skill neologisms can be learned to improve model capabilities on specific skills while being composable with out-of-distribution skills, and that independently trained skill neologisms can be composed zero-shot. Finally, we validate zero-shot composition of independently learned skill neologisms on the more realistic natural language setting of the Skill-Mix benchmark. These results suggest that skill neologisms may provide a scalable path towards skill-based continual learning.

paragraphs: Adding skills to a language model creates a tension: fine-tuning can overwrite previous capabilities, while teaching through context is constrained by expressiveness and effective context length. This paper explores skill neologisms, learned soft tokens added to the vocabulary and optimized for particular skills without updating the model’s existing weights.

The authors first observe that pretrained models already contain tokens associated with procedural knowledge. On a controlled synthetic task, they then show that new skill tokens can improve targeted capabilities and combine with out-of-distribution skills. Independently trained skill tokens can also be composed without additional joint training.

The study extends this composition test to the natural-language Skill-Mix benchmark, validating zero-shot combinations of independently learned tokens in a more realistic setting. The findings suggest a possible route toward skill-based continual learning: acquire separate skill representations and reuse them in combinations. The abstract presents this as a promising direction for scalability, with the evidence centered on targeted skill improvement and composability.
summary.tldr: Learned vocabulary tokens improve specific skills and compose without joint training, suggesting a possible route to skill-based continual learning.

title: Skill Neologisms: Towards Skill-based Continual Learning

abstract: Urgently needed generalizable robot object interaction and manipulation requires high-quality Cross-Category object perception. As a pioneer of this area, Generalizable and Actionable Parts (GAParts) understanding has attracted increasing attention from relevant researchers. However, most recent works either have insufficient design regarding the symmetry issue or require rich symmetry annotation, which severely impedes precise GAPart pose estimation in data-lacking scenarios. In this paper, we propose SAFAG, a novel Symmetry Annotation-Free framework for Generalizable and Actionable Parts Pose Estimation. Specifically, we suggest a stepwise refinement two-stage framework for candidate-to-final quaternion regression, and tackle the symmetry prediction as a probability distribution problem with self-supervised learning strategy. The experimental results demonstrate the superior performance and robustness of our SAFAG. We believe that our work has the enormous potential to be applied in many areas of embodied AI system.

paragraphs: SAFAG addresses perception of object parts that robots can interact with across different object categories. Accurate pose estimation is important for this goal, but symmetry complicates the task. The paper argues that existing approaches either handle symmetry inadequately or depend on extensive symmetry annotations, making precise estimation difficult when annotated data are scarce.

The proposed framework removes the need for symmetry annotations. It estimates pose through a two-stage process that progressively refines candidate quaternion predictions into final predictions. Alongside this refinement, it treats symmetry prediction as a probability-distribution problem and learns it through self-supervision. This combines a structured pose-estimation process with a way to learn symmetry without explicit symmetry labels.

The experiments report superior performance and robustness for SAFAG. Those findings support the framework’s approach to the symmetry problem in generalizable, actionable part perception. The authors also describe potential applications across embodied AI. That broader application claim remains a statement of potential, while the reported experimental contribution concerns the quality and robustness of part pose estimation.
summary.tldr: SAFAG combines progressive pose refinement with self-supervised symmetry prediction to estimate actionable part poses without symmetry annotations.

title: Generalizable and Actionable Parts Pose Estimation with Symmetry Annotation-Free Learning Strategy

abstract: As large language models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, there is a growing need for tools that audit not only model outputs but also the internal computations that produce them. Circuit analysis is a central approach in mechanistic interpretability, but it is typically target-conditioned, explaining a single prompt paired with a chosen completion. This target-conditioned setup can obscure heterogeneity across a model’s continuation distribution. We introduce distribution-level unsupervised feature discovery, which clusters sampled continuations using both semantic content and sequence-level mechanistic attributions, without manually specifying target outputs. Our method represents each continuation with a semantic embedding and a prefix-to-continuation attribution signature, then optimizes a rate-distortion objective that trades off semantic coherence, mechanistic consistency, and cluster granularity. Across clustering and steering analyses, the discovered clusters expose continuation modes that single-view baselines miss and provide interventional evidence that cluster signatures correspond to actionable mechanistic factors. Overall, our approach complements circuit analysis and behavioral evaluation by providing a scalable audit of the mechanisms underlying a model’s continuation distribution.

paragraphs: Circuit analysis commonly explains a chosen completion for a particular prompt. This paper argues that such target-conditioned analysis can hide differences across the model’s possible continuations. It introduces an unsupervised approach that examines sampled continuations together, looking for groups that share both semantic content and patterns of internal mechanistic attribution.

Each continuation receives two representations: a semantic embedding and an attribution signature linking the prefix to the continuation. A rate-distortion objective balances semantic coherence, mechanistic consistency, and the number or granularity of clusters. This allows the grouping to reflect what continuations mean and how their attributed computations differ, without manually choosing target outputs.

Clustering and steering analyses reveal continuation modes missed by single-view baselines. Interventions provide evidence that the cluster signatures correspond to mechanistic factors that can be acted upon. The approach therefore complements circuit analysis and behavioral evaluation by organizing a model’s continuation distribution into interpretable groups, with empirical evidence connecting those groups to controllable aspects of model behavior.
summary.tldr: Joint clustering of continuation meanings and mechanistic attributions reveals model behaviors missed by single-view analyses and supports targeted interventions.

title: Shared Semantics, Divergent Mechanisms: Unsupervised Feature Discovery by Aligning Semantics and Mechanisms

abstract: Generative AI disrupts the practice of giving credit to work that came before. Ideally, a generative model would give credit to any work on which its output depends in a significant way. Counterfactual credit attribution (CCA) is a technical condition formalizing this goal—a relaxation of differential privacy—recently introduced by Livni, Moran, Nissim, and Pabbaraju (2024) who studied it in the PAC learning setting. We initiate the study of CCA generative models. Specifically, we consider autoregressive models giving credit to a deployment-time dataset (e.g., a RAG database). We uncover barriers to two natural approaches to CCA autoregressive models. First, we show that imposing CCA on the underlying next-token predictor does not guarantee that the model is CCA: CCA does not compose autoregressively (unlike DP). Second, we consider a different approach to building CCA models which we call retrofitting. Retrofitting takes a model that does not attribute credit, and adds credit onto it. Given black-box access to the starting model, retrofitting requires query complexity exponential in the length of the model’s outputs.

Given black-box access to the starting model, retrofitting requires query complexity exponential in the length of the model’s outputs.

paragraphs: Counterfactual credit attribution formalizes the goal of crediting source material on which a generated output significantly depends. This paper brings that condition to autoregressive generation, focusing on credit assigned to a dataset available at deployment time, such as a retrieval database. It studies whether two natural construction strategies can provide the required attribution.

The first strategy imposes the condition on the next-token predictor. The authors show that this does not guarantee the condition for the complete generated output. Even if individual prediction steps satisfy the attribution requirement, their autoregressive composition need not do so. This differs from the composition behavior of differential privacy, of which the attribution condition is a relaxation.

The second strategy adds attribution to an existing model through black-box access. For this retrofitting approach, the required number of queries grows exponentially with output length. Together, the results identify barriers to these two routes: local next-token guarantees do not automatically extend to full outputs, and black-box retrofitting can be prohibitively query-intensive.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual attribution does not automatically compose across generated tokens, and black-box retrofitting requires exponentially many queries in output length.

title: Barriers to Counterfactual Credit Attribution for Autoregressive Models

abstract: Existing Meta-Black-Box Optimization (MetaBBO) methods focus on how to search when controlling optimizers, but largely overlook where to search. We propose MetaSG-SAEA, a bi-level MetaBBO framework for expensive constrained multi-objective optimization problems (ECMOPs), in which a meta-policy provides search guidance to the low-level Surrogate-Assisted Evolutionary Algorithm (SAEA). To achieve this, we introduce Max–Min Constraint-Calibrated Inequality (MM-CCI), a compact, problem-agnostic region abstraction that maps heterogeneous constraint evaluations to an ordered scalar level; we further provide a theoretical analysis of its fundamental properties. Building on this region abstraction, we adopt diffusion-based population initialization to translate the meta-policy’s region-level guidance into solution-level priors for the SAEA. To make MetaSG-SAEA scalable, we construct an attention-based state representation across varying problem dimensions, population sizes, and numbers of objectives and constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that MetaSG-SAEA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks and exhibits the ability to generalize across problem distributions.

title: Meta-Black-Box Optimization Can Do Search Guidance for Expensive Constrained Multi-Objective Optimization

abstract: Machine-learned (ML) XC functionals aim to replace human-designed density functional approximations by learning directly from reference data, but they still do not consistently outperform traditional $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$-scaling hybrid functionals. We therefore study a hybrid-distillation setting, where $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$-scaling semilocal ML-XC functionals are trained to reproduce B3LYP/def2-SVP targets. We introduce Derivative Informed XC-Loss (DI-Loss), a loss that incorporates additional information from the reference hybrid functional by supervising first and second derivatives of the energy on the Grassmannian of admissible density matrices. Rather than only matching the self-consistent fixed point, DI-Loss aligns the local first- and second-order response of the learned functional with that of the target functional. Across four evaluated architectures, DI-Loss consistently improves the main energy metrics. Averaged uniformly across architectures, the total-energy MAE decreases by 66% relative to energy and density supervision alone. The density-sensitive mean-field energy metric $E_\rho$ improves from 1.2 to 0.8 mEh on average, while dipole and $\mathcal{L}_2$ density errors do not improve uniformly. We further show that densities from the distilled functionals reduce hybrid-functional SCF iterations by up to 55%. In downstream TDDFT calculations, Hessian supervision improves excited-state predictions, with XCdiff reducing the mean excitation-energy MAE by 24-35% across molecule sizes on QM40.

The goal is to transfer the reference functional’s behavior into a cheaper approximation.

This gives training additional information about the shape of the reference energy function.

Across four architectures, the loss improves the main energy metrics, reducing total-energy mean absolute error by 66% when averaged uniformly across architectures. summary.tldr: Supervising energy derivatives improves cheaper learned approximations of a hybrid functional, with benefits for energy accuracy and downstream calculations.

title: Derivative Informed Learning of Exchange-Correlation Functionals

abstract: Quantization can drastically increase the efficiency of large language and vision models, but typically incurs an accuracy drop. Recently, function-preserving transforms (e.g. rotations, Hadamard transform, channel-wise scaling) have been successfully applied to reduce post-training quantization error, yet a principled explanation remains elusive. We analyze linear-layer quantization via the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SQNR), showing that for uniform integer quantization at a fixed bit width, SQNR decomposes into (i) the concentration of weights and activations (capturing spread and outliers), and (ii) the alignment of their dominant variation directions. This provides an actionable insight: enhancing alignment between weight and activation variation directions can reduce quantization error, complementing concentration-focused approaches. Motivated by this, we introduce Concentration–Alignment Transforms (CAT), a lightweight linear transformation that uses a covariance estimate from a small calibration set to jointly improve concentration and alignment, approximately maximizing SQNR. Experiments across several LLMs show that CAT consistently matches or outperforms prior transform-based quantization methods at 4-bit precision.

paragraphs: Quantization makes models more efficient by representing their numerical values at lower precision, but it often reduces accuracy. Function-preserving transformations can lessen that damage, although why they help has lacked a principled explanation. This paper analyzes quantization in linear layers using the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio, a measure of useful signal relative to the error introduced.

For uniform integer quantization at a fixed bit width, the analysis separates this ratio into two factors. Concentration describes the spread and outliers of weights and activations. Alignment describes how their dominant directions of variation relate. The resulting insight is that improving alignment can reduce quantization error alongside approaches that focus on concentration.

The proposed Concentration–Alignment Transforms use a covariance estimate from a small calibration set to improve both factors jointly. This lightweight linear transformation approximately maximizes the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio. Across several language models at 4-bit precision, it consistently matches or exceeds earlier transformation-based methods. The findings connect a mathematical decomposition of quantization error to a concrete calibration procedure for reducing it.
summary.tldr: CAT reduces quantization error by jointly improving the concentration and directional alignment of weights and activations.

title: Dissecting Quantization Error: A Concentration-Alignment Perspective

abstract: Diffusion models are widely used for high-quality generation, but their performance is sensitive to the accuracy of the estimated score. We first derive a stepwise Wasserstein error bound in a Gaussian-mixture setting, where the score admits a closed-form structure, and the score Hessian can be controlled explicitly, leading to sharp Wasserstein estimates. We then extend the analysis to general data distributions, which yields a more general but typically looser upper bound. This general bound can be sharpened under mild regularity: when the initial distribution has a globally Lipschitz score, the curvature contribution at small times is uniformly bounded, avoiding the worst-case blow-up. The results hold for both variance-preserving (VP) and variance-exploding (VE) diffusions, and apply to both the reverse-time SDE and the associated probability-flow ODE.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation depends on an estimated score that guides the reversal of noise. Errors in this estimate can accumulate during sampling and change the generated distribution. This paper analyzes that accumulation using stepwise bounds in Wasserstein distance, connecting local estimation errors with distribution-level discrepancies.

The analysis begins with Gaussian mixtures, where the score has an explicit form and its Hessian can be controlled directly. That structure enables sharp error estimates. The authors then extend the argument to general data distributions, obtaining a broader upper bound that is typically looser. This progression separates what can be established with tractable distributional structure from what remains available more generally.

A regularity condition improves the general result: if the initial distribution’s score is globally Lipschitz, the curvature contribution stays uniformly bounded at small times, avoiding the worst-case blow-up. The conclusions cover variance-preserving and variance-exploding diffusions, as well as both reverse-time stochastic dynamics and the associated probability-flow ordinary differential equation. The work clarifies how score accuracy and curvature jointly influence error accumulation across these sampling formulations.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how score-estimation errors accumulate in diffusion sampling and shows when regularity prevents a small-time curvature blow-up.

title: The Accumulation of Score Estimation Error in Diffusion Models

abstract: Regularization is a core component of recent Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms. Mirror Descent Value Iteration (MDVI) uses both Kullback-Leibler divergence and entropy as regularizers in its value and policy updates. Despite its empirical success in discrete action domains and strong theoretical guarantees, the performance of KL-entropy-regularized methods does not surpass that of a strong entropy-only-regularized method in continuous action domains. In this study, we propose Mirror Descent Actor Critic (MDAC) as an actor-critic style instantiation of MDVI for continuous action domains, and show that its empirical performance is significantly boosted by bounding the actor’s log-probability terms in the critic’s loss function, compared to a non-bounded naive instantiation. Further, we relate MDAC to Advantage Learning by recalling that the actor’s log-probability is equal to the regularized advantage function in tabular cases, and theoretically discuss when and why bounding the advantage terms is validated and beneficial. We also empirically explore effective choices for the bounding functions, and show that MDAC performs better than strong non-regularized and entropy-only-regularized methods with an appropriate choice of the bounding functions.

paragraphs: Mirror Descent Value Iteration combines divergence and entropy regularization and has strong results for discrete actions. Translating that success to continuous actions has been difficult: methods with both regularizers have not surpassed a strong entropy-only approach. This paper introduces Mirror Descent Actor Critic, or MDAC, as an actor-critic realization for continuous-action problems.

The central modification bounds the actor log-probability terms appearing in the critic’s loss. Compared with a straightforward unbounded implementation, this substantially improves empirical performance. The authors connect the modification to Advantage Learning through a tabular identity between the actor’s log-probability and the regularized advantage function. They then theoretically discuss conditions under which bounding advantage terms is justified and beneficial.

The paper also studies which bounding functions work well in practice. With an appropriate choice, MDAC outperforms strong methods using no regularization or entropy alone in the reported evaluation. The result makes the bounding choice central to the method’s success, while the tabular connection provides an explanation for why modifying these terms can help.
summary.tldr: Bounding actor log-probability terms strengthens a continuous-action mirror-descent actor-critic method, with gains depending on the bounding function.

title: Mirror Descent Actor Critic via Bounded Advantage Learning

abstract: Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (HTE) from observational data is essential in fields such as healthcare and policy-making, where randomized experiments are often impractical. While representation learning-based methods have shown promise, recent studies suggest that tree-based approaches may offer superior performance on tabular data, particularly in the presence of uninformative features. We introduce GRAdient-based Causal tree Ensembles (GRACE), a novel tree-based architecture for HTE estimation that incorporates multi-way, oblique, and soft splits, enabling end-to-end training via backpropagation. GRACE can be seamlessly integrated into existing models as a replacement for fully-connected neural network layers. Across diverse benchmarks involving binary and non-binary treatment settings, GRACE consistently surpasses neural network and tree-based baselines, often by a substantial margin. We further analyze GRACE as an extension of fully-connected neural network layers and conduct ablation studies to isolate and quantify the contribution of each architectural component to the improvement in performance. These results position GRACE as a promising new foundation for flexible, robust, and accurate HTE estimation. GRACE code is available at https://github.com/ysk-kano/GRACE

paragraphs: Heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation asks how an intervention’s effect varies across individuals. The paper focuses on learning these differences from observational data, where randomized experiments may be impractical. It develops a tree-based architecture motivated by evidence that trees can perform well on tabular data, especially when some features are uninformative.

GRACE combines multi-way, oblique, and soft splits. These allow branches with several outcomes, decisions based on combinations of features, and gradual routing between branches. The resulting architecture can be trained end to end with backpropagation and can replace fully connected neural-network layers inside existing models.

Across benchmarks covering binary and non-binary treatments, GRACE consistently outperforms the evaluated neural-network and tree-based baselines, often substantially. The authors also analyze its relationship to fully connected layers and use ablation studies to measure the contributions of individual architectural components. The work presents differentiable tree ensembles as a reusable building block for treatment-effect models, bringing tree-like structure into the same gradient-based training process used by neural architectures.
summary.tldr: GRACE uses differentiable tree ensembles as replacements for neural layers, improving heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation across the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Gradient-Based Causal Tree Ensembles: A Backbone Architecture for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

abstract: On-policy preference learning algorithms for language model alignment such as online direct policy optimization (DPO) can significantly outperform their offline counterparts. We provide a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon by analyzing how the sampling policy’s coverage evolves throughout on-policy training. We propose and rigorously justify the coverage improvement principle: with sufficient batch size, each update moves into a region around the target where coverage is uniformly better, making subsequent data increasingly informative and enabling rapid convergence. In the contextual bandit setting with Bradley-Terry preferences and linear softmax policy class, we show that on-policy DPO converges exponentially in the number of iterations for batch size exceeding a generalized coverage threshold. In contrast, any learner restricted to offline samples from the initial policy suffers a slower minimax rate, leading to a sharp separation in total sample complexity. We further propose a hybrid sampler based on a novel preferential G-optimal design, which removes dependence on coverage and guarantees convergence in just two rounds. Finally, we develop principled on-policy schemes for reward distillation which achieve faster noiseless rates. Experimentally, we confirm that on-policy DPO and our proposed reward distillation algorithms outperform their off-policy counterparts and enjoy stable gains across iterations.

paragraphs: On-policy preference learning collects training examples using the policy being updated. This paper explains why that can outperform learning from a fixed collection generated by the initial policy. Its central idea is coverage improvement: with sufficiently large batches, each update enters a region around the target where coverage is uniformly better, making later samples more informative.

The main convergence result applies to contextual bandits with Bradley-Terry preferences and a linear softmax policy class. The authors also introduce a hybrid sampler based on preferential G-optimal design that removes coverage dependence and guarantees convergence in two rounds within the analyzed framework. Additional reward-distillation schemes obtain faster noiseless rates. Experiments support the theoretical direction: the proposed on-policy methods outperform their off-policy counterparts and show stable improvements across iterations.
summary.tldr: Under specified modeling and batch-size conditions, on-policy preference updates improve sampling coverage and enable faster convergence than fixed offline data.

title: Coverage Improvement and Fast Convergence of On-policy Preference Learning

abstract: The maximal update parameterization ($\mu P$) provides an approach to scale parameters while preserving feature learning in deep neural networks. In fixed data distribution settings it has been found to yield more stable learning dynamics, more consistent learned features, and enable optimal hyperparameters such as learning rate to transfer from small models to larger ones. However, it is unclear if these benefits readily transfer to reinforcement learning problems, where learning dynamics are coupled to the non-stationary data distribution induced by an agent’s own actions. We empirically study how two regimes, the ”rich” CompleteP and ”lazy” Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) parameterizations affect hyperparameter transfer, feature and policy consistency, and learning behavior as we scale reinforcement learning agents. Ultimately, we show that agents trained using CompleteP consequentially improves compute and reward efficiency compared to the NTK parameterization across multiple control tasks and variants.

paragraphs: Increasing a neural network’s size changes how its parameters and learned representations behave during training. Parameterization schemes aim to manage those changes so that larger models remain trainable and settings chosen for smaller models remain useful. Such benefits have been observed with fixed data distributions, but reinforcement learning introduces a complication: the agent’s actions change the data it subsequently learns from.

This paper empirically compares two scaling regimes for reinforcement learning agents. CompleteP represents a rich regime that maintains feature learning, while the Neural Tangent Kernel parameterization represents a lazy regime. The study examines whether hyperparameters transfer across model sizes, how consistent learned features and policies remain, and how learning behavior changes as agents grow.

Across multiple control tasks and variants, agents trained with CompleteP achieve better compute and reward efficiency than agents using the NTK parameterization. The finding supports preserving representation learning when scaling reinforcement learning systems. Its significance is empirical: parameter scaling choices influence how productively additional model capacity translates into learning and control performance.
summary.tldr: CompleteP improves compute and reward efficiency over NTK parameterization when scaling reinforcement learning agents across the studied control tasks.

title: CompleteP for RL: Maintaining Feature Learning When Scaling Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong potential in complex reasoning, yet their progress remains fundamentally constrained by reliance on massive high-quality human-curated tasks and labels, either through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL) on reasoning-specific data. This dependence renders supervision-heavy training paradigms increasingly unsustainable, with signs of diminishing scalability already evident in practice. To overcome this limitation, we introduce CPMöbius, a collaborative Coach–Player paradigm for data-free reinforcement learning of reasoning models. Unlike traditional adversarial self-play frameworks, CPMöbius inspired by multi-agent collaboration treats the Coach and Player as independent but cooperative roles. The Coach proposes instructions targeted at the Player’s capability and receives rewards based on changes in the Player’s performance, while the Player is rewarded for solving the increasingly instructive tasks generated by the Coach. This cooperative optimization loop is designed to directly enhance the Player’s mathematical reasoning ability. Remarkably, CPMöbius achieves substantial improvement without relying on any external training data, outperforming existing unsupervised approaches. For example, on the Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, our method improves accuracy by overall average +4.9 and out-of-distribution average +5.4, which exceed RENT for +1.5 on overall accuracy and R-zero for +4.2 on OOD accuracy.

paragraphs: Improving language-model reasoning commonly depends on large collections of human-prepared tasks and answers. CPMöbius explores a training loop that generates its own mathematical reasoning tasks without external training data. It assigns separate, cooperative roles to a Coach that proposes instructions and a Player that learns to solve them.

The Coach targets tasks to the Player’s current capabilities and receives rewards based on changes in the Player’s performance. The Player receives rewards for solving the Coach’s tasks. This couples task generation to learning progress: the Coach is encouraged to produce increasingly instructive problems, and the Player is encouraged to improve through solving them.

The authors report substantial improvements over existing unsupervised approaches. For Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, they report average accuracy gains of +4.9 overall and +5.4 on out-of-distribution evaluations. They also report advantages over RENT on overall accuracy and R-zero on out-of-distribution accuracy. These results support cooperative task generation as a route to further reasoning improvement without supplying external data to this training process.
summary.tldr: CPMöbius improves mathematical reasoning through cooperative task generation and solving without external training data.

title: CPMöbius: Iterative Coach–Player Reasoning for Data-Free Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Optimization problems are fundamental across science and industry, including planning, scheduling, and resource allocation. While LLMs show promise in automating optimization, they struggle to bridge the gap between real-world requirements and both mathematical formulations and effective heuristic designs. Furthermore, the field lacks a unified framework that spans problem formulation and heuristic discovery for NP-hard settings. To address these challenges, we propose OptMaster, a unified framework that spans optimization from formulation to heuristic discovery, structuring the process as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) where each node represents a candidate solution. The DAG architecture enables cross-branch knowledge transfer when search progress stagnates. Within each node, we further replace textual self-reflection with independently generated verification code, grounding the evaluation in deterministic computation to suppress hallucinations. OptMaster achieves competitive performance across two optimization paradigms. In Formulation Intelligence, OptMaster achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across the three most challenging benchmarks in the field. In Heuristic Discovery, OptMaster surpasses the best known solutions on Circle Packing ($n=26, 32$) and achieves a cut of 9,590 on Gset70 with significantly reduced time and search budgets.
