paragraphs: OptMaster addresses two steps in automated optimization: translating practical requirements into mathematical formulations and discovering useful heuristics for difficult problems. Language models show promise in both, but can struggle to connect requirements with effective solutions. The paper combines these activities in a single search framework.

Candidate solutions are organized as nodes in a directed acyclic graph. This structure allows knowledge to move between branches when progress stalls, so different search paths can inform one another. Within each node, independently generated verification code replaces textual self-reflection. Evaluating candidates through deterministic computation is intended to suppress hallucinations and give the search more grounded feedback.

For formulation tasks, the authors report leading accuracy on three challenging benchmarks. For heuristic discovery, they report improvements over the best known circle-packing solutions for 26 and 32 circles, plus a cut value of 9,590 on Gset70 using significantly reduced time and search budgets. These results demonstrate the framework across both mathematical formulation and computational search, with graph organization and executable verification serving complementary roles.
summary.tldr: OptMaster combines graph-structured candidate search with executable verification to automate optimization formulations and heuristic discovery.

title: OptMaster: A DAG-Based Framework for Formulation and Heuristic Discovery in Optimization

abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can invalidate safety alignment of large language models, exposing significant safety risks. In this paper, we utilize the attention sink mechanism to mitigate harmful fine-tuning. Specifically, we first measure a statistic named sink divergence for each attention head and observe that different attention heads exhibit two different signs of sink divergence. To understand its safety implications, we conduct experiments and find that the number of attention heads of positive sink divergence increases along with the increase of the model’s harmfulness when undergoing harmful fine-tuning. Based on this finding, we propose a separable sink divergence hypothesis – attention heads associating with learning harmful patterns during fine-tuning are separable by their sign of sink divergence. Based on the hypothesis, we propose a fine-tuning-stage defense, dubbed Surgery. Surgery utilizes a regularizer for sink divergence suppression, which steers attention heads toward the negative sink divergence group, thereby reducing the model’s tendency to learn and amplify harmful patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Surgery improves defense performance by 5.90%, 11.25%, and 9.55% on the BeaverTails, HarmBench, and SorryBench benchmarks, respectively. Source code is available on https://github.com/Lslland/Surgery.

abstract: We study how we can leverage only a handful of characteristics of a transformer’s architecture to closely predict the number of different sequences it can output, both qualitatively and quantitatively. We provide an upper bound depending on the length of the prompt, which we show empirically to be tight up to a factor less than 10, across architectures and model sizes. Our analysis also provides a theoretical explanation for previously observed empirical failures of transformers on simple sequence tasks—such as copying and cramming. Formally, we prove that (i) the maximal length of accessible sequences (those that the transformer can output for some prompt) grows linearly with the prompt length, (ii) beyond a critical threshold, the proportion of accessible sequences decays exponentially with sequence length, and (iii) the linear coefficient relating prompt length to accessible sequence length admits a theoretical upper bound. Notably, these results hold even with unbounded context and computation time.

paragraphs: This paper studies the range of sequences a transformer can produce from prompts, asking how much that range can be predicted from a few architectural characteristics. It defines an accessible sequence as one the transformer can output for some prompt and develops a prompt-length-dependent upper bound on the number of distinct outputs.

The theoretical results connect prompt length to several restrictions. The maximum accessible sequence length grows linearly with prompt length, and the coefficient in that relationship has a theoretical upper bound. Beyond a critical threshold, the fraction of sequences that are accessible shrinks exponentially as sequence length increases. The stated results continue to hold with unbounded context and computation time.

Empirical tests across architectures and model sizes find the output-count bound tight within a factor smaller than ten. The analysis also explains previously observed failures on copying and cramming tasks. Together, these findings connect architectural constraints to output diversity and sequence-task behavior, showing that additional context and computation alone do not remove the restrictions established by the analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper derives architectural bounds linking prompt length to the number and length of sequences a transformer can output.

title: How Many Different Outputs Can a Transformer Generate?

abstract: Meta reinforcement learning (RL) allows agents to leverage experience across a distribution of tasks on which the agent can train at will, enabling faster learning of optimal policies on new test tasks. Despite its success in improving sample complexity on test tasks, many real-world applications, such as robotics and healthcare, impose safety constraints during testing. Constrained meta RL provides a promising framework for integrating safety into meta RL. An open question in constrained meta RL is how to ensure safety of the policy on the real-world test task, while reducing the sample complexity and thus, enabling faster learning of optimal policies. To address this gap, we propose an algorithm that refines policies learned during training, with provable safety and sample complexity guarantees for learning a near optimal policy on the test tasks. We further derive a matching lower bound, showing that this sample complexity is tight.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning uses experience across training tasks to help an agent learn new tasks faster. In applications with safety constraints, faster adaptation is only part of the objective: the policy used on a new task must also satisfy those constraints. This paper studies how to combine these requirements within constrained meta reinforcement learning.

The proposed algorithm refines policies learned during training when confronting test tasks. Its theoretical guarantees address both policy safety and the number of samples needed to learn a near-optimal policy. The training setup allows experience across a distribution of tasks on which the agent can train at will, making transferred experience central to the approach.

The authors also establish a matching lower bound on sample complexity. This means the upper bound achieves the corresponding theoretical limit in the setting studied. The contribution is therefore a characterization of how efficiently safe adaptation can proceed, alongside an algorithm that attains that efficiency while learning a near-optimal test-task policy.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a constrained meta-RL algorithm with provable test-task safety and a sample complexity matched by a lower bound.

title: Constrained Meta Reinforcement Learning with Provable Test-Time Safety

abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can improve through self-evolution (SE), using supervision signals generated by the model itself. In this work, we ask: under a strict closed-loop setup, where the SE algorithm has access only to an unlabeled prompt set and a base model, how close can internally generated supervision come to oracle-supervised training? We analyze four representative strategies in a unified offline self-evolution framework, including single-round verification, multi-turn revision with feedback, iterative training, and curriculum learning. Our primary experiments use Knights and Knaves (KK) logical reasoning tasks, which provide deterministic solutions, controlled difficulty levels, and a clean testbed for easy-to-hard generalization. We first show that SE consistently improves over the base model, but plateaus after excessive training compute is invested, and eventually still leaves a non trivial gap to oracle supervision. We find that multi-turn critic-revision with large models could reach strong self-evolution performance, where Gemma 12B nearly matches oracle-supervised training. Beyond KK, we also evaluate SE on real-world reasoning benchmarks, where gains are also modest. Overall, our results characterize when closed-loop SE can help, and show how internally generated supervision remains insufficient under this minimal formulation.

paragraphs: Can a language model train itself nearly as well as it could learn from correct external supervision? This paper studies that question under a strict closed loop: the learning algorithm receives only a base model and an unlabeled set of prompts. It compares four approaches within a common offline framework, covering verification, feedback-based revision, iterative training, and curriculum learning.

The main experiments use Knights and Knaves logic tasks, whose deterministic answers and controlled difficulty make them suitable for examining transfer from easier to harder problems. Self-evolution consistently improves on the starting model, but gains plateau with excessive training compute. A nontrivial gap to oracle-supervised training generally remains.

Multi-turn critique and revision with larger models can perform strongly; Gemma 12B nearly matches oracle-supervised training in the reported setting. Additional real-world reasoning evaluations show modest gains. Together, these findings identify both the promise and the limits of internally generated supervision under the minimal setup, showing that additional self-training compute alone does not reliably close the generalization gap.
summary.tldr: Closed-loop self-evolution improves reasoning but generally plateaus below oracle supervision, with strong results from larger-model critique and revision.

title: On the Generalization Gap in Self-Evolving Language Model Reasoning

abstract: Autoregressive (AR) modeling has recently emerged as a promising new paradigm in visual generation, but its practical adoption is severely constrained by the slow inference speed of per-token generation, which often requires thousands of steps to produce a single sample. While several Speculative Decoding (SD)-based methods have been proposed to solve this problem by generating multiple tokens in a single forward step, they suffer from limited speedup, degraded quality, or require the training of a draft model. To solve these problems, we propose a new training-free, lossless SD framework, Speculative Coupled Decoding (SCD), by extending the recently proposed Speculative Jacobi Decoding (SJD). While SJD shows strong potential for accelerating AR generation by combining Jacobi iteration and SD, we found that its acceptance rate is still significantly limited due to the instability arising from the independent sampling process used during draft token generation. To overcome this, we introduce an information-theoretic approach, Coupling, which stabilizes the drafting trajectory of SJD by maximizing the probability of sampling identical draft tokens across consecutive iterations, significantly enhancing the acceptance rate while preserving its lossless property. Remarkably, this method requires only a single-line modification to the existing algorithm with almost zero overhead, yet achieves substantial performance gains, delivering up to a 4.2$\times$ speedup in image generation and 13.6$\times$ speedup in video generation compared to standard AR decoding, without any degradation or the need for additional training.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image and video generation can require thousands of sequential token-generation steps. Speculative decoding tries to accelerate that process by producing multiple tokens in a forward step. This paper builds on Speculative Jacobi Decoding, which combines speculative decoding with Jacobi iteration, but whose draft acceptance rate is limited by instability from independent sampling.

Speculative Coupled Decoding stabilizes the drafts through an information-theoretic coupling approach. It maximizes the probability that consecutive iterations sample identical draft tokens, making the drafting trajectory more consistent and increasing acceptance. The change preserves the method's lossless property and requires only a single-line modification with almost no added overhead.

The reported gains reach up to 4.2 times faster image generation and 13.6 times faster video generation than standard autoregressive decoding. These are maximum observed speedups, achieved without additional training or degradation. The result shows that the way randomness is coordinated across drafting iterations can substantially affect useful acceleration, even when the underlying generative model and the broader decoding procedure remain the same.
summary.tldr: Coupling draft samples across iterations accelerates lossless visual decoding by up to 4.2× for images and 13.6× for video.

title: Speculative Coupled Decoding for Training-Free Lossless Acceleration of Autoregressive Visual Generation

abstract: For reinforcement learning in data-scarce domains like real-world robotics, intensive data reuse enhances efficiency but induces overfitting. While prior works focus on critic bias, representation-level instability in Self-Predictive Learning (SPL) under high Update-to-Data (UTD) regimes remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose Robust Representation via Redundancy Reduction (R2R2), a regularization method within SPL. We theoretically identify that standard zero-centering conflicts with SPL’s spectral properties and design a non-centered objective accordingly. We verify R2R2 on SPL-native algorithms like TD7. Furthermore, to demonstrate its orthogonality to prior advancements, we extend the state-of-the-art SimbaV2, which originally lacks SPL, by integrating a tailored SPL module, termed SimbaV2-SPL. Experiments across 11 continuous control tasks confirm that R2R2 effectively mitigates overfitting; specifically, at a UTD ratio of 20, it improves TD7 by $\sim$22% and provides additional gains on top of SimbaV2-SPL, which itself establishes a new state-of-the-art. The code can be found at this link.

paragraphs: R2R2 addresses overfitting when reinforcement-learning agents repeatedly reuse limited experience. High update-to-data ratios allow more learning steps per unit of collected data, but can destabilize learned representations. The paper examines this problem within self-predictive learning, complementing prior work that emphasizes bias in the critic’s value estimates.

The authors theoretically identify a conflict between standard zero-centering and the spectral properties of self-predictive learning. They design a non-centered redundancy-reduction objective in response. The method is tested with TD7, which already uses self-predictive learning, and with SimbaV2 extended through a tailored self-predictive module. This extension is called SimbaV2-SPL.

Across 11 continuous-control tasks, R2R2 mitigates overfitting under intensive experience reuse. At an update-to-data ratio of 20, it improves TD7 by approximately 22%. It also adds gains to SimbaV2-SPL, which itself establishes a new state of the art in the reported evaluation. These results indicate that stabilizing representations can complement other algorithmic improvements when data must support many learning updates.
summary.tldr: R2R2 uses non-centered redundancy reduction to stabilize self-predictive representations when reinforcement-learning agents intensively reuse experience.

title: R2R2: Robust Representation for Intensive Experience Reuse via Redundancy Reduction in Self-Predictive Learning

abstract: Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) play a fundamental role in scientific computing, and recent efforts have sought to extend the success of foundation models to PDE solving. However, multi-physics PDE pre-training faces the unique challenge of disentangling dynamic heterogeneity to learn universal, elementary patterns that generalize to new PDEs. Additionally, cross-physics transfer lacks a theoretical framework for interpretability—specifically, understanding which pre-trained operator knowledge is effectively transferred to target PDEs. To bridge these gaps, we introduce the theory of neural operator splitting, which decomposes PDE evolution into a modulated global spectral operator and sparse local constitutive mechanisms. A key innovation is Origo, which provides a neural operator bank that enables the identification of operator-level generalization patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization and mechanism-level interpretability on unseen PDEs.

paragraphs: Foundation models for partial differential equations aim to reuse learned knowledge across different physical systems. A central challenge is separating the varied dynamics in pretraining data into elementary patterns that generalize. Another is explaining which learned components actually help solve a new equation. Origo addresses these linked problems of transfer and interpretability.

The paper introduces neural operator splitting, which decomposes PDE evolution into a modulated global spectral operator and sparse local constitutive mechanisms. This separates a global component of the dynamics from local mechanisms. Origo organizes learned operators into a bank, providing a basis for identifying generalization patterns at the operator level.

The significance of this organization is that transfer can be examined in terms of the model’s constituent mechanisms. The authors report strong zero-shot generalization on unseen PDEs, together with mechanism-level interpretability. Their experiments support using the proposed decomposition to learn across different physics while making the transferred operator knowledge more understandable.
summary.tldr: Origo decomposes PDE dynamics into reusable global and local operators, supporting zero-shot transfer and interpretable generalization to unseen equations.

title: Origo: Interpretable Multi-physics PDE Foundation Model through Neural Operator Splitting

abstract: We present Causal-Adapter, a modular framework that adapts frozen text-to-image diffusion backbones for counterfactual image generation. Our method enables causal interventions on target attributes while preserving all other aspects of the image, including the core identity. In contrast to prior approaches that rely on prompt engineering without explicit causal structure, Causal-Adapter leverages structural causal modeling augmented with two attribute regularization strategies: prompt-aligned injection, which aligns causal attributes with textual embeddings for precise semantic control, and a conditioned token contrastive loss to disentangle attribute factors and reduce spurious correlations. Causal-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art results on synthetic and real-world datasets, outperforming other baselines in effectiveness, composition, realism, and minimality. These results demonstrate that the approach enables efficient, robust, and generalizable counterfactual image editing with faithful attribute modification and strong preservation of core identity.

paragraphs: Counterfactual image generation asks how an image would change if selected attributes were different while the remaining content, including identity, stayed consistent. Causal-Adapter tackles this through a modular addition to a frozen text-to-image diffusion model. Keeping the backbone frozen allows the framework to adapt an existing generator for controlled attribute changes.

The method uses structural causal modeling to represent interventions explicitly. Two regularization strategies connect that structure to image generation. Prompt-aligned injection aligns causal attributes with text embeddings, providing semantic control over the requested change. A conditioned token contrastive loss separates attribute factors and reduces spurious correlations that could otherwise entangle the target edit with unrelated features.

On synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art results across effectiveness, composition, realism, and minimality. These findings indicate that the framework can produce the intended attribute modification while strongly preserving core identity. Its central contribution is connecting explicit causal structure with a pretrained diffusion backbone to make counterfactual edits more faithful and controlled.
summary.tldr: Causal-Adapter adds explicit causal control to frozen diffusion models for targeted image edits with strong identity preservation.

title: Causal-Adapter: Taming Text-to-Image Diffusion for Faithful Counterfactual Generation

abstract: Interpretable time series deep learning systems are often assessed by checking temporal consistency on explanations, implicitly treating this as evidence of robustness. We show that this assumption can fail: Predictions and explanations can be adversarially decoupled, enabling targeted misclassification while the explanation remains plausible and consistent with a chosen reference rationale. We propose TSEF (Time Series Explanation Fooler), a dual-target attack that jointly manipulates the classifier and explainer outputs. In contrast to single-objective misclassification attacks that disrupt explanation and spread attribution mass broadly, TSEF achieves targeted prediction changes while keeping explanations consistent with the reference. Across multiple datasets and explainer backbones, our results consistently reveal that explanation stability is a misleading proxy for decision robustness and motivate coupling-aware robustness evaluations for trustworthy time series tasks.

We propose TSEF (Time Series Explanation Fooler), a dual-target attack that jointly manipulates the classifier and explainer outputs. In contrast to single-objective misclassification attacks that disrupt explanation and spread attribution mass broadly, TSEF achieves targeted prediction changes while keeping explanations consistent with the reference. Across multiple datasets and explainer backbones, our results consistently reveal that explanation stability is a misleading proxy for decision robustness and motivate coupling-aware robustness evaluations for trustworthy time series tasks.

paragraphs: A time-series classifier can appear trustworthy when its explanations remain temporally consistent. This paper shows why that signal can be misleading: an adversarial change can alter the predicted class while preserving an explanation that looks plausible and agrees with a chosen reference rationale. Stable explanations therefore do not, by themselves, establish robust decisions.

The proposed Time Series Explanation Fooler, or TSEF, attacks two outputs jointly. It aims to induce a particular misclassification while keeping the explainer's output aligned with the reference. This differs from attacks concerned only with changing predictions, which can also disrupt explanations and spread attribution broadly. TSEF makes the separation between prediction behavior and explanation behavior an explicit objective.

Across multiple datasets and explanation backbones, the experiments consistently demonstrate this vulnerability. The implication is that evaluation should examine how explanations and decisions behave together under attack. The results establish that explanation stability can coexist with targeted prediction failure, motivating robustness checks that assess their coupling rather than interpreting consistency alone as reassurance.
summary.tldr: TSEF induces targeted time-series misclassifications while preserving reference-consistent explanations, showing that explanation stability can conceal decision failures.

title: Exposing Vulnerabilities in Explanation for Time Series Classifiers via Dual-Target Attacks

abstract: Learning robust navigation policies remains a core challenge in robotics. Offline imitation learning suffers from distribution shift and compounding errors at rollout, while reinforcement learning requires reward engineering and learns inefficiently. In this paper, we propose NavOL, an online imitation learning paradigm that interacts with a simulator and updates itself using expert demonstrations gathered online. Built upon a pretrained navigation diffusion policy that maps local observations to future waypoints, NavOL trains in a rollout–update loop: during rollout, the policy acts in the simulator and queries a global planner which has privileged access to the global environment for the optimal path segment as ground truth trajectory labels; during update, the policy is trained on the online collected observation–trajectory pairs. This online imitation loop removes the need for reward design, improves learning efficiency, and mitigates distribution shift by training on the policy’s own explored rollouts. Built on IsaacLab with fast, high-fidelity parallel rendering and domain randomization of camera pose and start-goal pairs, our system scales across 50 scenes on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs, collecting over 2,000 new trajectories per hour, each averaging more than 400 steps. We also introduce an indoor visual navigation benchmark with predefined start and goal positions for zero-shot generalization. Extensive evaluations on simulation benchmarks, including the NavDP benchmark and our proposed benchmark, as well as carefully designed real-world experiments, demonstrate the effectiveness of NavOL, showing consistent performance gains in online imitation learning.

paragraphs: A navigation policy trained on fixed demonstrations can encounter unfamiliar situations once its own actions determine where it goes. Errors may then compound. NavOL addresses this distribution shift by collecting expert labels during the policy’s simulated rollouts, allowing training examples to reflect situations the policy actually visits.

Starting from a pretrained diffusion policy that maps local observations to future waypoints, NavOL alternates between rollout and update phases. During rollout, a global planner with privileged environmental access supplies optimal path segments as labels. During update, the policy learns from the resulting observation–trajectory pairs. This supplies direct supervision without requiring a designed reward function.

The system uses IsaacLab, parallel rendering, and randomization of camera poses and start–goal pairs. Across 50 scenes on eight RTX 4090 GPUs, it collects over 2,000 trajectories per hour, averaging more than 400 steps each. The authors also introduce an indoor navigation benchmark and report consistent gains in simulation and real-world experiments, supporting online imitation as an effective navigation-training approach.
summary.tldr: NavOL improves navigation through simulated rollout–update cycles that obtain expert path labels for situations visited by the policy itself.

title: NavOL: Navigation Policy with Online Imitation Learning

abstract: Synthesizing realistic time series with generative models has wide-ranging applications in real-world scenarios. Despite recent progress, most existing methods are trained under the assumption of abundant training data, which substantially limits their effectiveness in data-scarce settings. In this paper, we propose TimeMoDE, a novel framework that integrates Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts to exploit both domain adaptability and diffusion-stage awareness for time series generation under data scarcity. It is pre-trained on a large-scale collection of multi-domain datasets to extract domain-agnostic temporal representations and domain-specific information benefiting generalization during fine-tuning. We propose Domain Prompts to condition expert assignment for indistinguishable noised tokens, mitigating the limitations of capturing inter-dataset relationships. Moreover, we incorporate diffusion timestep signals to equip the experts with awareness of time series degradation variations, facilitating adaptive calibrate to stage-dependent denoising requirements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TimeMoDE outperforms existing methods under diverse low-data settings. It establishes an innovative paradigm for advanced time series few-shot generation.
originalAbstract: Synthesizing realistic time series with generative models has wide-ranging applications in real-world scenarios. Despite recent progress, most existing methods are trained under the assumption of abundant training data, which substantially limits their effectiveness in data-scarce settings. In this paper, we propose TimeMoDE, a novel framework that integrates Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts to exploit both domain adaptability and diffusion-stage awareness for time series generation under data scarcity. It is pre-trained on a large-scale collection of multi-domain datasets to extract domain-agnostic temporal representations and domain-specific information benefiting generalization during fine-tuning. We propose Domain Prompts to condition expert assignment for indistinguishable noised tokens, mitigating the limitations of capturing inter-dataset relationships. Moreover, we incorporate diffusion timestep signals to equip the experts with awareness of time series degradation variations, facilitating adaptive calibrate to stage-dependent denoising requirements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TimeMoDE outperforms existing methods under diverse low-data settings. It establishes an innovative paradigm for advanced time series few-shot generation.

paragraphs: TimeMoDE addresses time-series generation when only a small amount of target-domain training data is available. It combines a Diffusion Transformer with a mixture of experts and pretrains on a large collection of datasets from multiple domains. This pretraining aims to learn both shared temporal structure and domain-specific information that can support later fine-tuning.

The framework uses Domain Prompts to guide expert assignment when noisy tokens are otherwise difficult to distinguish. This provides domain information for routing and helps represent relationships across datasets. It also supplies diffusion timestep signals, allowing experts to adjust to how degraded the time series is and to the denoising requirements of the current diffusion stage.

These mechanisms connect two kinds of adaptation: selecting expertise relevant to the data domain and adjusting that expertise to the stage of generation. Experiments across diverse low-data settings report improvements over existing methods. The results support transferring knowledge from broad pretraining while retaining domain and diffusion-stage information for few-shot time-series synthesis.
summary.tldr: TimeMoDE combines multi-domain pretraining with domain-guided and diffusion-stage-aware experts to improve time-series generation with scarce target data.

title: Towards a Unified Generative Model for Scarce Time Series with Domain Experts

abstract: In this paper, we propose a discrete roto-reflection group equivariant vision transformer with convolutional attention. Roto-reflection equivariant networks preserve the rotational, flip and positional symmetry in feature maps, making them useful for tasks where orientation of the inputs is relevant to the model outputs. In image classification and object detection, most of the studies on roto-reflection equivariant models have focused on using convolutional neural networks rather than vision transformers. In this paper, we examine the challenges involved in achieving equivariance in vision transformers, and we propose a simpler way to implement a discretized roto-reflection group equivariant vision transformer. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the existing approaches for developing discrete roto-reflection group equivariant neural networks for image classification.

paragraphs: An image model can be designed so that rotating or flipping its input produces a corresponding transformation in its internal features. This property, equivariance, preserves a structured relationship between input orientation and representation. The paper studies how to build that behavior into a vision transformer for a discrete set of rotations and reflections.

Earlier work on these symmetries has concentrated largely on convolutional neural networks. REViT examines the obstacles to achieving equivariance in transformers and proposes a simpler implementation using convolutional attention. Its feature maps preserve rotational, flip, and positional symmetries, giving the architecture explicit structure for handling changes in input orientation.

Image-classification experiments show that the approach outperforms the compared methods for constructing discrete roto-reflection equivariant networks. The reported finding concerns classification, while the motivation also discusses the relevance of such models to object detection. The central contribution is an architectural route for bringing these symmetry-preserving properties into vision transformers, together with evidence that the resulting design can improve classification performance.
summary.tldr: REViT uses convolutional attention to build a vision transformer that preserves discrete rotation and reflection symmetries.

title: REViT: Roto-reflection Equivariant Convolutional Vision Transformer

abstract: Bokeh rendering and depth estimation share a fundamental optical connection, yet existing methods fail to fully exploit this reciprocity. Conventional bokeh pipelines rely heavily on noisy depth maps that inevitably introduce visual artifacts. Conversely, existing monocular depth models typically follow two flawed paradigms. Generative diffusion-based frameworks often lack consistent metric scale. Meanwhile, feed-forward metric depth models frequently fail in textureless or distant regions where defocus blur can provide geometric information. We propose BokehDepth, a two-stage framework that treats synthetic defocus as a supervision-free geometric signal. In the first stage, a physically grounded generative model produces calibrated bokeh stacks from a single sharp input without requiring prior depth input. Subsequently, a lightweight defocus-aware aggregation module integrates these stacks into the encoder of a depth estimation framework. This mechanism allows the model to extract consistent geometric features from the defocus dimension while keeping the decoder architecture unchanged. Experiments demonstrate that BokehDepth achieves superior visual bokeh fidelity compared to depth-dependent rendering baselines and consistently enhances the metric accuracy of state-of-the-art monocular depth models.

paragraphs: BokehDepth uses the relationship between defocus blur and scene depth to improve distance estimation from a single image. Existing bokeh methods can inherit artifacts from noisy depth estimates, while depth models can struggle with consistent physical scale or with textureless and distant regions. The paper treats synthetic defocus as an additional source of geometric information.

The framework has two stages. First, a physically grounded generative model creates calibrated stacks of bokeh images from one sharp image, without needing a depth map as input. A lightweight aggregation module then extracts information across those defocus variations and integrates it into a depth model's encoder. The decoder stays unchanged, allowing the added geometric cues to enter through the representation used for prediction.

Experiments report better visual bokeh fidelity than depth-dependent rendering baselines and consistent metric-depth improvements for state-of-the-art monocular models. The approach matters because the generated blur variations serve as a supervision-free geometric signal. Bokeh generation and depth estimation become connected parts of a framework in which synthetic optical variation helps inform physical distance predictions.
summary.tldr: BokehDepth generates calibrated defocus variations from one image and uses them to improve monocular metric-depth estimation.

title: Boosting Monocular Metric Depth Estimation via Bokeh Rendering

abstract: Long-Text Understanding (LTU) at million-token scale requires balancing reasoning fidelity with computational efficiency. Frontier long-context LLMs can process millions of token contexts end-to-end, but they suffer from high token consumption and attention dilution. In parallel, specialized LTU agents often sacrifice fidelity through task-agnostic abstractions like graph construction or indexing. We identify a key insight for LTU: query-relevant information is typically sparse relative to the full document, so effective reasoning should rely on a query-sufficient subset rather than the entire context. To address this, we propose SCOUT, a new paradigm for LTU that shifts from passive processing to active information foraging. It treats the document as an explorable environment and answers from a compact, provenance-grounded epistemic state. Guided by state-level gap diagnosis, SCOUT adaptively alternates between coarse-to-fine exploration and anchored state updates that progressively contract its epistemic state toward query sufficiency. Experiments show that SCOUT matches state-of-the-art proprietary models while reducing token consumption by up to 8 times. Moreover, SCOUT remains stable as context length scales, substantially alleviating the practical cost–capability trade-off in long-context reasoning. Resources are available at our Project Page.

paragraphs: SCOUT addresses understanding documents at million-token scale, where processing everything can consume many tokens and dilute attention. Its starting observation is that information relevant to a particular question is typically sparse. The framework therefore seeks a subset sufficient to answer that question, treating the document as something to explore actively.

Answers are developed from a compact epistemic state: a representation of what the system currently knows, grounded in its source evidence. SCOUT diagnoses gaps in that state and alternates between coarse-to-fine exploration and anchored updates. As it gathers what the question requires, it progressively contracts the state toward query sufficiency. The question therefore guides both evidence acquisition and what information remains in the working representation.

Experiments show that SCOUT matches state-of-the-art proprietary models while reducing token consumption by up to eightfold. It also remains stable as context length increases. These findings support active, evidence-grounded exploration as a way to reduce the practical cost of long-context reasoning while preserving the evaluated answer quality.
summary.tldr: SCOUT actively gathers question-relevant evidence from long documents, matching leading proprietary models with up to eightfold lower token consumption.

title: SCOUT: Active Information Foraging for Long-Text Understanding with Decoupled Epistemic States

abstract: Multi-view clustering effectively exploits rich information from multiple views, yet real-world applications are frequently challenged by missing views and cross-view sample misalignment, hindering cross-view modeling and resulting in inferior clustering performance. To address these challenges, this paper presents a novel method, OPtimal Transport–GuIded flOw MatchiNg for incomplete and unaligned multi-view clustering (OPTION). Specifically, OPTION employs conditional flow matching to learn deterministic transport paths for missing-view imputation, enabling stable manifold-preserving recovery and more discriminative representations. To support alignment-free fusion, we introduce a Gromov-Wasserstein-inspired structural regularization that aligns intra-view geometric structures in the latent space without solving hard correspondences. Furthermore, an optional contrastive regularization is incorporated to enhance cross-view consistency specifically for aligned settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OPTION outperforms state-of-the-art methods across ideal, incomplete, and unaligned scenarios evaluated separately. Code: https://github.com/TimoZhou1024/OPTION.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different views of data to form useful groups. Missing views remove information, while misalignment makes it unclear which samples correspond across views. OPTION addresses these obstacles through learned recovery of missing information and structural alignment of representations, allowing cross-view information to support clustering.

For missing-view recovery, conditional flow matching learns deterministic transport paths intended to preserve the data manifold and produce discriminative representations. For fusion without known sample alignment, a Gromov-Wasserstein-inspired regularizer aligns the internal geometric structures of views in latent space. This avoids requiring hard cross-view correspondences. When samples are aligned, an optional contrastive regularizer can further encourage consistency.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods in ideal, incomplete, and unaligned scenarios, which are evaluated separately. That distinction matters when interpreting the results: the abstract reports evidence across those individual settings rather than a joint evaluation of every difficulty at once. The overall contribution combines missing-view imputation and structural consistency within one clustering method, with an additional mechanism tailored specifically to aligned data.
summary.tldr: OPTION combines flow-based missing-view recovery with geometric alignment to improve clustering across separately evaluated incomplete and unaligned settings.

title: OPTION: Optimal Transport–Guided Flow Matching for Incomplete and Unaligned Multi-View Clustering

abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) models and foundation models (FMs), are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains, ensuring their trustworthiness has become a central challenge. However, the core trustworthy AI objectives, such as fairness, robustness, privacy, and explainability, are hard to achieve simultaneously, especially while preserving utility. This position paper argues that causality is necessary to understand and balance trade-offs in performance and multiple objectives of trustworthy AI. We ground our arguments in re-interpreting trustworthy AI trade-offs as incompatible invariance requirements under different changes to the data-generating process. We then illustrate this argument through case-study analyses from the literature and a stylized synthetic-data simulation, showing that causality provides a unifying framework for understanding how trade-offs in trustworthy AI arise and how they can be softened or resolved through selective invariance. This perspective applies to both classical ML models and large-scale FMs. Our paper discusses how causal assumptions may be applied explicitly or implicitly in modern large-scale systems. Finally, we outline open challenges and opportunities for using causality to build both trustworthy and high-performing AI.

Finally, we outline open challenges and opportunities for using causality to build both trustworthy and high-performing AI.

paragraphs: This paper examines why fairness, robustness, privacy, explainability, and predictive usefulness can be difficult to achieve together. The authors reinterpret these tensions as conflicts between invariance requirements: different objectives demand that particular aspects of a system remain unchanged under different changes to how data is generated. Those demands can be incompatible.

The paper argues that causal reasoning is necessary to understand and balance these conflicts. It develops the argument through case studies from existing literature and a stylized simulation with synthetic data. Causality provides a common framework for describing why a trade-off arises and for deciding which changes a system should remain insensitive to.

The proposed response is selective invariance. Rather than demanding every form of stability simultaneously, causal assumptions guide which invariances are appropriate. The authors show how this perspective can soften or resolve trade-offs and discuss its relevance to both conventional machine learning and foundation models. They also examine how causal assumptions can appear explicitly or implicitly in large systems and identify remaining challenges. The proposal offers a framework for reasoning about competing objectives, rather than asserting that all conflicts disappear.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that causal reasoning can explain conflicting trustworthiness requirements and guide selective invariance to soften or resolve trade-offs.

title: Position: Trustworthy AI Suffers from Invariance Conflicts and Causality is The Solution

paragraphs: This paper builds decision trees around the combined cost of classification mistakes and obtaining information. The objective reflects diagnostic tasks in which making an incorrect decision has a cost, but measuring an attribute can also require payment or effort. The authors introduce a splitting criterion that accounts for both costs when selecting attributes during tree construction.

They also address prediction when test cases have many missing values. Several proposed strategies suggest which missing values to obtain, taking acquisition costs into account. This extends cost-sensitive reasoning beyond tree construction to the decisions made while using the tree on an incomplete case.

Experiments compare the proposed strategies with C4.5 and its variations, reporting significant improvements. The authors also state that their algorithm has complexity similar to C4.5 and substantially below previous work. The practical contribution is an approach that considers the expense of acquiring information together with the expense of mistakes, both when building a tree and when applying it.
summary.tldr: The proposed decision-tree methods account for both misclassification and information-acquisition costs during training and prediction.

title: Decision trees with minimal costs

abstract: Learning the structure of graphical models is an important task, but one of considerable difficulty when latent variables are involved. Because conditional independences using hidden variables cannot be directly observed, one has to rely on alternative methods to identify the d-separations that define the graphical structure. This paper describes new distribution-free techniques for identifying d-separations in continuous latent variable models when non-linear dependencies are allowed among hidden variables.
authors: Ricardo Bezerra de Andrade e Silva
originalAbstract: Learning the structure of graphical models is an important task, but one of considerable difficulty when latent variables are involved. Because conditional independences using hidden variables cannot be directly observed, one has to rely on alternative methods to identify the d-separations that define the graphical structure. This paper describes new distribution-free techniques for identifying d-separations in continuous latent variable models when non-linear dependencies are allowed among hidden variables.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model's structure becomes difficult when some variables are hidden. Relationships that involve those variables cannot be checked directly in the observed data. The paper focuses on identifying d-separations, the graphical relationships that encode conditional independence and help determine how a model's variables can be connected.

The authors introduce distribution-free techniques for identifying these relationships in continuous latent-variable models. Their setting allows nonlinear dependencies among the hidden variables. The contribution therefore addresses structural identification without restricting the hidden relationships to linear dependencies, while describing the techniques as independent of a prescribed distributional form.

The significance lies in finding an indirect route to structural information that direct conditional-independence checks involving hidden variables cannot supply. Identifying d-separations provides information about the graphical structure even when the relevant variables are unobserved. The stated result is a set of identification techniques for this setting, rather than a claim that every possible latent-variable graph can be completely recovered.
summary.tldr: Distribution-free techniques identify d-separations in continuous latent-variable models that allow nonlinear dependencies among hidden variables.

title: New d-separation identification results for learning continuous latent variable models

abstract: Feature selection aims to reduce dimensionality for building comprehensible learning models with good generalization performance. Feature selection algorithms are largely studied separately according to the type of learning: supervised or unsupervised. This work exploits intrinsic properties underlying supervised and unsupervised feature selection algorithms, and proposes a unified framework for feature selection based on spectral graph theory. The proposed framework is able to generate families of algorithms for both supervised and unsupervised feature selection. And we show that existing powerful algorithms such as ReliefF (supervised) and Laplacian Score (unsupervised) are special cases of the proposed framework. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first attempt to unify supervised and unsupervised feature selection, and enable their joint study under a general framework. Experiments demonstrated the efficacy of the novel algorithms derived from the framework.

paragraphs: Feature selection reduces the number of input variables with the aim of producing understandable models that generalize well. Methods using class labels and methods operating without labels are often studied separately. This paper looks for shared principles underlying both kinds of selection and expresses them through spectral graph theory.

The resulting framework can generate families of supervised and unsupervised feature-selection algorithms. The authors show that ReliefF, a supervised method, and Laplacian Score, an unsupervised method, appear as special cases. This connection matters because it places established methods within a common formulation, allowing their relationships to be studied alongside new algorithms derived from the same framework.

Experiments support the effectiveness of the newly derived algorithms. The contribution combines a conceptual unification with a route to constructing further selection methods, rather than offering only one new feature-ranking procedure. The authors describe the work, to their knowledge, as the first attempt at this unification. That priority claim remains qualified, while the inclusion of the two named methods is a stated technical result.
summary.tldr: A spectral graph framework unifies supervised and unsupervised feature selection, includes ReliefF and Laplacian Score, and generates new algorithms.

title: Spectral feature selection for supervised and unsupervised learning

abstract: We discuss how the runtime of SVM optimization should decrease as the size of the training data increases. We present theoretical and empirical results demonstrating how a simple subgradient descent approach indeed displays such behavior, at least for linear kernels.
originalAbstract: We discuss how the runtime of SVM optimization should decrease as the size of the training data increases. We present theoretical and empirical results demonstrating how a simple subgradient descent approach indeed displays such behavior, at least for linear kernels.

paragraphs: The paper examines an unusual relationship between dataset size and the time required to optimize a support vector machine. Its central argument is that optimization runtime should decrease as the training set grows. The quantity under discussion is the runtime of the optimization procedure, making the relationship between data volume and computational effort the main subject.

The authors investigate a simple subgradient descent approach and provide both theoretical and empirical results showing this behavior. Subgradient descent is the specific optimization method supporting their claim. The contribution therefore includes an analysis of the proposed runtime relationship and observations that demonstrate it for the studied approach.

The stated scope is at least the case of linear kernels. Within that scope, the results give a concrete example in which more training data accompanies less optimization time. The paper’s significance lies in this counterintuitive computational finding and its support from both analysis and experiments, with the kernel qualification remaining part of the claim.
summary.tldr: Theoretical and empirical results show that simple subgradient SVM optimization can become faster as training data increases, at least for linear kernels.

title: SVM optimization: inverse dependence on training set size

abstract: We study the problem of selecting a subset of $k$ random variables from a large set, in order to obtain the best linear prediction of another variable of interest. This problem can be viewed in the context of both feature selection and sparse approximation. We analyze the performance of widely used greedy heuristics, using insights from the maximization of submodular functions and spectral analysis. We introduce the submodularity ratio as a key quantity to help understand why greedy algorithms perform well even when the variables are highly correlated. Using our techniques, we obtain the strongest known approximation guarantees for this problem, both in terms of the submodularity ratio and the smallest $k$-sparse eigenvalue of the covariance matrix. We also analyze greedy algorithms for the dictionary selection problem, and significantly improve the previously known guarantees. Our theoretical analysis is complemented by experiments on real-world and synthetic data sets; the experiments show that the submodular ratio is a stronger predictor of the performance of greedy algorithms than other spectral parameters.

paragraphs: The paper studies choosing k variables from a larger collection to obtain the best linear prediction of a target variable. This is relevant to feature selection and sparse approximation. Its focus is understanding the performance of widely used greedy selection methods, including settings where candidate variables are highly correlated.

The analysis combines ideas from submodular maximization and spectral properties of the covariance matrix. The authors introduce the submodularity ratio as a quantity for explaining greedy performance. They derive what they report as the strongest known approximation guarantees, expressed through that ratio and the smallest k-sparse eigenvalue. They also substantially improve existing guarantees for greedy dictionary selection.

Experiments on real and synthetic datasets complement the theoretical results. In these tests, the submodularity ratio predicts greedy performance better than the other spectral parameters examined. This gives the new quantity both a role in formal guarantees and an empirical interpretation. The contribution helps explain why greedy methods can succeed with correlated variables, without claiming that correlation is harmless in every selection problem.
summary.tldr: The submodularity ratio sharpens guarantees for greedy selection and empirically predicts performance better than the spectral parameters compared.

title: Submodular meets Spectral: Greedy Algorithms for Subset Selection, Sparse Approximation and Dictionary Selection

abstract: We analyze a method for nonparametric density estimation that exhibits robustness to contamination of the training sample. This method achieves robustness by combining a traditional kernel density estimator (KDE) with ideas from classical M-estimation. The KDE based on a Gaussian kernel is interpreted as a sample mean in the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This mean is estimated robustly through the use of a robust loss, yielding the so-called robust kernel density estimator (RKDE). This robust sample mean can be found via a kernelized iteratively re-weighted least squares (IRWLS) algorithm. Our contributions are summarized as follows. First, we present a representer theorem for the RKDE, which gives an insight into the robustness of the RKDE. Second, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for kernel IRWLS to converge to the global minimizer, in the Gaussian RKHS, of the objective function defining the RKDE. Third, characterize and provide a method for computing the influence function associated with the RKDE. Fourth, we illustrate the robustness of the RKDE through experiments on several data sets.

paragraphs: The paper studies density estimation when the training sample contains contamination. It combines kernel density estimation with robust M-estimation. The starting observation is that a Gaussian-kernel density estimator can be viewed as a sample mean in its associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, creating a route to robustifying that mean.

Using a robust loss to estimate the mean produces the robust kernel density estimator, or RKDE. A kernelized iteratively reweighted least-squares algorithm computes this estimate. The authors present a representer theorem that helps explain its robustness and give necessary and sufficient conditions for the algorithm to converge to the defining objective's global minimizer in the Gaussian kernel space.

They also characterize the estimator's influence function and provide a method for computing it, supplying a way to analyze sensitivity to contamination. Experiments on several datasets illustrate robustness. The contribution combines a robust formulation, a computational procedure, and theoretical tools for understanding both the procedure's convergence and the estimator's sensitivity.
summary.tldr: Robust estimation of a kernel-space mean yields a density estimator with analyzed contamination sensitivity and conditional global-convergence guarantees.

title: On the Robustness of Kernel Density M-Estimators

abstract: Visualization techniques for complex data are a workhorse of modern scientific pursuits. The goal of visualization is to embed high dimensional data in a low dimensional space, while preserving structure in the data relevant to exploratory data analysis, such as the existence of clusters. However, existing visualization methods often either entirely fail to preserve clusters in embeddings due to the crowding problem or can only preserve clusters at a single resolution. Here, we develop a new approach to visualization, tree preserving embedding (TPE). Our approach takes advantage of the topological notion of connectedness to provably preserve clusters at all resolutions. Our performance guarantee holds for finite samples, which makes TPE a robust method for applications. Our approach suggests new strategies for robust data visualization in practice.

paragraphs: Visualizing high-dimensional data requires compressing it into a low-dimensional space while retaining structure useful for exploration. Clusters are one such structure. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: crowding can prevent clusters from being preserved, and some methods preserve them only at a single resolution.

Tree preserving embedding uses the topological concept of connectedness to address cluster preservation across resolutions. The idea is to make the grouping structure central to the embedding's objective. The authors prove that their approach preserves clusters at all resolutions, supporting exploration of both broader groupings and finer distinctions within the data.

The performance guarantee applies to finite samples, connecting the theoretical result to the finite datasets encountered in applications. The contribution is therefore a visualization approach with a specific structural guarantee, rather than only a visual assessment of whether a projection looks informative. The paper presents this result as a foundation for more robust practical visualization strategies.
summary.tldr: Tree preserving embedding uses connectedness to provably preserve clusters across all resolutions, with guarantees for finite samples.

title: Tree preserving embedding
